"You have only been in the palace two days, yet you have already surpassed someone who's been here two years."
"Take your cousin, for instance — the Emperor has never once favored her."
This was the first time Xi Rongyan had heard this.
Her cousin had never spoken to her of her situation with the Emperor in the palace. She was genuinely surprised.
She paused: "How can that be..."
The Empress Dowager smiled: "Did you think the Emperor must favor every woman in the inner palace?"
"Many of them will never lay eyes on the Emperor even once in their lives, growing old and dying within these palace walls."
"Those of lower rank do not even have the right to attend the Empress's morning gathering."
"In the past, women plotted desperately for the chance of a chance encounter with the Emperor — but none of them came to a good end."
The incense in the burner on the altar table coiled lazily in the still, quiet air. The Empress Dowager turned her teacup slowly and looked at Xi Rongyan's eyes with a measured, unhurried gaze: "Rongyan, the Emperor is spending his nights with you. That is your fortune."
"Your mother wrote to me about what happened at the Flower Viewing Festival. Do you think the Emperor would issue a decree to bring you into the palace if he had no intention of having you?"
"Knowing the Emperor's temperament, if you had offended him, he would have had you punished."
Xi Rongyan suddenly remembered what the Emperor had said to her this morning — that he had long been fond of her.
In truth, she found it difficult to believe.
The Emperor had left for the north at fifteen and earned considerable military merit. His returns to the capital had been rare. He had come back only when the late Emperor fell gravely ill at twenty-one, and it had been barely three years since then. The number of times the two of them had truly crossed paths was small.
Even when they had crossed paths, it had been nothing more than a passing exchange of pleasantries.
Before her thoughts had fully settled, the Empress Dowager dismissed the attendants around them. She then lifted another box from the side table and handed Xi Rongyan a bracelet, saying quietly: "This bracelet is hollow inside. It contains emotion incense."
"Wear it on your wrist when the Emperor comes. He will not be able to leave your side."
Xi Rongyan looked at the item and felt it was something she did not wish to hold.
The Empress Dowager frowned: "Rongyan, your aunt has been through everything in the inner palace these many years. Whatever methods exist, I have seen them all."
"The Emperor is a man, and men have desires. You are only amplifying that desire. Once you have a child, you will no longer need it."
"A man's love passes in an instant — if you do not seize this opportunity, it may not come again."
"Your aunt used this herself once. I conceived through this as well."
"Trust your aunt. How could I ever harm you?"
Xi Rongyan looked at the bracelet in the Empress Dowager's hand, her thoughts in turmoil.
She had come to the palace hoping for a quiet, settled life — but she did not want to use such means.
From what she had seen, the Emperor did not appear to be a man of excessive desire. Moreover, the Emperor was devoted to state affairs and spent little time in the inner palace to begin with. If the Emperor were to discover she had used something like this, it might well backfire.
But she hesitated for a long while, and in the end accepted it.
She would treat it as accepting her aunt's kind intention — to set her mind at ease.
When she returned, Xi Rongyan held the bracelet and examined it by the window. She lifted it to her nose and smelled it. There truly was a faint scent.
She could not quite describe it, but it was pleasant — and not easy to detect.
Baozhu, curious, asked: "Can it truly be so effective?"
Yuzhu looked at Xi Rongyan and asked: "The Empress Dowager's things should work well. If the Emperor comes tonight, perhaps you should try?"
But Xi Rongyan placed the bracelet in Yuzhu's hands and shook her head: "Put it away in the case. I do not wish to use it."
Yuzhu could only say: "Mistress, now that you are in the palace, you should at least think of your own future."
Xi Rongyan sat on the couch, turned her head, and said softly to Yuzhu: "I know you both wish me well. But I do not want to use such a method — and I fear it would do more harm than good."
"It has not come to that yet."
Yuzhu had no choice but to take it and put it away.
Xi Rongyan then called Baozhu over to look at her face. There was still a faint pink mark, but it was slowly fading — which was a relief.
That evening the Emperor came again. Xi Rongyan had just finished bathing. She tended to sleep early, had asked for the time, and thinking the Emperor would likely not come tonight, had already gotten into bed.
She had been propped up chatting with Baozhu when the palace maid outside hurried in with the announcement that the Emperor had arrived. She was briefly startled, and had just sat up when the Emperor's tall figure was already striding inside.
Baozhu, ever perceptive, quickly stepped back and withdrew.
The Emperor carried the chill of the night air with him as he entered, and the warm room seemed to grow cooler with his presence. That black-robed figure walking in made Xi Rongyan feel a breath of cold.
Wei Qi's gaze swept over Xi Rongyan's wrists, and he lowered his gaze without a word. He pulled her close, taking in the warmth of her body.
Xi Rongyan, held within the Emperor's arms, felt as though the Emperor knew she would feel cold and had pulled the quilt up around her waist.
The warmth of his palm covered her back.
By now she found the Emperor's scent familiar. She was no longer as afraid of him as she once had been. She had not expected the Emperor to come tonight. Listening to the quiet sigh at her ear, she looked up.
She saw the Emperor was also looking at her. In those cool, long eyes was the flicker of candlelight — and the reflection of her face.
Her heart wanted to take the initiative, yet she did not know how.
Even now, with the Emperor holding her so gently, she did not know how she ought to respond.
She hesitated, and then lightly leaned against the Emperor's chest. It was the only proactive gesture she could manage.
Wei Qi had not dared to hope Xi Rongyan would take any initiative. And yet she was actually leaning her soft body toward him.
His heart hammered. The fingers at her back actually trembled with excitement.
He suddenly cupped Xi Rongyan's face in his hands, looked at her quietly, his excitement flickering and dancing in the candlelight in his eyes.
The eardrops at her ear were brushing against his thumb ring, giving off a faint, clear, chiming sound — a sound like the coaxing notes of an intoxicating melody. Her face, luminous as the moon, was no longer a moon's reflection in the water — it was the real, warm sensation beneath his hands.
He could not hold himself back. Beneath that clear, innocent gaze, he bent his head and kissed her.
The fragrance on her body made his body taut. The soft warmth of her made the blood that had so long craved her surge. He pressed her against him, his hands moving across her body, no longer under his own control.

chapters.title: Did I Frighten You Just Now?
chapters.content:
Wei Qi's kisses were so heavy that Xi Rongyan could barely close her lips. Overcome, she let out a few soft sounds, yet she did not stop him.

The broad hand slipped beneath the hem of her robe — still carrying the coolness of his cuff — and Xi Rongyan shivered slightly at the chill.

She knew what might happen next.

Yuzhu had just had her carefully study the little manual, which was still under her pillow.

She also knew it would hurt. Her mother had said to endure — it would pass; every woman went through this, and it got better afterward.

Though Xi Rongyan was afraid, the Emperor's movements were urgent and heavy, and she felt a soreness even in her lips. But she told herself to endure — it would pass.

She dared not open her eyes. When the Emperor finally released her lips, she heard his suppressed, labored breathing at her ear.

Just like in the dream.

The man in that dream had breathed like this too.

The same heavy force.

She began to feel a faint trembling of fear again.

She barely opened her eyes — and found herself looking directly into the Emperor's gaze.

Those dark eyes were bottomless. Colored by desire, they turned a little fearsome, and in one particular moment they were exactly like the eyes in her dream.

In the dream, that man had bound her hands and made her whole body ache — an endless torment.

She could not tell dream from reality. The word came out of her without thinking: "No..."

Wei Qi's hands stilled in an instant.

He pulled himself from the flood of desire and saw Xi Rongyan's frightened eyes looking back at him.

Only a moment ago she had been so yielding beneath him, her fingers even resting lightly at his waist.

He had thought she was ready. Ready to give herself to him.

Why was she looking at him with such fear again?

Instinctively he glanced at his reflection in the nearby lamp column. He had been hiding his possessiveness of her perfectly well — yet the reflection there was warped and twisted, like a grotesque specter. Even he could not see clearly what he looked like in that moment.

The fingers that had been gripping Xi Rongyan's waist were white with tension. Wei Qi lowered his lashes, letting all the dark emotion sink into the shadows.

His half-removed outer robe hung loose on his shoulders. He bent down and gathered Xi Rongyan gently into his arms. Looking into her frightened eyes, without a trace of reproach, he pressed his lips softly to her forehead and asked in a low voice: "Did I frighten you just now?"

Xi Rongyan looked at the Emperor's eyes now — gentle, watching her. Her heart beat hard, and then a sudden wave of guilt rose in her.

She could not understand why she kept being haunted by that nightmare. The Emperor had been tender with her, yet she had blurted out those words just now, and the Emperor had not blamed her even so.

Xi Rongyan quickly shook her head, then lowered her eyes in shame, not daring to meet the Emperor's gaze. She said quietly: "Just now this concubine did not mean to..."

Wei Qi soothed her with patient care: "It's all right. I don't blame you."

"It was my own movements that were too rough."

Wei Qi lifted her chin and asked: "Did I hurt you just now?"

It had hurt, a little — the Emperor's movements had been heavy.

Xi Rongyan hesitated, and in the end did not admit it. She gave a small shake of her head. "No..."

Wei Qi had already read the answer in Xi Rongyan's earlier hesitation.

He also understood that Xi Rongyan still feared his station and dared not tell him the truth. This woman had always been timid, frightened of everything.

Yet she had been so devoted to that dead husband of hers — refusing to yield to him alone.

In the previous life, she had feared him, yet had still resisted him at every turn.

He pressed his lips together. His gaze fell to the red marks on Xi Rongyan's neck. His fingers gently drew aside one edge of her robe.

There were red marks on her waist too, from the force he had used.

Wei Qi paused, and bent down to press his lips tenderly to those marks, then looked up at her with remorse: "Yan'er, I'm sorry."

"I'll be gentler next time."

When the Emperor had pressed his lips to her waist just now, Xi Rongyan had trembled — that spot still carried a faint, lingering tingle.

She seemed to recall the Emperor saying something about being gentler before.

But Xi Rongyan had no experience with such things and did not know whether what the Emperor did was too rough or simply how things were.

She gave a small nod. The Emperor's fingers kneaded at her waist — such a light touch, yet she felt his tenderness clearly.

After a long while, Wei Qi let Xi Rongyan rest first while he went to bathe.

Xi Rongyan watched the Emperor's retreating figure and thought quietly that tonight would again come to nothing.

Though she felt a small pang of regret, she also felt a relieved exhale — as though she had escaped something. All together it was a tangle of complicated feelings.

She closed her eyes and again the dream scenes with that man came to her. She did not want to dream of him again, so she lay with her eyes open, willing herself to forget.

When Wei Qi came back, he was surprised to find Xi Rongyan still awake — as though she had been waiting for him.

His heart warmed. He pulled the warm, soft person into his arms and looked at her bashful, pale face. Without thinking, he softened his voice. "Were you waiting for me?"

In truth that had not been Xi Rongyan's intention — but seeing the Emperor's downward gaze, she instinctively nodded.

That obedient nod pleased Wei Qi. It was rare for her to know to wait for him — so she was not entirely indifferent to him after all.

His body was again threatening to run away from him. He suppressed the impulse and only lightly ran his fingers through her hair.

Seeing that the Emperor seemed to be in quite a good mood, Xi Rongyan weighed her words carefully before finally asking: "This concubine would like to have her cousin come and live in Guanju Palace. Would Your Majesty agree?"

This was already the second time Xi Rongyan had raised the matter.

Wei Qi gave a noncommittal murmur, his gaze passing over Xi Rongyan's face for a moment. Then, as if tired, he patted her back. "Sleep now."

Xi Rongyan paused. With an answer like that, she could not tell whether the Emperor had agreed or not.

She hesitated and looked up again. "Has Your Majesty agreed?"

Wei Qi looked down at her and thought for a moment about how to discourage her without making her unhappy.

He did not want Xi Rongyan to be disappointed, but he also did not want her cousin coming here.

Setting aside Xie Yumian's dubious motives from the previous life, he also had no wish for Xi Rongyan to be drawn back into memories of her time with Gu Yunyu.

Xie Yumian's presence would inevitably stir up some of those recollections.

He wanted Gu Yunyu to become the past, completely and thoroughly.

Wei Qi regretted it a little — he had forgotten about Xie Yumian. Had he remembered earlier, he would have sent her away long ago.

His fingertips shifted at her waist. After a brief silence, he said quietly: "This matter has been left for the Empress to arrange. I have already given her instructions."

Hearing the Empress mentioned, Xi Rongyan knew in her heart this would likely be difficult. Yet the Emperor had already said as much, and it would seem unreasonable to press further.

She knew Imperial Consort Qi was the Empress's ally, and was not sure the Empress would arrange anything at all. The uncertainty sat in her heart.

She was most afraid that Imperial Consort Qi would know, and make things difficult for her cousin.

She was about to speak again when the Emperor had already reached up to lower the bed curtain. The heavy drape shut out the light from outside, and the Emperor's husky voice came from above her head: "Are you settling in well here in the palace?"

Xi Rongyan faintly understood the Emperor did not wish to continue that conversation. She could only set aside the matter of her cousin for now and answered softly: "Yes, well enough."

The Emperor seemed to have asked only in passing. He gave a single murmur of assent and said nothing more.

It was Xi Rongyan who could not sleep — turning from side to side, unable to settle.

Wei Qi opened his eyes in the dark and glanced at the person in his arms who was still awake. He held her waist to keep her from fidgeting, then drew her over to lie against his chest and asked: "Can't sleep?"

Xi Rongyan lay half-propped against Wei Qi's chest and said quietly: "There is no one to talk to in this palace. It's cold and lonely."

As she said it, she nuzzled her face against Wei Qi's chest in something almost like a pout, her arms circling his broad, firm waist. She even rubbed her face gently against him — which made Wei Qi's breath catch.

chapters.title: A Rare Initiative
chapters.content:
Wei Qi knew perfectly well why Xi Rongyan was doing this.

It was rare for her to take such initiative.

But it was only for the sake of someone else that she could be this attentive and persistent.

He pressed his lips together and said nothing. Her soft body made him taut all over — especially because she was wearing only thin clothes, and she pressed against him with no idea at all how enticing that was.

Perhaps she truly believed he would not touch her.

He quietly looked down at her. In his heart, he had already begun to relent. In the end, he could not bear to let her down.

In the previous life he had desperately wished she would be able to coax him like this. But she had never once done so.

His fingers settled in her dark hair. He sighed quietly. "I will arrange it. Just wait a few more days."

Hearing the Emperor's words, the anxiousness that had been sitting in Xi Rongyan's heart eased a little. She held him tighter and said softly: "This concubine thanks Your Majesty."

Wei Qi silently tugged at the corner of his mouth. His fingers slid from her hair down to her waist. "Is there anything else you want to say to me?"

In fact, Xi Rongyan did.

She brought up what the Empress had said to her about Noble Consort Xian, then added quietly: "About the Noble Consort's matter, Your Majesty..."

Her voice trailed off into a low laugh from the Emperor.

She looked up but could not make out the Emperor's expression in the dark — she did not understand why he had laughed.

She only heard his low voice: "Even if I release her, she will not believe it was you who pleaded for her."

"This is something I wanted to do long before — punishing Noble Consort Xian is not your concern. I will speak with the Empress about it."

Xi Rongyan paused at that, and then felt reassured.

She nodded and leaned comfortably back against the Emperor's chest.

She found herself puzzled. The Emperor always spoke to her gently, as though he was never truly angry. She was genuinely no longer so afraid of him, and found that having him near actually gave her a feeling of calm in which she could fall asleep.

She had always been cold-blooded since childhood — even in spring she needed a warming jar inside her quilt. The Emperor was warm, and held in his arms through the night she would not feel cold once.

She felt the Emperor press his lips to her forehead — soft, warm, and tender. Her heart skipped a beat. The fingers resting against his chest tightened of their own accord, and she closed her eyes in peace.

When Wei Qi woke the following morning, Xi Rongyan was still sleeping.

He looked at her for a long time — eyes closed, buried in his arms — then lightly touched her cheek. The warm, soft sensation made everything feel real.

He could not help but think of the moment she had left him, her body covered in blood.

Wei Qi closed his eyes, cutting off the thought, and quietly rose.

When Xi Rongyan finally woke with a start, she found the Emperor had long since gone.

In the days that followed, the Emperor continued to spend his nights at Hanyuan Hall.

Whispers ran through the inner palace, and the looks cast Xi Rongyan's way shifted again and again.

On one particular morning, as Xi Rongyan was leaving the Empress's palace hoping to find her cousin and talk with her about the move, someone suddenly blocked her path.

She looked over — she recognized the person by now, after all these days.

It was Wang Xiuyi — the one her mother had mentioned as the most favored woman in the inner palace.

Wang Xiuyi was, naturally, quite beautiful: delicate and graceful, wearing a peach-red spring dress, holding a jade-handled fan, jade bracelets on both wrists, her adornments chosen with great care.

But her brows were drawn up high, at odds with the otherwise gentle impression of her face.

Xi Rongyan had already guessed at some of Wang Xiuyi's hostility toward her.

Yet even though Wang Xiuyi regarded her with such antipathy, Xi Rongyan felt no displeasure at all.

Wang Xiuyi had been favored before. Perhaps it was Xi Rongyan's turn now. And after her, who would be next?

If one hated every woman who received favor, would there be enough hatred to go around?

As youth faded, younger and more beautiful women would continue to enter. By then, would the Emperor even remember the faces that had come before?

Xi Rongyan had no wish to be the target of anyone's hatred, so she asked in a soft voice: "Sister, do you have something you wished to say to me?"

Wang Xiuyi looked Xi Rongyan up and down. In truth she had seen her before, at banquets, though only from a distance.

Back then, Xi Rongyan had been the model and center of attention among the noble daughters — not only for her striking looks, but for her ever-gentle and refined manner.

She had always been impeccably gracious in company.

Her own elder brother had secretly liked her once. But unfortunately Xi Rongyan had already been engaged.

Wang Xiuyi had once wished to become someone like her — and had felt a quiet envy.

She still remembered one banquet where Xi Rongyan had worn only a simple blue orchid-patterned dress, yet she had gleamed in the sunlight. With the begonias in bloom, she had sat before the flowers and drawn every eye in the room.

Now she had entered the palace, and Wang Xiuyi knew herself to be no match for her. Yet she was not willing to accept it.

She had once been the only place in the inner palace the Emperor would visit — even though he had never touched her even then. But ever since Xi Rongyan had entered the palace, on the days that should have been the Emperor's visits to her, he had shown no intention of coming at all. She could not help the resentment in her heart.

The sisters who used to fawn over her now looked at her with tepid pity. The cutting and sarcastic remarks — she heard them all too clearly.

Even Imperial Consort Qi and Consort Hui, who had once been relatively civil with her, now barely acknowledged her.

The little eunuchs who used to rush to please her no longer came.

Even her daily meals, in just these few short days, had fallen far below what they used to be.

Of course she was bitter. How could she not be?

If Xi Rongyan had never entered the palace, none of this would have changed.

Wang Bao'ran squeezed her fingers tight. She wanted to contain the jealousy on her face, yet she could not.

The inner palace was like this — everyone was a quick reader of the room, always watching for cues. The moment the Emperor stopped visiting her, they changed their tune in an instant.

She took a deep breath and forced a smile. "I do have something I'd like to say to you."

"Would it be convenient for me to come sit with you for a while, sister?"

Seeing her expression, Xi Rongyan nodded and agreed.

Not far behind them, Imperial Consort Qi and Consort Hui watched Wang Xiuyi and Xi Rongyan walk away together. Consort Hui laughed. "Look at that — I had someone tamper with Wang Xiuyi's food just a few days ago, had people mock her for a couple of days, and she's already lost her composure."

Imperial Consort Qi gave a slow, lazy smile. "The Empress has the right idea. Let's just sit back and watch the show."

The two of them chatted and laughed as they turned and went their separate ways.

Not far away on the palace path, Xie Yumian stood watching Xi Rongyan and Wang Xiuyi walk away side by side. Her face went rigid.

She had assumed Xi Rongyan would actually make good on her word and bring her to Hanyuan Hall. With the Emperor staying there night after night, showing her such favor — she could not believe a request as simple as this would be refused.

Unless Xi Rongyan had never truly intended to help her at all. Perhaps she feared she would go to Guanju Palace and draw away the Emperor's attention.

Xie Yumian clutched the handkerchief in her hands until her knuckles went white. She kept her eyes on Xi Rongyan's retreating figure until it disappeared — and then the hatred that surfaced in her eyes was unmistakable.

Wang Bao'ran followed Xi Rongyan into Hanyuan Hall. Her gaze swept over every corner of the spacious palace, and seeing Xi Rongyan living here alone in such grandeur, the envy rose in her again, unstoppable.

The two of them sat down together. Wang Bao'ran looked at Xi Rongyan — and promptly reddened around the eyes. She pressed her handkerchief to them and bowed her head, letting the tears fall.

chapters.title: More and More Favored
chapters.content:
Xi Rongyan was taken aback at Wang Bao'ran's behavior. She did not understand why she had burst into tears the moment she sat down, and quickly asked in a hushed voice: "Sister, what is the matter?"

Wang Bao'ran looked at Xi Rongyan through her tears, her voice choked. "Nothing. I only envy your good fortune, sister."

Xi Rongyan did not know what to say. She offered softly: "Sister need not envy me. You and I are not so different."

Wang Bao'ran wiped her tears. "Ever since the Emperor began going to you, I fear he has forgotten all about me — the one who was here first."

Xi Rongyan replied sincerely: "How does sister know I will not one day be the one who is forgotten?"

"Perhaps it will not be long before the Emperor stops coming to me as well."

Wang Bao'ran was startled, and stared at Xi Rongyan.

She saw Xi Rongyan sitting gracefully beside her, her face genuinely free of any satisfaction or gloating at being favored. By contrast, she felt like an undignified fool reaching for something out of her grasp.

Wang Bao'ran murmured in a daze: "Sister is joking. Who in the inner palace can compare to you right now?"

"Everyone can see the Emperor treats you differently."

Xi Rongyan did not wish to argue the point. She only said quietly: "Sister, whether you believe me or not, what I said came from my heart."

Wang Bao'ran stared at Xi Rongyan's face for a long moment.

She could find not one crack in her manner — as though the Emperor's favor truly meant very little to her.

She genuinely seemed unwilling to compete for it.

She was receiving so many benefits from that favor, yet here she was acting so serene and detached. What was the purpose of such a performance?

She suppressed the irritation in her heart, dried her tears, and gripped Xi Rongyan's hand tightly. "May I ask sister, what method you've used to keep the Emperor with you for so many consecutive days?"

Wang Bao'ran wept again. "I ask for nothing else — only for the Emperor to spend one night with me."

Xi Rongyan's hand was gripped so tightly it had begun to ache.

Looking at Wang Bao'ran's relentlessly tearful, heartbroken face, she felt another kind of sorrow entirely.

She had long known that she herself would also be locked inside these walls for the rest of her life. She had made her peace with being swallowed up among so many women.

If she could not be open-minded enough to let herself go, she would only live in misery.

Wang Xiuyi had clearly not been able to let herself go.

She thought: would she herself become this one day? Clinging to an obsession, unable to release it from her heart, only tormenting herself?

The thought filled her with dread for the future.

Something lodged in Xi Rongyan's throat. She bowed her head for a moment — the cold jade eardrops brushing her cheek, the string of white jade beads at her neck hanging in the air — and gently dabbed at Wang Bao'ran's tears with her handkerchief, knowing she could not help anyone.

As for Wang Bao'ran's true reason for coming to her, she had a vague sense of it — and did not think it was only for this.

Besides, to ask her what method she used to please the Emperor — was Wang Bao'ran truly so naïve, or did she simply think Xi Rongyan had no guard against her?

She said simply: "Sister, please do not grieve so. In truth, I have used no method whatsoever. Why the Emperor comes to my quarters, I myself do not understand."

"Sister has been in favor before — what could I possibly teach you?"

"But as we both live here in the inner palace, we could spend our days together in conversation and keep each other company."

A handkerchief scented with fragrance settled softly against Wang Bao'ran's eyes. She paused for a moment. Her gaze fell to the silver-threaded orchid fan on Xi Rongyan's lap.

She looked upward slowly — the neatly gathered collar, the gentle luster of the beads reflecting her own tears, and then above that, the composure beneath Xi Rongyan's beautifully drawn brows.

Poised, graceful, slender, lovely. Who would not be drawn to her?

That the Emperor liked her suddenly seemed not so hard to understand.

She suddenly felt that she could never, in all her life, be a match for her.

She did not have Xi Rongyan's fortune. From the moment of entering the palace, she had lived alone in her own hall with no faction pressing down on her, the Empress Dowager standing behind her. Even if she fell out of favor, the Empress would not dare go too far.

She was different.

A woman in the inner palace without the Emperor's love was no better than a nameless weed at the base of the palace wall — even a eunuch could tread on her. A whole year might pass without catching the Emperor's eye even once. If she died, she would be wrapped in white cloth and carried out.

It forced her to compete.

She did not have Xi Rongyan's family background or her standing.

A tear rolled down Wang Bao'ran's cheek. She spoke from her heart: "I am not like you, sister. I cannot afford to pass the days in such idle leisure."

"All I want is even a little of the Emperor's favor — just enough to live a little better in this palace."

Xi Rongyan looked at that single tear, her dark brows faintly raised then let go. She said quietly: "Sister entered the palace before me and should better understand the ways of survival here, and the Emperor's temperament. You would know I truly cannot help you."

Xi Rongyan could not even manage to bring her own cousin to live in Guanju Palace — how was she to help Wang Bao'ran?

In that moment, Wang Bao'ran suddenly understood.

Xi Rongyan was still the same gentle, well-bred lady she had always been. Everyone loved her — because she truly could nourish people like a soft spring rain.

Even though she had genuinely resented and envied her just now, there came a moment when, suddenly, she did not hate her anymore.

She knew what Xi Rongyan said was true. She understood even more that the Emperor was not someone who could be controlled by anyone.

And some people were simply born to have everything.

Even when the Gu family had its catastrophe and everyone mocked Xi Rongyan, she had turned around and entered the palace — and effortlessly won the Emperor's favor.

She could not hold back the tears. She bent her head and pressed it against Xi Rongyan's shoulder, sobbing. "May I come often and talk with you?"

Xi Rongyan had not expected Wang Bao'ran to lean on her like this. She felt a dampness at her shoulder, and said quietly: "Of course you may. I am lonely here alone."

When Wang Bao'ran finally left, she turned to look back at the peach blossoms filling the courtyard.

She had heard long ago that Xi Rongyan loved peach blossoms. That one backward glance, and she gave up completely.

Because she understood now that perhaps the Emperor truly loved Xi Rongyan — had planted this entire courtyard full of peach blossoms for her. She, who mattered so much to the Emperor, was perhaps the only one.

She had no more desire to compete. She even found herself hoping Xi Rongyan would grow more and more favored.

Between that Empress who looked gentle and kind on the surface yet was cold-hearted beneath — and Xi Rongyan — she found herself wanting Xi Rongyan to have the upper hand.

Then perhaps the inner palace would truly be peaceful.

Wang Bao'ran returned to Xingqing Palace.

The main hall there was occupied by Consort Hui; the Xiyu Hall on the other side housed Noble Lady Lin. Only she lived in the Jingyi Study — a narrow two-room western-facing apartment with poor light.

She could hear the sounds of Consort Hui and Noble Lady Lin laughing together in the main hall. She sat alone and cold at the window.

The palace maid standing behind her stepped forward and asked: "Did you not prepare something earlier, my lady? Why did you not give it to Consort Zhen?"

"If you had gotten rid of her, the Emperor would have come back to remember you again."

Wang Bao'ran looked at the palace maid. There was no real deference in those eyes — only a kind of reproach.

She was silent.

All the palace maids assigned to her after she entered the palace had been carefully chosen by the Empress. What could she say?

Her every step was watched by another's eyes.

A single misstep was all the Empress needed to deal with her — nothing could be easier.

Wang Bao'ran was quiet for a long while before saying softly: "Wait a little longer."

After Wang Bao'ran left, Xi Rongyan's mood was also subdued.

She sat sideways on the couch, gazing at the peach blossoms outside the window, lost in thought. Her fingers turned the fan, and Wang Bao'ran's tearful face drifted back before her eyes.

A sorrow stirred for her — the kind that lived in the deep places of the heart.

She propped her cheek on her hand beside the small table, sitting in this cold and exquisite palace hall, and looked at the old keepsake on her wrist that her mother had given her. As though that alone was her one remaining comfort.

Something that could remind her of the easier days that had come before.

In Xuanzheng Hall, Wei Qi listened to Gao Yi relay the news that Wang Bao'ran had gone to Hanyuan Hall to speak with Xi Rongyan. The fingers resting on the imperial desk paused.

books.title: Peeking at Spring's Affection
books.author: Qiong Yu
books.synopsis:
After her mother's death, Shen Weici is left utterly alone, drifting like a rootless weed. She travels a great distance to the capital to seek out her relatives.

Upon first entering the Marquis's estate, she treads carefully, facing difficulties at every turn — yet throughout it all she remains quiet and gentle, with no desire to take a single thing from the household. She only wishes to find herself a suitable marriage and a small corner of peace to call her own.

Song Zhang, the capital's notorious "Lord of Hell," is a man of noble lineage who holds great power and regards everyone beneath him with contempt.

When he first lays eyes on Shen Weici, he is full of disdain and makes things difficult for her.

Later, he notices her smiling shyly at another man, her beautiful eyes alluring as a fox spirit's — and he scoffs coldly as he walks away, only to secretly destroy the promising match behind her back.

He watches her face him with reddened eyes, demanding to know why. He answers with a lazy, wicked smile: *"Zhang the Second placed first in the imperial exams young and comes from a distinguished family — who do you think you are to cling to him? If you want a peaceful life, why not beg me? I might just grant you the position of honored concubine."*

But the tables turn swiftly. In the end, it is he who kneels at her door, eyes red and pleading:

*"Ah Ci… I'm begging you…"*

*"Don't carve out my heart…"*

He had used every dark means at his disposal for her sake — and only in the end did he realize he had already fallen beyond saving.

chapters.title: First Encounter
chapters.content:
A humble carriage rumbled slowly along the wide, imposing hutong from the far end of the Vermillion Wall Alley.

Before the front gates of Jian'an Marquis Manor, Shen Zhaozhao regarded the approaching carriage with unconcealed disdain, then turned to her personal maidservant beside her with a displeased air: "To think Father would actually agree to let her come — isn't this just asking for trouble for Mother and me?"

"Someone from some backwater village, who knows what uncouth habits she's picked up — eight out of ten chances she'll be just as unrespectable as that mother of hers who died young."

"And Father actually agreed to let her come."

As she spoke, she turned to look at the young man standing beside her: "Brother Song, don't you think so?"

The man standing beside Shen Zhaozhao wore a round-collared, narrow-sleeved deep crimson robe with a ferocious tiger embroidered on his chest. His figure was tall and upright, and the black-and-gold crow-blade at his waist lent him an air of menace.

He merely cast a lazy sideways glance at Shen Zhaozhao and arched a brow with languid disinterest, showing no intention of speaking.

It was the old nanny standing beside Shen Zhaozhao who quietly said: "It is cold here, and the Old Madam and the Lady are waiting inside. You can see her once the servants bring her in — why would a young lady like yourself wait out here in person?"

Shen Zhaozhao gave a cold snort. "I simply want to see first what sort of creature she is."

"Everyone says my father and mother are an ideal couple — and now suddenly this base woman appears, an illegitimate daughter born of a kept mistress with no proper standing. I truly cannot stomach it."

She then added through gritted teeth: "I want her to make a fool of herself the moment she arrives — only then will I feel any satisfaction."

Song Zhang, standing on Shen Zhaozhao's other side, only now broke into a lazy smile at these words. The corners of his thin lips curved upward as a glint of amusement appeared in his phoenix eyes: "Is it not easy enough to make her embarrass herself?"

Shen Zhaozhao's eyes immediately lit up. She gave Song Zhang a sweet smile and tugged at his sleeve, her eyes bright and sparkling: "Brother Song, you have a way to make her humiliate herself?"

Song Zhang did not look at Shen Zhaozhao. His slender fingers rested on the long sword at his waist as his tall, straight figure — like a bamboo stalk — moved toward the carriage that had just halted before the gates of Dingguo Marquis Manor.

Shen Weici gently lifted a corner of the small window curtain on the carriage, took in the imposing gateway and the characters on the plaque, then let the curtain fall again.

Her maidservant Yuedeng supported her and murmured, "Miss, shall we get down from the carriage?"

Shen Weici gave a soft sound of agreement and was just reaching out to lift the curtain when it was suddenly flipped open from outside by the hilt of a sword.

The sword's blade was half drawn, pressed before her, its cold gleam directed straight at her — as if carrying a chill of murderous intent, or perhaps meant to give her a demonstration of power right from the start.

The maidservant Yuedeng let out an involuntary cry of fright at the sword that had suddenly intruded, her body reeling backward as she plopped down inside the narrow carriage.

Shen Weici only glanced at the sword before her, then raised her eyes to look at the young man holding it.

He was handsome in the manner of a noble gentleman — jade crown, phoenix eyes, long brows — yet his thin lips held a cool indifference, and two parts of unruly roguishness clung to him.

Looking further, his physique was imposing and his bearing beautiful, yet his eyes were careless and provocative; on closer inspection they carried a faint contempt and disdain, as though regarding an inferior object.

But seeing his official robes — deep purple with golden buckles — his distinguished identity was beyond question.

Their eyes met. Song Zhang looked at the young woman in the carriage: she wore a slightly faded crimson-pink scholar's skirt, yet her skin was white as snow, her bones delicate and slender, and her pair of slightly upturned peach-blossom eyes rippled like spring water. Below them was a full and vivid cherry mouth.

Her dark hair was adorned only with a simple, plain silver hairpin — no other ornament whatsoever, not even earrings — yet this made her red lips and white teeth all the more apparent, her jade bones and icy skin all the more striking.

He had expected merely a crude country girl, but this was an entirely unexpected beauty.

The contempt in Song Zhang's eyes deepened. She was nothing but an inferior plaything — her status was too low for him to regard with anything other than scorn.

Still, the fact that she had not been frightened by his sword surprised him slightly.

Shen Weici glanced at the man before her, then dropped her gaze to take in the gloating servants standing nearby. She understood that within the great aristocratic clans of the capital, birth and social standing were everything. She took the young man's contempt as something she had not seen, resolving to keep a low profile.

Moreover, she had long since prepared herself for the possibility of a cold reception upon arrival. Even knowing that the man before her intended to humiliate her, she still extended her slender pale fingers and gently pushed the sword hilt back into its scabbard.

She stepped out past the curtain, lowered her head modestly, gave a proper bow, and said in a soft, gentle voice: "Many thanks to the young master for lifting the curtain."

Song Zhang raised an eyebrow. He could not tell whether the woman before him spoke in irony or in sincerity.

From behind him came Shen Zhaozhao's laughter: "Brother Song, she is even thanking you."

The curve at Song Zhang's lips flattened. Having already made his boast, he could not now lose face.

He reached casually to his waist and yanked a jade pendant from the ornamental belt, flinging it over. There was a sound of a hairpin hitting the ground, and a cascade of ink-black hair spilled down, falling across that slightly pallid face.

Song Zhang glanced at the pair of humiliated peach-blossom eyes before him, then turned back to Shen Zhaozhao with a cool smile: "I, your lord, do not lift curtains for inferior creatures like her — that word of thanks is an insult to me, so striking her is what she deserves."

"She has also cost me my hour to attend court, and that account is not finished."

With that, Song Zhang swept up his robes, nimbly swung himself onto a jet-black steed, and rode off in a splendid flourish, leaving behind a scene of ruin.

Shen Zhaozhao looked at Shen Weici standing dazedly on the carriage step, hair disheveled, and felt a surge of satisfaction. She gave Shen Weici a cold snort: "Take a good look at your own origins — there are certain fortunes you are not fit to aspire to."

"The Marquis Manor keeps one extra person like you no differently than keeping an extra maidservant. If you know what is good for you, you will keep your tail between your legs from now on, and do not go speaking out of turn."

"My father has agreed to take you in only because he found your situation as pitiable as a stray dog's. You had better be careful around me. Do not think that entering the Marquis Manor means you get to live the comfortable life of a young lady."

"If you displease me, I will make your life worse here than it ever was in the countryside."

With that, Shen Zhaozhao turned up her chin, spun around, and walked away trailing four or five maidservants.

The maidservants following in Shen Zhaozhao's wake each turned to mock Shen Weici with a scornful smile.

Yuedeng, who had risen from the carriage floor and now stood behind Shen Weici, stared blankly at the scene, her hands clenching: "This is too much."

Shen Weici looked at the jade pendant lying on the ground, fought back the moisture rising to her eyes, clasped Yuedeng's hand tightly, and turned to step back into the carriage: "Pick up the hairpin."

Inside the carriage, Shen Weici redid her hair. The matron waiting outside impatiently pressed her: "What are you dawdling for? The Old Madam and the Lady are waiting inside. Do you think yourself some person of consequence in the capital, making the ladies wait for you?"

A maidservant chimed in with a laugh: "What face does a broken-down nobody have? Did the matron see what she's wearing? Even the big maidservants of the Marquis Manor wear better cloth than what's on her body. The embroidery on that garment is truly crude — and there are still loose threads!"

Another voice joined in: "Coming from a small place like Yuyang — what quality of fabric could she possibly wear?"

"Look at that petty manner of hers, truly beneath any standard. Not just anyone can be a miss of the Marquis Manor — one must have the blessing and the fortune for it."

"Our Lady is magnanimous to take her in. She should be burning incense in gratitude."

These words were spoken openly, without any attempt at discretion — clearly meant to be heard.

Yuedeng was already weeping with rage. Shen Weici lowered her lashes and silently re-pinned her hair with perfect care, then turned to gently wipe Yuedeng's tears with a handkerchief and murmured: "This is nothing. I had already expected this."

"It is still better than Yuyang."

Shen Weici climbed out of the carriage once more. Though her style was simple, it was impeccably neat and proper.

Yuedeng dried her tears and followed behind Shen Weici, biting her lip to hold back the rest, knowing her young mistress was right. If they were still in Yuyang right now, the young mistress would likely already have been sold by that black-hearted uncle to become some old man's concubine.

As the young mistress had said along the road: the great aristocratic houses of the capital cared deeply about their reputations. Even if they did not welcome her, at least on the surface they would not resort to those kinds of dirty tactics. Enduring a few cutting remarks was nothing.

chapters.title: Entering the Marquis Manor
chapters.content:
Everything she had brought with her was contained in a single small bundle. Shen Weici followed behind the matron with her eyes cast down at the path ahead, not looking around, and with a composed and humble expression on her face.

Yuedeng, however, gaped at the magnificently carved beams and painted rafters of the Marquis Manor, exclaiming repeatedly in wonder — until she drew a mocking snort from the matron beside her: "I am not saying this as a warning for nothing: if you dare let your eyes wander once you reach the main hall, you will be dealt with according to the Marquis Manor's punishments. Not just anyone is entitled to look upon the masters."

Yuedeng's face paled, and she dared not let her gaze stray again, imitating her young mistress ahead by walking with perfect propriety.

The Dingguo Marquis Manor occupied an entire hutong, and its interior was even grander. After winding through corridors, they had walked a good quarter of an hour before arriving at the main hall.

Inside the main hall, the Old Madam sat at the place of honor at the head. A matron stepped forward to announce: "Old Madam, Princess Consort, Second Lady — the person has been brought."

Not yet knowing the proper forms of address for those seated in the hall, Shen Weici stepped forward and curtseyed: "Weici pays her respects to the Old Madam, the Princess Consort, and the Second Lady."

Second Lady Wen's expression soured at the sight of Shen Weici standing in the hall. So this was the illegitimate daughter her husband had left behind during his dalliance years ago. With that fox-spirit's looks, she was likely the same sort as her mother.

Had it not been for the Old Madam insisting that the girl was still blood of the manor, and that letting her wander outside would make for unseemly talk, she would not — by her own temperament — have permitted such a person to enter.

She looked away in revulsion. All these years people had envied her for maintaining a clean household without concubines, and now this illegitimate daughter had to surface. She could only imagine what people would say outside.

The Princess Consort Huimin of the First Branch glanced at Lady Wen, leaned back in her chair, and sipped her tea at a leisurely pace, watching the scene unfold with detached amusement.

After Shen Weici finished speaking and silence fell over the hall, it was the Old Madam who finally spoke first: "I hear your mother fell ill and passed away — what illness was it?"

Shen Weici lowered her head respectfully and replied: "My mother spent her days doing embroidery to support the household. Working late into the night, she caught a chill in a draft and developed consumption. The funeral was only completed two months ago."

The Old Madam listened and sighed with a slow nod. "That is a pitiable fate."

She studied Shen Weici for a moment, then said: "Raise your head — let me have a look."

Shen Weici obediently lifted her face.

A clean, fair, and lovely countenance — the beauty of jade and bright flowers — was revealed before everyone. No powder or rouge adorned it, her gaze was calm, carrying a faint coolness, and her appearance was white and warm.

Her bearing was graceful and composed: a slender waist, fine shoulders, a straight back, standing there with a gentle elegance — nothing like the timidity one might expect from a small-town girl. Indeed, one could easily have mistaken her for the daughter of a distinguished family.

The Old Madam nodded: "Her looks are admirably fine, and her deportment is proper."

She continued: "How old are you? Have you received any schooling?"

Shen Weici replied quietly: "I have just turned fifteen."

She lowered her voice a little more: "I have only read the Admonitions for Women and the Four Books for two years, and can recognize a few characters."

The Old Madam gave a low murmur and studied Shen Weici carefully once more: "I had not expected your mother to have sent you to school."

"But from what I hear, yours is also a pitiable history. Now that you have come to the Manor, by your age you would be the Manor's Third Young Miss. Settle in here and live at ease from now on."

The Old Madam then looked at Lady Wen: "She is, after all, Rongshen's daughter. As her legitimate mother, you should arrange a small courtyard for her in the West Back Compound, and her food and clothing shall be in accordance with the standards set for the concubine-born."

Lady Wen's face stiffened. She looked at the Old Madam: "How can she be counted as the Lord's concubine-born? She is nothing more than the daughter of a woman the Lord kept outside with no name and no standing, never brought into the Manor, never formally acknowledged."

"Are we now to raise her as a proper young miss?"

"Moreover, what are we to say outside when a so-called concubine-born daughter of the Lord suddenly appears out of nowhere?"

Princess Consort Huimin smiled faintly at Lady Wen: "She is the blood of the Second Lord — whether born inside or outside the household, what does it matter? She has spent the last decade or more without seeking to attach herself to the Marquis Manor, and now that her mother has died, she is no doubt left with nowhere to turn. Does my sister-in-law truly have not even this much room in her heart?"

Lady Wen was nearly spitting blood at Princess Consort Huimin's words, yet unable to argue back given her inferior rank, so she plastered on a smile: "Sister-in-law speaks too strongly. If a person of unknown origins were to suddenly appear as an illegitimate daughter at your door, you too would feel unsettled, would you not?"

Princess Consort Huimin smiled: "I would not care in the least."

This left Lady Wen speechless.

The two sisters-in-law had never been close. The Princess Consort disdained Lady Wen's petty and shrewish jealousy, while Lady Wen resented what she saw as the Princess Consort's false superiority, propped up by her mother the Grand Princess.

The Old Madam cast a displeased look at Lady Wen as well: "What is said outside is your business to manage — or can you not even handle that much?"

With that, the Old Madam directly bypassed Lady Wen and summoned the housekeeper to make the arrangements, telling Shen Weici to follow him.

Shen Weici had listened quietly to the exchanges in the hall with her head slightly lowered throughout. Hearing the Old Madam's words, she gave a proper curtsey and then left.

In the moment she turned to go, she caught a glimpse of the Second Lady's eyes — a pair of eyes filled with deep, cold revulsion and loathing.

Her heart gave an involuntary lurch. She lowered her head and kept her eyes meekly downcast.

Once Shen Weici departed, the Princess Consort also found herself with nothing more to watch and took her leave as well.

Only Lady Wen and the Old Madam remained in the main hall, along with Lady Wen's daughter Shen Zhaozhao standing behind her.

Shen Zhaozhao at this moment pouted and ran to cling to the Old Madam's arm, wheedling: "Grandmother, I do not like her."

The Old Madam patted Shen Zhaozhao's hand fondly, then looked at Lady Wen below: "Rongshen has had御史中丞 Chen He filing memorials against him one after another these past days. Chen He and Rongshen have long been at odds, and Rongshen is in the Ministry of Revenue — there is no doubt he has had his hands in the till, and Chen He has seized some evidence against him; otherwise he would not continue pressing him so relentlessly."

"I managed to have Song Zhang suppress the matter somewhat in front of the Emperor, but it cannot hold back Chen He's constant memorials."

"Your sister-in-law, though a Princess Consort, has devoted herself to Buddhism for years and takes no part in worldly affairs — I cannot call upon her."

"It just so happens that I see this girl is uncommonly beautiful — even among the women of the capital, her looks are first-rate. That Lady Zhang is in great favor with the Emperor at the moment, and her elder brother Zhang Tingyi is also one of the Emperor's trusted favorites. He is adept at gauging the Emperor's wishes and currying imperial favor — his influence is most prominent."

"One word from him before the Emperor is worth ten words from anyone else."

"Fortunately, he is a man of lustful nature, and his two wives have both died. They say he has certain unsettling proclivities, and no noble family in the capital has been willing to give him a daughter in marriage."

"My plan is to send Weici to Zhang Tingyi as his wife once the new year comes. With her looks, getting Zhang Tingyi to agree will be no trouble at all. If the matter succeeds, it will draw his goodwill and shelter Rongshen, it will suppress that obstinate Chen He — best if he can be demoted outright — and in future Zhang Tingyi will continue to look after the Marquis Manor."

"It is an arrangement that achieves two things at once. Why should you have any objections?"

Lady Wen was startled, then brightened at once, for her husband had been fretting over exactly this matter in recent days: "It is the Old Madam who thinks of everything."

Shen Zhaozhao, upon hearing this, snuggled against her grandmother with a sudden lightening of spirit: "And here I thought Grandmother was truly going to keep her — it had me distressed for days."

The Old Madam smiled and took Shen Zhaozhao's hand: "You are the Manor's legitimate daughter. She is nothing more than the illegitimate child your father kept outside — her mother's status was low, and her origins are even more disreputable. How could she compare to you?"

"Taking her in is only to avoid gossip outside. Your father holds an official position at court, and reputation is paramount. If Chen He were to seize upon this matter as further grounds for censure, that would be even worse."

Lady Wen looked at the Old Madam: "But Zhang Tingyi is already past forty — what if Shen Weici refuses?"

The Old Madam smiled lightly: "Whether she is willing or not is not hers to decide."

"We shall find an opportunity in due course for them to meet, and we shall see. As long as Zhang Tingyi truly takes a liking to her, the matter will be easy to arrange."

Shen Zhaozhao leaned against her grandmother and smiled: "It seems her looks have some use after all. A fox-spirit face — that is its only purpose."

Lady Wen smiled at Shen Zhaozhao: "With those origins and that appearance, do you imagine she would have any future if the Manor did not take her in? She traveled all the way to the capital to throw herself on your father — surely she wants to cling to the Manor's wealth and prestige."

"Her mother was a plaything. She is the same."

"If she is sensible enough to keep Zhang Tingyi content, and becomes his proper wife with some wealth and standing, she may well end up grateful to our Marquis Manor."

"And if she is not sensible, I have any number of ways to torment her."

chapters.title: Meeting Father
chapters.content:
Meanwhile, Shen Weici followed behind the housekeeper. The housekeeper wore a thick silk-brocade blue robe of considerable quality, and his slightly plump figure had an air of comfortable prosperity.

Yuedeng walked beside Shen Weici and murmured: "The Marquis Manor is truly grand — even the housekeeper dresses this well."

"This kind of brocade in Yuyang would only be worn by the masters of the household."

Shen Weici glanced at Yuedeng and said softly: "Save that for later."

Yuedeng fell silent and walked quietly at Shen Weici's side.

The further they walked, the more tranquil their surroundings became. When they finally arrived before a secluded courtyard, Housekeeper Chang turned and looked Shen Weici over from head to toe. He showed no particular coldness, but neither was he warm — his manner was distant and politely formal.

He indicated the courtyard within: "This courtyard has been empty for some time, but it is cleaned every two months or so. Third Young Miss may go in and rest for now; I will have a few maids sent in presently to wait on you and do some tidying."

Housekeeper Chang glanced at Shen Weici once more: "If there is anything you are lacking, tell me now, and I will have the maids bring it along as well."

Having just arrived at the Marquis Manor, Shen Weici did not wish to make extra trouble, and shook her head, saying softly: "I have caused the housekeeper enough trouble seeing me here. There is nothing I need."

Housekeeper Chang nodded, said nothing further, turned, and left.

Yuedeng watched the retreating figure of the housekeeper and said to Shen Weici: "Everyone in this Marquis Manor looks difficult to get along with. But at least the Old Madam showed some pity for you — as long as she can speak in your favor, your days here need not necessarily be so hard."

Shen Weici looked up at the modest courtyard: "Let us hope so."

The lanterns hanging at the courtyard gate were like candles guttering in the wind — long faded — swaying faintly in the cool, damp air of an autumn afternoon.

She understood that the Old Madam's words in the hall earlier had been no more than pleasantries — the surface civility maintained by great families. As nothing more than a suddenly appearing illegitimate daughter, how much genuine compassion could the Old Madam have for her?

This cramped, run-down courtyard said it all. People are inclined to flatter the powerful and trample the weak — a man like Housekeeper Chang, who had spent years in this environment, surely understood the Old Madam's mind perfectly.

In settling her here, they had made it plain that she was not particularly important.

That was just as well. She had never wished to attract attention.

Wild grass had already sprung up across the courtyard, fallen leaves covered the flagstones, and the main three rooms at the center were flanked by two smaller side rooms. Within the grandeur of the Marquis Manor, the place looked remarkably humble — yet it was still far better than anywhere she had lived before.

She pushed open the door of the main room. A scent of aged wood drifted out, and only a light film of dust covered the furniture — a little cleaning and one could easily live here.

Shortly, the three maids the housekeeper had summoned arrived.

The three maids came in, acknowledged Shen Weici with a greeting of "Third Young Miss," listened to her instructions, and went off to tidy the courtyard.

The maids' movements were neither particularly efficient nor particularly slack — as if they neither wished to wait upon someone in such a place, yet were bound by propriety to follow orders.

Shen Weici paid no mind to any of this. She had spent the better part of a month riding in the carriage and had barely rested. Now she felt as though her bones had come apart; one more moment of exertion and she would not hold up. She sank into the armchair by the window and rested a while.

The light outside filtered through the window paper and fell upon her faded pink dress, casting a slender thread of serenity.

That evening, a maid came to relay a message: the Second Lord wished to see Shen Weici.

Shen Weici sat at the table, removed the silver hairpin from her hair, and placed it in a small box.

Yuedeng stood beside her and said quietly: "The Second Lord has returned and wishes to see you — would it not be too plain to go like this?"

Shen Weici looked at herself in the bronze mirror. The pale, tired face looking back at her gave a small shake of her head: "Plainer is better."

She added softly: "Also bring the boots I made."

Yuedeng immediately turned and rummaged through the bundle for the boots.

Shen Weici lowered her head and looked at the boots in her hands, stroking them gently for a moment before saying: "Let us go."

Yuedeng suddenly called out: "Miss, wait."

She held out a piece of jade and placed it in the open box on the table, then turned to Shen Weici with a smile: "Miss, this looks to be worth quite a bit of silver. When I was picking up your hairpin earlier, I quietly picked this up as well."

"We can keep it hidden in the box for now. Later I will find an excuse to leave the Manor and pawn it, so you will have some silver to spare."

"He threw it away and did not want it, so I picked it up to make use of something that would otherwise go to waste."

Yuedeng was genuinely thinking entirely of Shen Weici. This trip to the capital had spent every last coin of their travel money — not a copper remained. There were bound to be things to pay for within the Manor, and they could not go without any silver at all.

Besides, someone had thrown it away. Picking it up hardly seemed like anything wrong.

Shen Weici frowned at the contents of the box: a fine white jade qilin pendant — and it belonged to the man from that morning.

She knew Yuedeng meant no harm, but keeping this object would only invite trouble.

Moreover, no matter how impoverished she was, she drew the line at picking up what others had discarded.

She silently took the jade pendant from the box and held it in her palm, then looked at Yuedeng: "We cannot keep this. I will take it and throw it away later."

"Neither of us is familiar with the capital, and we do not know the relationships within this Manor. How could we leave the compound? And if someone were to see? Even if he threw it away himself, it was used to humiliate me — if I were to keep it, I would be truly inviting contempt."

"The temperaments of the other maids in this courtyard are something I have yet to gauge. We should be careful not to give anyone a handle against us."

Shen Weici tucked the pendant into her sleeve, then gave Yuedeng a look: "I will throw this away later. Do not mention it again."

She spoke, then lifted the curtain and walked out with Yuedeng.

The maid who had come to deliver the message was still waiting at the door. Seeing Shen Weici emerge, she seemed to feel she had taken too long — though she said nothing, she furrowed her brow and led the way ahead.

The maid brought them to a quiet little courtyard, then said: "This is the Listening Bamboo Study — the Second Lord's private library. Go in on your own."

Shen Weici looked inside and saw lamplight glowing in one room, with the faint shadow of a person within. She told Yuedeng to wait at the courtyard gate, then carried the boots inside.

Inside the courtyard, Shen Weici stood before the lit doorway and called out respectfully: "Father."

After a moment, a low, steady voice came from within: "Come in."

She pushed open the door before her, took a deep breath, and stepped inside with her head lowered.

The door was closed by a maid behind her. Shen Weici saw before her a tall, imposing back, which turned to face her at the sound of the door opening.

This was the first time Shen Weici had ever laid eyes on her father. Her mother had never spoken of him.

Though he was now in his middle years, he carried a refined and cultivated air — traces of handsome features from his youth still discernible.

She steadied the anxiety rising within her, set the boots down beside her feet, kept her gaze lowered, and gave her father a proper, obedient curtsey.

Shen Rongshen stood with his hands clasped behind his back, regarding the daughter standing before him. She was quietly still with her head lowered, yet at a single glance one could tell she was a great beauty in the making.

Seeing the old, plain clothing she wore, not a single jewel or pin upon her head, not a trace of rouge or powder on her face — he could not help but sigh.

Had it not been for Shen Weici's mother sending him a letter out of nowhere, he might nearly have forgotten the old debt of passion he had left behind.

chapters.title: Seeking a Proper Match
chapters.content:
Years ago, he had still been in the Hanlin Academy when he was sent by the Emperor to serve as Educational Commissioner in Jinzhou for three years. During his first year there, while making an inspection tour of the local education officials, his carriage had startled a young woman. At that moment he had been struck as if by divine revelation, marveling inwardly that such a beauty could be found in so small a place.

He had entertained certain thoughts, and under the guise of care and attention, having learned that she was merely an embroidery-woman, he had wooed her with tender sweetness until she followed him.

He had wanted only a gentle haven to ease his loneliness during his three years in Jinzhou — yet by the time he left, he had genuinely grown two parts truly fond of her.

However, he had already married his childhood sweetheart at home, and had made her a promise: there would only be one wife, and even taking a concubine would require her consent.

He dared not bring her home and cause chaos in the household, so he left her a sufficient sum of silver and departed without a word of farewell.

A decade and more passed. She had clearly known her own position, and had never come looking for him.

Then came that letter — written at the moment of death, entrusting their daughter to him. Reading it again, Shen Rongshen was brought back to the tenderness of those old days. On a rare occasion he held firm, quarreling with his wife for half a month, insisting on bringing his daughter home.

He was moved, and sighed softly: "Weici..."

The name brought a sudden sting to his throat. He recalled that the name had been given by him; when he had left, Shen Weici had been barely a year old.

Shen Weici raised her head, tears brimming in her eyes: "Father."

Only then did Shen Rongshen take in the beauty of the face before him — startlingly lovely — and seeing the tears in her eyes, he could not help but ask: "How did your mother fall ill and pass away?"

Shen Weici dabbed at her tears with a handkerchief, but could not stop them from streaming down, and choked out: "Mother took the silver Father left behind and brought me to Yuyang, raising me alone. But later the silver and the house were taken over by my uncle and grandmother. To earn money for the household, Mother worked on embroidery day and night without rest. Working so late into the night, her health declined over time, and eventually she fell ill..."

"Even the physicians could not help..."

The rest of the words died in Shen Weici's throat, as though the grief had made it impossible for her to continue.

Shen Rongshen was overcome with emotion and murmured: "She never remarried, and this is how she went..."

Shen Weici looked up at Shen Rongshen, her eyes red-rimmed: "Before Mother passed, she told me to listen to Father in all things from now on, and said that if Father was in any difficulty, I should show understanding and not add to his troubles."

She opened her mouth carefully, her voice hoarse: "Has Weici added to Father's troubles?"

As Shen Weici lifted her face, that countenance stirred memories in Shen Rongshen — two parts resembling her mother, yet more vividly beautiful. And he noticed the tiny black mole at the corner of her eye, just as he had once remarked when cradling the newborn Shen Weici: that mole had fallen beautifully.

This was unmistakably his own daughter.

A tide of emotion swept through him. He stepped forward, looked at the tears in his daughter's eyes, and guilt welled up in full. He said quietly: "You are my daughter. Bringing you home — how could that add to my troubles?"

"From now on, live here in the Marquis Manor without worry. Whatever Zhaozhao has, I will see to it that someone brings it to you as well."

"You shall not go on wearing these old clothes, and you shall not be left so plainly adorned."

"Your appearance surpasses even your mother's — dressed up properly, you will be every bit a daughter of this Marquis Manor."

Shen Weici gently lowered her head, and with tears clouding her eyes, spoke in a faint, husky voice: "Weici would not dare compare herself to Elder Sister. It is enough simply to have a place to belong."

"After Mother died, my uncle moved in and seized the house, and then intended to sell me to the county magistrate as a concubine. Only then did I have no choice but to come and seek Father's shelter. Father has already taken me in — I cannot dare ask him for more love and care."

"I only ask that Father show Weici some compassion, and help find a suitable marriage for her. I do not seek wealth or prestige — only a person of decent character from a plain household will do. Then I will leave the Manor early and spare Father from having to make things work on two fronts."

In truth, by asking the maids in the half day since her arrival, Shen Weici had already learned that her father almost never intervened in the inner household, deferring in all things to the Second Lady; there was not a single concubine in the inner quarters, which showed how little say her father had there.

Her words expressed that she understood her father's difficulty — and it was genuinely true that she did not wish to remain here.

At this moment her father still harbored some guilt toward her, but with time, that guilt would erode away.

And judging by the Second Lady's attitude in the main hall today, she would certainly never be able to tolerate her presence in future. With her father unable to hold sway, the longer she stayed, the more resentment she would accumulate, until she was left entirely at the Second Lady's disposal — who might marry her off to anyone she chose, with her father not lifting a finger to speak for her.

While she could still draw upon her father's sense of lingering old feeling and guilt, settling herself into a good household now was the best plan Shen Weici could devise for herself.

Shen Rongshen heard these sensible words from Shen Weici and felt a pang of tenderness.

His other daughter, Zhaozhao, had grown up from infancy in silks and finery, waited on by crowds of servants, surrounded by admiring attention all her life — yet this daughter before him was dressed in such coarse clothing, not a single ornament on her body, and yet this poised and gentle.

He gave his word at once: "You need not worry about your marriage. Though you are not my legitimate daughter, finding you a good match is not beyond my means."

"I will choose carefully for you — consider it my way of making amends."

Shen Weici was moved to tears, lifting her face to look at Shen Rongshen with a soft voice: "Before Mother passed, she said Father would care for me — and that Father had no choice but to leave back then. I grew up without a father, and I thought that if I could only see him once, I would be content."

"Today I have finally seen Father at last. Weici's heart is moved, and there is nothing left to regret."

As she spoke, Shen Weici picked up the boots from beside her feet and offered them to Shen Rongshen, her teary eyes holding a look of reverence and careful deference: "These are boots Weici made for Father in Yuyang. I did not know your size, Father, so Mother told me."

"Please try them when you get home. If they do not fit, Weici will make another pair — consider it a small token of filial devotion from your daughter."

Not even his own wife had ever made him a pair of boots. Yet this daughter, reunited with him after more than a decade apart, had had the thoughtfulness to make boots for him.

This child was so sensible and gentle — Shen Rongshen felt a deepening tenderness in his heart. He reached out to take the boots from Shen Weici's hands, and his eyes actually grew warm. Looking at her tearful gaze, he seemed, in a blur, to see the woman of those days who had looked upon him with such devoted affection.

With her beauty, had she not followed him, she could surely have married into a fine family.

In the end it had been he who had let her down. She had never remarried, had raised their daughter alone, had remembered even the size of his boots...

And he, all these years, had never once thought of her — had even forgotten about their daughter.

Consumed with guilt, Shen Rongshen looked down at Shen Weici and said: "From now on, if you are in any difficulty at the Manor, do not go to your stepmother — come here and find me instead."

Shen Weici looked at the expression on Shen Rongshen's face, and a look of heartfelt gratitude spread across hers. With moist eyes still glistening, she said softly: "Thank you, Father."

Shen Rongshen nodded and sighed once more.

chapters.title: What Does Young Lord Song Want?
chapters.content:
Coming out of the Listening Bamboo Study, Yuedeng saw Shen Weici's reddened eyes — clearly she had been crying — and immediately asked anxiously: "Miss, what happened?"

Shen Weici shook her head and walked on ahead with Yuedeng, lantern in hand.

The tears she had shed inside had been performed for her father's benefit — to win some measure of his care and attention, and to have him find her a stable, proper match. That was all.

She had arrived only today, but she already knew she was far from welcome in the Marquis Manor. She held little feeling for this father of hers, yet for now he was all she had to rely on.

Stepping out into the cool, deep autumn air, she lifted her face to look at the moonlight. Her old clothes stirred faintly in the breeze, and her eyes held a vague, drifting sorrow.

Was it worth it — this person her mother had longed for?

Yuedeng walked alongside her and asked curiously: "What did the Lord say? Does he miss you, Miss?"

Shen Weici was quiet. Her father's face in there had carried the look of a caring parent, and she did not know whether those promises were real or not. She had wept herself rather tired just now. She gave her head a small shake and said softly: "Let us talk when we are back."

Then she turned to Yuedeng: "First let us go throw that thing away."

Yuedeng understood what the "thing" was. Though she felt it was a shame, she still asked: "Where shall we throw it?"

Shen Weici replied gently: "Just follow me."

On her way to her father's earlier, she had noticed a pond and rockery garden in the back compound, not far from the path — and she had made a note of its location.

She had by now formed a rough understanding of the people in the Marquis Manor. The young woman who had mocked her that morning was the one who had stood behind the Second Lady in the main hall — she must be the Zhaozhao her father had mentioned this evening.

She had heard that Zhaozhao address the sword-wielding man as "Brother Song," and she had made a specific inquiry: he was the Young Lord of the Song Ducal Manor. Given that, the pendant could not simply be thrown anywhere — if a maid were to pick it up later and make something of it, that would be trouble. The best place was into the pond. Even if someone were to find it afterward, suspicion would not fall on her.

Shen Weici led Yuedeng toward the pond at the back garden. It was dark now, and the hour was late — with no one on the paths, the timing was perfect.

The water in the pond was pitch-black, lit only by the moonlight and the dim glow of their lantern.

Shen Weici glanced around to be sure no one was nearby, then drew the jade pendant from her sleeve. She was just about to throw it into the pond when a sudden bark rang out, and a half-man-tall wolf hound, black all over, came bounding toward her and leapt upon her.

She had been standing right at the water's edge. The great black dog's lunge knocked her off balance — and to the sound of Yuedeng's startled cry — Shen Weici felt a rush of cold water close over her as her body plunged into the pond.

Yuedeng tried to reach down into the water and pull Shen Weici out, but the great black dog turned on her with bared fangs, frightening her into sitting down hard on the bank.

Shen Weici flailed in the water and managed to seize the bank's edge. Fortunately the pond was shallow — the water only reached her waist. With a face gone deathly pale, she gripped the weeds at the edge of the bank and looked at the dog snarling ferociously at her, her eyes stinging with tears that she refused to let fall, her whole body trembling with cold.

The water in late autumn was bitterly cold. Her teeth were chattering, yet she quietly said to Yuedeng: "This dog is dangerous — stay back for now. Hurry and fetch the housekeeper. Let us see where it came from."

Yuedeng nodded frantically and was just about to scramble up and run when the wolf hound suddenly made as if to lunge at her, and she did not dare move a single step.

Just then, a languid voice called out: "Cangyu, come."

Shen Weici looked in the direction of the voice and saw a figure in blue emerge from the shadows.

The man's eyes still held their careless, provocative glint — his red lips, jade-white face, phoenix eyes — supremely noble and arrogant.

Shen Weici watched as the great black wolf hound obediently trotted to its master's side at the sound of his voice, the sharp fangs and ferocious eyes vanishing as it became a docile and gentle creature walking at its master's feet.

She then looked up at the man who now stood at the water's edge, gazing down at her.

She could see clearly the contempt and coldness in the man's eyes, tinged with a cold-blooded mockery — utterly indifferent to the fact that his dog had knocked her into the water.

Or perhaps it had been intentional all along.

She thought of the words he had said that morning: the account was not finished.

Simply because her status was too low for his regard — she had to bear this gratuitous malice.

The knuckles of the fingers gripping the weeds had gone white. She refused to show any weakness before this man, refused to give him the satisfaction of watching her break.

She raised her water-drenched face and called: "Young Lord Song."

Song Zhang raised an eyebrow. In the moonlight, the woman in the water looked as though bathed in a layer of lunar radiance — her skin paler still, damp strands of hair clinging to her cheeks, throwing the tiny black mole at the corner of her peach-blossom eyes into sharp relief. She was devastatingly, bewilderingly beautiful.

Those eyes were clearly awash with light and moisture, their rims red, as if tears might fall in the next instant — yet not a single one fell.
