He crouched down at his leisure to meet Shen Weici's eyes, his fingers cupping her ice-cold chin. He felt the faint trembling of her body.

His gaze lingered on the curves shifting beneath the water, and on the parted neckline of her clothing, beneath which the white underdress revealed glimpses of smooth, pale skin.

Her delicate bones were perfectly proportioned, draped in a snowy hue — and it momentarily clouded his mind.

His lips curved with a cruel edge. Looking into those eyes that seemed innocent and pitiful, he said softly: "Something worn on my person — Cangyu can smell it from a hundred paces away. Who gave you the nerve to steal what I had discarded?"

Shen Weici met the gaze of those phoenix eyes. Her expression was blank, but her voice was light: "If Young Lord Song had discarded it, how does it constitute theft?"

She opened her palm before the man's eyes, showing the pendant lying in it: "It was wrong of my maid to pick it up — but my intention was also to return it to Young Lord Song."

Song Zhang looked at that slender, fair, perfectly formed hand before him — the fine, soft skin completely unlike what he had imagined.

A contemptuous smile touched his face: "Something you have already handled — do you think I would still want it?"

Shen Weici paused. Her damp lashes concealed a delicate storm in her eyes. She suppressed the humiliation and asked the man before her: "Then what does Young Lord Song want?"

Song Zhang listened to Shen Weici's voice — gentle and meek as though she had no temper at all. He smiled thinly: "Touching something of mine naturally calls for punishment. Stay in the water for a full half-hour, then you may leave. How does that sound?"

These words rang in Shen Weici's ears with a particular irony. She pushed away the fingers at her chin, and her voice — though husky — remained soft and obedient: "Very well."

Song Zhang looked down at the figure before him, whose eyes were cast downward — water droplets still trailing from her hair, sliding across her smooth jaw, gathering at her chin and trembling there, neither falling nor not falling.

Not the slightest intention of begging for mercy.

Not the slightest show of temper.

Even the slight tilt of her head, her pale eyes not lifting toward him again.

He found her, quite suddenly, rather interesting.

Even from their encounter that very morning, those eyes had held not a trace of cringing or fawning.

He straightened up and patted the head of Cangyu beside him: "Stay here and watch carefully. If she dares to run, bite her throat."

Then he turned to a manservant behind him and ordered: "Keep a close watch. After a quarter-hour, take Cangyu back to the kennel."

The manservant shot Shen Weici a gleeful look and quickly agreed.

Shen Weici's face went a shade paler. She knew those words were meant for her ears. Her fingers dug into the mud at the pond's edge, her teeth clenched tight, and she did not make a single sound.

Song Zhang took one last look at Shen Weici — motionless in the water — and felt, for a passing moment, that he had been rather cruel.

The thought made even him find himself vaguely ridiculous.

chapters.title: Bullying
chapters.content:
When Shen Weici returned, she was drenched from head to toe. Yuedeng frantically called for maids to heat water, then helped Shen Weici strip off her wet clothing and led her to soak in the hot bath.

In the swirling steam, Shen Weici lay face-down over the edge of the bathtub, her gaze lost upon the water's surface. Hot vapor drifted into her eyes, and tears fell one by one into the water.

Behind her came the sound of Yuedeng's choked, anguished voice: "It is my fault, Miss."

"But that man is truly too cruel! Miss should go to the Second Lord tomorrow — how can anyone bully someone like this?"

"Miss already has a cold ailment, and the water was so freezing — even a grown man could not endure it that long."

Yet when her words fell away and a long silence followed, Yuedeng turned to look — and found Shen Weici's face an alarming shade of white in the steam.

She gave a start and called again: "Miss."

After a long moment, a hoarse voice finally came: "I am all right."

Then, with exhaustion: "We have only just arrived at the Manor. Do not stir up trouble. And the jade really was something we had taken — let it be..."

Yuedeng's throat tightened. She looked into Shen Weici's weary, reddened eyes, bit the corners of her lips, and lowered her head to cry silently.

Dressed in clean white garments, Shen Weici lay on her side, her moon-white clothes against ink-black hair, her eyes half-closed as if adrift between mountains and sky. Beneath the elegant line of her nose, her lips were flushed red, and an unnatural crimson bloom spread across her cheeks.

She lay with her eyes shut, enduring the clammy chill of cold sweats, curling her body inward, fingers covering her knees — seeking what little warmth might ease the ache that had settled there.

Yuedeng sat at the bedside and wiped Shen Weici's damp hair, weeping as she spoke: "Ever since that night Miss knelt in the snow as a young child, she has had trouble in her legs — they ache in rain and snow. And today she fell into that cold water again. I do not know if it will get worse."

Shen Weici slowly exhaled a long breath of burning heat, letting her voice fall with reassurance: "It will be all right."

She was dizzy, her thoughts drifting. The past surfaced before her eyes, one image at a time.

She remembered that snowy night.

She had been eleven, on a heavy snow night. Her mother had vomited blood and fainted at night, and she had gone to her grandmother to beg for silver to send for a physician — but the cold response from inside was to wait until morning.

She had knelt outside in the snow the entire night. She had wept and kowtowed, but could not make her grandmother open the door. The east wing where her uncle lived had never opened its door either, from beginning to end.

That night, she had looked up at the vast, bleak whiteness of the snow, taken in this courtyard that had once felt warm and harmonious, gazed at the warm glow of charcoal fires burning in the main room and the east wing — while the west wing where they lived had been given only broken, crumbled coal fragments. In a single night, she came to understand the coldness of the human heart.

What family was there? Outside of her mother, she had no family.

Yuedeng looked down at Shen Weici's pale sleeping face, and thought of how the young mistress had once lived the life of a proper young lady — with schooling and people to look after her — only to be reduced to this state when her uncle seized the family's money and property.

Had her mother not died, why would she have had to come here and suffer this indignity?

Even if they had lacked great wealth or prestige, she would not have had to lower her head like this at every turn.

Yuedeng's heart burned with indignation, but she held her tongue. Looking at the half-dried strands of hair in her hands, she called for a maid outside to bring another dry cloth.

But when she called the maid's name four or five times and received no response from outside, she set down the hair and walked out — only to find two maids sitting on the doorstep cracking melon seeds and chatting.

She walked over and frowned: "Did you not hear the call from inside?"

One of the maids glanced at Yuedeng, then languidly cracked another seed: "Maids are people too. We've been cleaning this courtyard all day — and now we're expected to keep night watch on top of that?"

"In any other courtyard, after a whole day of sweeping, they'd at least get a few silver melon seeds or silver beans as a reward. But we got nothing — not even a word. And now we're being ordered around till this late hour. Do they think we're not human?"

She gave a cold snort and muttered in the direction of the other maid: "Who knows — maybe she wasn't any better off than us before."

"And now that she's playing the role of a young miss, she's already giving orders."

The low mutter was not quite inaudible. Yuedeng had not caught the words, but she had seen the two maids exchange a glance and laugh. She immediately stepped forward and pointed at them, her face flushing with anger: "What did you just say?!"

The maid looked at Yuedeng with contempt: "Mind your own business."

Yuedeng was furious enough to leap forward, had already rolled up her sleeve to teach them a lesson — when a low, hoarse voice came from behind her: "Yuedeng, let it be."

Yuedeng started, spun around, and found Shen Weici stepping out from behind the curtain, wrapped in a pink outer robe.

The two maids on the doorstep also froze and looked up at Shen Weici.

Her black hair was still slightly damp, lying loose and soft against her shoulders, with a few strands falling across her cheeks.

And her fair skin was flushed a rosy crimson, her eyes bright and watery. Plain and simple in the morning light, she now looked, with that flush of color, utterly, almost dangerously lovely.

The two maids stared, a little dazed. They thought she truly looked like someone who had come out of the moonlit river — even lovelier than the Second Young Miss.

Shen Weici walked to stand before the two maids. She steadied herself against the lightheadedness and the ache in her body, pressed her pale fingers against the flower stand beside her, drew a quiet breath, and said softly: "I have nothing with which to give you a reward. I know it has been an inconvenience to be sent to my courtyard."

"This Linchun Courtyard has been quiet and secluded for a long time. I understand I cannot compare to the mistresses of the other main courtyards, who can casually give gifts and rewards to their maids. I do not blame you for being lax, and I understand that every maid wants a good mistress to serve."

Yuedeng, hearing these words, hurried to Shen Weici's side: "Miss..."

Shen Weici's gaze remained on the two maids: "I will not make things difficult for you. If you stay, I will treat you with sincerity. If you have somewhere else to go, feel free to seek another position elsewhere. If the housekeeper asks, I will naturally say I agreed to it."

With that, Shen Weici released her fingers from the stand and turned to go back behind the curtain.

Yuedeng followed close behind Shen Weici with an astonished expression, watching as her young mistress settled back against the bed. The sweat standing out on her brow made Yuedeng burst out: "Why should Miss bother about what they think? They were sent here to serve — there is no need to show them a kind face."

Shen Weici turned to look at Yuedeng, rubbing her aching temples with a tired sigh: "Do you think if they had good prospects, they would have been sent to me?"

"On my way back from Father's just now, I took a careful look at the layout of this courtyard. It is in the most secluded corner of the West Back compound — all the good courtyards are in the East compound. The only small courtyard around here is mine, and the paths to it are all overgrown and long untended. It is clearly a spot that rarely sees visitors."

"Would the maids not know what sort of place this is? If they were summoned here, it means they have no backing or connections."

"I noticed just now that their hands are broad and coarse — much thicker than those of ordinary women. Clearly they have been doing rough labor before. Even if I sent them away, they would either go back to rough labor, or find no other courtyard willing to take them. They will have to stay with me."

"Since they have to stay, let them stay with peace of mind and no other ideas. I will not be cruel to them."

"And if they still insist on leaving — that is also fine. It saves the trouble of having people who are fickle and resentful cluttering up the courtyard."

Yuedeng nodded at that: "Miss always thinks things through."

Then, with worry, she used a cloth to dab the sweat from Shen Weici's forehead: "Miss — have you caught a chill?"

"Shall I go to the Second Lord and ask him to send a physician?"

Shen Weici rubbed her temples and sighed: "In the old days when I caught a chill at Grandmother's and there was no silver for medicine, did I not recover all the same? Wait until tomorrow."

And she was already too exhausted to keep her eyes open: "Tomorrow morning I still need to go pay respects to my stepmother. Let us rest now."

With that she turned on her side, and her eyes closed with the weight of fatigue.

chapters.title: Not Calling for Help This Time?
chapters.content:
The next morning, Shen Weici rose early. Behind the partition screen, two maids were already waiting with warm water.

It seemed they had made their decision overnight. Shen Weici asked no questions and went to wash up.

Yuedeng brought out a half-new, half-worn moon-white crossed-collar padded jacket: "Miss has only brought two changes of clothes. I wonder if this Manor will have any made for you."

"With winter coming on, shall we ask the Second Lady?"

Shen Weici steadied herself through her aching body and went to put it on, looking down as Yuedeng fastened the sash at her waist: "We have come to seek shelter here — not to hold out our hands and demand things."

"Two changes of clothing were enough to get by in Yuyang, and they will be enough here in the Manor as well."

Yuedeng's hands stilled. She looked up at Shen Weici: "But Miss is different now. Yuyang is nothing but a remote, backwater county — many people there can only wrap themselves in paper to get through the winter."

"Yesterday I saw the fabric on Second Young Miss's clothes — the style and the patterns, so refined and exquisite. I had never seen such a beautiful garment before. I cannot even say what fabric it was."

"Now Miss is also the Third Young Miss of Jian'an Marquis Manor in the capital. With a different standing, why should she not wear fine cloth?"

Shen Weici met Yuedeng's eyes: "Setting aside the fact that my standing in this Manor cannot compare to Shen Zhaozhao's — simply put, I came here as a dependent, and I am not welcome. If I were to compare myself to the Manor's legitimate daughter at every turn and covet a few sets of clothing, it would only invite people to look down on me, and it would disgrace the upbringing my mother gave me."

Yuedeng, hearing Shen Weici say so, said no more and returned to her tasks.

At the dressing table, after combing her hair, Yuedeng brought out a small box. Nearly all the compartments were empty — only two silver hairpins, a pair of jadeite earrings whose color was not particularly good, and nothing else.

In truth, Shen Weici had once owned a set of silver hair ornaments and an agate hairpin, but they had been taken by her grandmother afterward, leaving only these two worthless silver pins.

Yuedeng put the earrings on for Shen Weici, then inserted a silver hairpin at a slant into her hair. The preparations were complete.

Shen Weici was by nature somewhat provocatively beautiful — her slightly upturned eye corners and cherry lips, her skin fine and white beneath no powder or rouge — giving her, even in simple dress, a faint and fragile gentleness.

Shen Weici did not linger before the bronze mirror. She checked the sky, asked for the hour, then took up a lantern and set out from the courtyard.

This was her first time coming here, and she did not know where the Second Lady's courtyard was, so she had a maid lead the way.

The autumn chill crept down the collar, making her already-uncomfortable back, damp with a thin sweat, go cold again. She could not help but cough once.

Passing through the side gate into the East compound, all she could hear in the dark was the rustle of wind.

Along the way, the leading maid explained that the East compound housed the First and Second Branches, and the Old Madam resided in the West Small Compound; the Third Branch was adjacent to the East Main Compound. Shen Weici listened attentively and quietly memorized the route.

The East compound was vast. Though both the First and Second Branches lived there, one could see from the garden shadows that the pavilions and terraces were not crowded but spread out in an extraordinary expanse.

Only now, after so long a walk, did she realize how secluded her own courtyard truly was. She had been installed somewhere far removed — clearly reflecting how little she was welcome.

She kept her eyes to the ground as she walked, yet caught sight of lantern light approaching. She looked carefully: four or five servants followed behind someone, lanterns held to the left and right, the procession bearing a certain air of importance.

When she looked again and recognized the face of the person walking in the center, she stiffened — then quietly pulled her sleeves together, composing herself with perfect calm, and stepped to one side to make way, eyes respectfully downcast.

Song Zhang passed by Shen Weici, glancing down at her as he went. In the warm orange-yellow lantern glow, her face seemed to carry a faint otherworldly air — yet she remained forever without spirit, cautious and self-effacing.

A strand of hair, stirred by the breeze, lifted against her face. Her complexion was a shade too pale.

He had heard her cough faintly from a distance earlier, and thought of what his servant had reported last night: that she had stood without a word in the cold water for a full half-hour, and when she finally left, she could barely stand.

The jade pendant had also been returned to him by his servant afterward. It seemed to carry the scent of her on it — a faint fragrance of magnolia. He had intended to discard it, but the memory of her quiet, still eyes — not a word of protest, yet carrying a certain resilience — had stayed his hand, and it now sat on his desk.

He looked again at the half-new, half-worn moon-white garment on her — old-fashioned in cut and crude in embroidery — and yet it did not look ill on her. He simply had not expected the Second Branch to have sent no decent clothing at all.

That faint fragrance drifted past once more. It was impossible to name — unlike the perfumes the women of the capital preferred. It was something more like a wildflower from the hills, brushed by a passing wind.

As the two of them drew level and passed each other, Song Zhang could not help glancing at her again. Her haggard features were nonetheless richly lovely, and her bearing seemed deliberately distant from him — eyes forever downcast as if she had not noticed him at all. Something inexplicably stirred in him.

He halted in front of her, with a slightly mocking air, and asked: "Not calling for help this time?"

Shen Weici had only wanted to pass this man by quickly and have no further dealings with him. She had not expected him to ask this of her, and though she had little desire to engage, she answered with the intention of not creating more trouble: "Young Lord Song."

Those words — faintly husky, slightly stiff and distant — came with eyes that never once lifted toward him.

As if she were avoiding him at great pains.

Song Zhang had never in his life been so thoroughly ignored by anyone. A flash of displeasure rose in him, followed by a strange arrest of his expression. His face gradually darkened.

He had been displeased by her coolness — and had deliberately slowed his pace for her.

Song Zhang looked down once more at the person in front of him, eyes meekly downcast. In the dim candlelight, warm shadows played over those lowered dark brows, like the gentle rippling of a calm lake.

With a darkened expression, he lifted his foot and walked on.

Shen Weici did not stir, waiting until Song Zhang had passed before moving again.

Yuedeng, relieved to see that Song Zhang had gone straight past without troubling her young mistress, exhaled a long breath. Once the procession had moved far enough away, she hurried over to ask the leading maid: "Was the person who just passed not the Young Lord of the Song Ducal Manor? Why is he also living in the Marquis Manor?"

The maid replied: "That is not only the Young Lord of the Song Ducal Manor — he is also the Second Young Master of the Marquis Manor's First Branch, and moreover the Commander of the Left and Right Feathered Guards. His standing is most exalted."

Yuedeng puzzled: "How can he be the First Branch's Second Young Master as well?"

The maid gave a little laugh: "It is a long story — I will tell you later when there is time."

Yuedeng drew out a long sound of understanding and glanced back at Song Zhang once more.

No wonder that person always had a sword at his waist and kept such a massive dog. He was terrifying.

Arriving at the Second Lady's courtyard, the rooms within were already fully lit. Heavy curtains hung outside the main chamber, with a matron stationed at the entrance. Seeing Shen Weici approach, she looked her over with her chin raised.

Taking in the half-worn clothing, the style unlike anything worn in the capital, and the jadeite earrings — worse than those of the First Lady's senior maids — the contempt in her eyes deepened.

She spoke in a languorous tone: "Third Young Miss, please wait a moment. Allow this old servant to have someone go in and announce you."

With that, the matron pointed to a maid and had her go inside.

Yuedeng, watching the matron's imperious manner, silently resented it on her young mistress's behalf.

Inside, Shen Rongshen was bent over, kneading Lady Wen's shoulders, placating her: "My lady, Weici is a pitiful child. I have not been there for her all these years — please be kind to her."

Lady Wen cast Shen Rongshen a sideways glance, leaned back in her armchair, and gave a cold snort: "When you married me, you said I was the only one you loved. And then you went off as Educational Commissioner and took up with a low woman. I never even settled that account with you, and now you dare say such things to me — do you think I have been unkind to her?"

"Shen Rongshen, that is something you owe me. I remember every word of that old vow."

Shen Rongshen hurriedly bent to take Lady Wen's hand: "I was blindsided back then, bewitched by that woman — otherwise I would never have done such a thing."

He watched Lady Wen's expression carefully: "But she is still my blood and flesh. Her mother has died, and she is adrift outside with nowhere to go — it is a pitiable situation. You are gracious and magnanimous, my lady. Simply give her a place to stay — that is all I ask."

Lady Wen smiled and looked at Shen Rongshen: "Seeing as that woman who died had too little nerve to come looking for you herself, I will let her daughter be. You need not worry."

Shen Rongshen let out a breath of relief, then leaned in to press a kiss to Lady Wen's cheek.

Outside, Shen Weici endured the cold wind, her fingers already frozen stiff.

From behind, a rush of fragrance swept in, followed by a bright and vivid voice: "Matron Tan, is my mother awake yet?"

Matron Tan transformed, a smile springing instantly to her face — nothing like the coldness she had shown Shen Weici: "The Lady is up, Third Young Master, Second Young Miss — please go in quickly and get out of the wind."

Shen Weici looked back and saw a young man and a young woman walking over side by side, both smiling.

They wore cloaks of scattered golden medallions on clustered flowers, their robes of richly lustrous brocade. Several servants followed in their wake. They strolled to the doorway, needing no announcement at all — the maids on either side automatically lifted the curtain to let them through.

chapters.title: Morning Greetings
chapters.content:
Shen Yanli, walking behind Shen Zhaozhao, glanced curiously at Shen Weici standing beside the main entrance and could not help asking Matron Tan: "Is this a new maid Mother bought? She looks rather lovely."

He leaned closer and studied her a moment more, and the more he looked, the more startling her beauty — he clicked his tongue approvingly: "Truly a fine appearance. A maid is something of a waste for someone like this."

The already-entered Shen Zhaozhao turned back to look at her elder brother and pulled at his sleeve, not bothering to lower her voice as she sneered: "Is she not just a maid in her destiny? Her mother was a fox-spirit, and she carries the same foul stench. Brother should not stand too close — you might catch it."

Shen Yanli understood at that and glanced back at Shen Weici: "So she is that country girl who came to throw herself on the family?"

Shen Zhaozhao pulled Shen Yanli inside: "Who else would come around at this hour to make people's day worse?"

Shen Rongshen, coming out from inside, heard Shen Zhaozhao's words just in time and immediately turned cold-faced: "Zhaozhao, do not speak of your sister that way."

Shen Zhaozhao had never before been reprimanded by her father, who had always been warm and indulgent toward her. Hearing his cold rebuke now, she ran over and threw herself into the arms of Lady Wen, who had followed Shen Rongshen out, weeping in aggrievement: "Mother, Father is scolding me because of that base woman."

Shen Rongshen sat in the principal seat and frowned at Shen Zhaozhao's words, then reproached her: "Where is this manner of speaking from a young lady? Your lessons at the clan school have been wasted, it seems."

Lady Wen comforted Shen Zhaozhao while glancing at Shen Rongshen: "Zhaozhao has always spoken her mind — you know that. And we are not outside. What is there for you to be displeased about?"

"How can someone born of a base woman not be called base? A person appears from nowhere, and Zhaozhao is unwilling too, is she not?"

Shen Rongshen gave a long sigh at Lady Wen: "The form of address is after all improper. Saying such things in private I will not press, but if overheard outside, people will say the daughters of the Marquis Manor are lacking in refinement — take care of that in the future."

Lady Wen looked at Shen Rongshen: "Is there anyone outside who does not praise Zhaozhao?"

Shen Rongshen sighed again and rose: "I must go to court. That is enough."

Shen Weici was still standing outside the curtain, listening to the conversation within. Her expression did not change, yet her fingers had dug into her own flesh.

Only after Shen Rongshen emerged did he remember Shen Weici still waiting outside. Seeing her cheeks flushed from the cold wind and her body in those old clothes, his guilt rose again. He glanced at the curtain, and quietly said to her: "Do not take Zhaozhao's words to heart. She was spoiled from a young age — she does not mean any real harm."

"Go inside in a little while and defer to your stepmother in all things. She will not make things overly difficult for you."

Shen Weici nodded obediently, then lifted her face to look at Shen Rongshen and said sensibly: "Father need not worry about me. I understand, daughter knows what to do."

"The morning is cold and the path is dark, Father — please take care on the road."

Shen Rongshen found that even his daughter, whom he barely knew, was showing concern for him. He sighed heavily, nodded, then quietly said to her: "I will keep your matter in mind. Endure a little while longer."

With that, he told Matron Tan at the door to lift the curtain and let Shen Weici inside, then departed.

Shen Rongshen did have a measure of compassion for this daughter who had come to him. Her looks were fine, and he could see that her life in the Manor going forward would not be easy. He wanted to find her a good match as soon as possible — to avoid further quarrels with his wife, and to spare the child further suffering.

Hearing her father's words, Matron Tan finally lifted the curtain and said to Shen Weici: "Third Young Miss, go in please."

Shen Weici gathered her sleeves and stepped over the threshold with her head lowered.

The moment she entered, a wave of warmth hit her. She glanced sideways to one corner — a charcoal brazier was burning there, which was why it was so warm.

The sudden warmth meeting the chill still clinging to her sent color flooding up into her pallid cheeks. She lowered her head and gave Lady Wen a proper curtsey: "Weici pays her respects to the Second Lady."

By custom, Shen Weici should have addressed Lady Wen as "Mother" — but Shen Weici naturally knew the title would be intolerable for Lady Wen to hear, and she herself could not bring herself to say it. This arrangement suited both of them.

Lady Wen was instantly irritated by the sight of Shen Weici's face, but thinking of the Old Madam's words, she kept it in check.

She had not told Shen Rongshen about this matter, for she could see that Shen Rongshen's heart had softened toward this daughter. He was, by nature, a wavering sort — if she told him now, he might not agree and might even quarrel with her. But when the time came, if he refused, he could go argue with the Old Madam himself. Whether he put his career first or this half-way daughter of his, that would be none of her fault.

She set down the teacup on the small side table and looked at the girl standing in the middle with mild indifference: "Go and sit."

Shen Weici glanced at the chairs to one side. On Lady Wen's immediate left and right sat Shen Zhaozhao and Shen Yanli respectively. Going to sit meant sitting beside Shen Zhaozhao — who clearly had no desire to be next to her — so she skipped a seat and sat one chair removed.

Lady Wen gave Shen Weici a brief look, then summoned a nanny to explain the Manor's rules and etiquette.

The nanny stood before Shen Weici with an air of superiority and began to speak in a tone of careless condescension.

She went through the list of rules and then looked at Shen Weici, who sat listening quietly and composedly in her chair: "The Marquis Manor is no ordinary household — deportment and propriety are paramount. Do not go out there and let people say the daughters of the Marquis Manor lack refinement, and do not bring any provincial habits with you. In your daily conduct, watch Second Young Miss more carefully and learn from her example."

Shen Zhaozhao gave a cold sound in Shen Weici's direction: "You had better remember well. If you violate the rules, do not blame my mother for punishing you."

Lady Wen looked at Shen Zhaozhao with mild resignation, then turned to Shen Weici: "Look at you — not a single piece of jewelry on you anywhere, and that silver hairpin is worn out. To go about looking like this as a daughter of the Marquis Manor would be a disgrace."

She looked at Shen Zhaozhao: "Every year you have one or two new sets of hair ornaments made, and you never wear them all. Go back later and pick out a few pieces to send to your Third Sister."

Shen Zhaozhao shot up from her seat at this and glared at her mother: "I would sooner give those to the servants than give them to her. She does not even leave the Manor — who is there to show off to? What face does she even need?"

Lady Wen frowned and spoke low: "This is not the time for your temper. Weici is your Third Sister, and if the other branches see her looking this plain, what will they think of our Second Branch?"

Shen Zhaozhao was about to say more, but caught the rare stern look in her mother's eyes and turned her face away with a discontented sound, saying nothing further.

Lady Wen looked at Shen Weici again: "As for clothing, I will have a seamstress come shortly to take your measurements. It is deep autumn now, and what you have on is rather plain."

Shen Weici slightly bowed her head and said in soft, gentle tones, her face carrying a look of genuine gratitude: "Thank you, Second Lady."

Lady Wen studied Shen Weici's expression. From yesterday until now, she had been quiet and composed, obedient and deferential in her presence. This was satisfying.

Since the girl was here, as long as she remained compliant — and then married off to Zhang Tingyi in due course — she would not trouble her further, lest it create a rift with her husband.

She nodded and continued: "For this month's allowance, have someone go to the stewardship to collect it later. And you need not come so early in the future — autumn and winter nights are long; a little later is perfectly fine."

Shen Weici quietly agreed.

chapters.title: A Fine Figure
chapters.content:
After sitting in Lady Wen's quarters a while longer, Lady Wen dismissed Shen Weici.

Shen Weici rose, gave Lady Wen a respectful and proper curtsey, then gently retreated from the room.

Shen Zhaozhao looked at Shen Weici's old clothing and the plain silver pin in her hair, and said with a cold, contemptuous laugh: "Look at that pauper's appearance. I was truly afraid she might dirty the carpet in here."

"I wonder if she brought any smell from the countryside with her."

Shen Weici heard these words in silence, lifted the curtain, and walked out with her eyes lowered.

Lady Wen looked at the composed expression on Shen Weici's face until she had disappeared from sight, then turned to Shen Zhaozhao: "Your father is not wrong. Say less of this in future and do not forget your grandmother's words."

"She will not be here long. She can never compare to you, and if she misbehaves, I have ways enough to deal with her."

"But if you overdo it too much, your father will rebuke you."

"Besides, your own temperament needs reining in. You are to be married into the Yong'an Marquis Manor next year — you cannot carry on this way."

Shen Zhaozhao burrowed into Lady Wen's embrace and said aggrievedly: "I was just upset on Mother's behalf, that is all. I cannot bear seeing those fox-spirits come in and make trouble for Mother."

Lady Wen smiled and stroked Shen Zhaozhao's hair: "Leave the rest to me and do not trouble yourself. This is no concern of yours. You simply wait contentedly for your marriage."

----

Out in the courtyard, Shen Weici had already emerged. It was just beginning to get light outside — the path no longer needed a lantern.

When she made it back to Linchun Courtyard, Yuedeng finally could not hold back any longer: "They call themselves ladies of a noble family, but no amount of fine hair ornaments can cover up the black hearts beneath. Saying 'base woman' this and 'base woman' that — even Miss has never used such coarse words."

"In my view, this Marquis Manor only looks grand from the outside. Under all that glitter is hollow rot — every one of them rotten to the core inside."

"And those servants know exactly how to fawn on the powerful and trample on the weak. Just a matron — and she dares to look down on Miss? She is a person who waits on others for a living, and she thinks herself the mistress of the house?"

"And that heavy, suffocating perfume on her — I nearly gagged. As if she needs everyone to know she smells fragrant."

Shen Weici sat at the writing table in the inner room, her head throbbing badly. She heard Yuedeng's indignant outpouring as though from a distance and gave a helpless smile, then reached out and took Yuedeng's hand: "I am not angry — and yet it is you who are angry on my behalf."

Unable to help herself, she pressed a cloth to her lips to stifle a few coughs: "Let her say whatever she wishes — it cannot hurt me. My only wish right now is to find a proper and suitable match. Once I have settled that, life will be stable, and I want no more trouble."

Yuedeng still looked resentful: "But she also insulted your mother..."

Shen Weici's fingers tightened then — just slightly — and she looked at Yuedeng: "I know what sort of woman my own mother was. Their words cannot change that. But this is not the moment for me to argue back. Doing so would only do me harm."

Shen Weici's gaze drifted to a spot beyond the window, and she murmured quietly: "Father cannot take my side entirely. If I stir up too much trouble, Father will grow tired of it. Endure these few months, and it will pass."

Just then, a maid announced from beyond the curtain that breakfast was ready. Shen Weici patted Yuedeng's hand and went out.

After eating, Shen Weici had a maid go to the stewardship to collect her monthly allowance, and sent Yuedeng along to learn the route.

When Yuedeng returned, she was beaming as she pushed aside the curtain — only to see her young mistress lying on the daybed, face ashen, forehead damp with cold sweat.

She rushed over and crouched beside her: "Miss, what is wrong with you?"

Shen Weici shook her head and murmured, eyes half-open: "How much was collected?"

Yuedeng quickly opened the pouch in her hand and placed it in Shen Weici's palm: "Miss, look — a full one tael of silver, and half a string of cash!"

"This Manor is truly grand — even the allowance is this generous."

She leaned close to Shen Weici's ear and whispered: "I sneaked a look at the account book of the stewardship manager just now, and some people's allowances are even five taels!"

"When the mistress worked herself half to death making embroidery for two weeks, she earned only three or four hundred wen. Five taels of silver could make several winter garments in Yuyang."

Shen Weici smiled faintly and pressed the pouch back into Yuedeng's hand: "To the people of this Manor, this allowance is pocket change they hardly notice."

"Did you not hear what Shen Yanli said just now? The Manor's daily expenses are managed from the common fund, each main courtyard has its own stipend and shops, and the ladies have their dowry income as well. This small allowance is nothing more than their spending money."

Yuedeng's face puckered: "Truly, behind the crimson gates there is no limit to the feast."

"Five taels of silver could feed a small family for half a year."

Shen Weici smiled and patted Yuedeng's hand: "Keep the silver safe. There will come a time when it is needed."

A maid called from outside the curtain just then: "Miss, the seamstress from the Manor has come to take your measurements."

Shen Weici rose and invited the woman inside.

The seamstress who entered was around forty, her face pleasant and smiling — unlike the other cold-faced servants. The moment she came in, she curtseyed to Shen Weici and then launched into a stream of compliments.

She walked a full circle around Shen Weici, then reached out to take a few measurements. Noting the full bosom and the slender waist, she could not help letting out an admiring laugh: "Third Young Miss has a truly fine figure — every part of her is exactly as it should be, perfectly proportioned."

"And with such snowy skin — she absolutely must have moon-glory silk, with elegant landscape embroidery on it. I guarantee it will make Third Young Miss look like an immortal descended from the heavens."

Shen Weici hurried to decline modestly: "Something plain would suit me better. I prefer simplicity."

The seamstress looked at Shen Weici — the luminous gaze, the hair dark as a waterfall, the pallor that could not quite conceal a subtle and devastating beauty — not the brazen allure of a temptress, more like a bewitching grace entirely unaware of itself.

She had never seen a face like this before, and smiled: "Third Young Miss is a beauty. Why stay so plain?"

"Besides, the Second Lady gave specific instructions that I must make Third Young Miss some handsome garments. If I make them too plain, the Second Lady will find fault with me."

Hearing that the Second Lady had personally given instructions, Shen Weici chose not to make things difficult for the seamstress and only said: "As long as the style is not too showy. I have only just arrived at the Manor, and you surely understand my situation — I do not wish to attract unnecessary attention."

The seamstress had not expected Shen Weici to have not a trace of haughtiness or impatience, to speak in a soft and gentle manner, and to be so self-effacing — none of the flightiness you might expect from someone dazzled by sudden wealth. She was remarkably low-key.

She nodded with a smile: "Third Young Miss may rest assured — nothing too bright or vivid."

Shen Weici nodded and held out her arms to let the seamstress measure.

Shortly after the seamstress left, another maid came to deliver a small box. Shen Weici recognized her — she was the one who usually followed Shen Zhaozhao — and though her manner was somewhat perfunctory, Shen Weici accepted the box in good spirit and asked her to go back and pass on her thanks.

The maid gave a huff, said offhandedly, "These are things my young mistress never wears, but Third Young Miss probably has never seen the like of them. My young mistress is kind-hearted to have picked out several pieces to send over." Then she turned and left.

Shen Weici smiled slightly and asked Yuedeng to see the maid out.

Yuedeng, now capable of keeping a better hold on her feelings, stretched a false smile to see the maid to the door, then let it drop: "Giving away what she does not want — as if Miss wants it."

Shen Weici stood before the dressing table, gently unlatched the copper clasp, and opened the box. Inside were two pairs of earrings and a few hairpins and bracelets. They were, truly, things Shen Weici had never seen before in her life.

She had never seen pearls, or white jade, or fine jadeite — even these cast-off pieces of Shen Zhaozhao's were exquisite enough in her eyes.

She stood quietly for a moment, then gently closed the lid of the box and told Yuedeng to put it at the very bottom of the cabinet. She had no intention of touching any of it — she was waiting for the day she could return it.

chapters.title: The Gathering at the Veranda Annex
chapters.content:
Half a month passed. During those two weeks, Shen Weici went each morning to pay her respects to Lady Wen and then returned — Lady Wen had not made things difficult for her. She spent the rest of each day in her room, tending to her health.

But this bout of cold had been worse than her usual ones. Normally she would recover in two or three days, but this time the cough only grew worse, and she had no choice but to send Yuedeng out to buy a couple of doses of medicine.

In the veranda annex of the main hall, the whole extended household was gathered and chatting. This day was a rest day, and the Old Madam had established a rule that once a month the whole family must spend a day together, so as not to grow distant from one another.

The Old Madam still sat at the head, with Shen Zhaozhao nestled warmly beside her. The Third Branch lady-of-the-house sat to the Old Madam's right and slightly below, while the men sat on the left, some standing, some seated, conversing in clusters of two or three. Maids circulated with trays of fruit, and charcoal braziers glowed in the room, making it lively and warm.

The Old Madam glanced around and asked Lady Wen: "Where is Weici? Why have you not brought her?"

"I have not seen her these past several days. They are all daughters of the Manor — you should not make it too conspicuous."

Lady Wen's expression tightened. She felt the meaningful glances from those around her and said: "Daughter-in-law was thinking that she had only just arrived, and feared she might be uncomfortable among the other younger members of the family. I was planning to bring her along when I came to see the Old Madam again a little later."

No sooner had Lady Wen's words landed than Princess Consort Huimin let out a faint, unhurried sound of cold amusement.

Lady Wen shot the Princess Consort a sharp look, then turned back to the Old Madam: "If the Old Madam wishes to see her, I will have someone fetch her at once."

The Old Madam gave Lady Wen a cool look, one that carried a warning. She had reminded her once before not to go too far — if Zhang Tingyi learned that this concubine-born daughter was mistreated at home, he would feel uncomfortable. And she most certainly did not want Shen Weici to develop a rebellious streak and then turn against the Marquis Manor once she was married into Zhang Tingyi's household.

Lady Wen caught the warning in the Old Madam's eyes and immediately had a matron go and summon Shen Weici.

At that moment, Shen Weici had just finished taking her medicine and was propped against the writing table, slowly exhaling.

Yuedeng stood beside her, watching anxiously. She had heard that the Manor had a physician who would come for a sum, and had been thinking of going to inquire about it.

She was about to leave when the curtain was suddenly lifted from outside, and a matron marched in without so much as a greeting. Spotting Shen Weici seated inside, she lifted her chin and announced: "The Old Madam and the Second Lady are asking for you in the main hall's veranda annex, Third Young Miss. You had best go and freshen up quickly."

She then cast a contemptuous look at the simple furnishings in the room: "If you take too long and the Old Madam holds it against you, my Lady cannot very well speak up for you."

Shen Weici heard this, turned to look at the matron — recognized her as Lady Wen's close personal matron — and released the fingers she had been pressing to her forehead, responding with the same warm politeness: "I thank the matron for coming to relay the message. Please go back and tell them I will come directly, once I have made myself presentable."

The matron kept a haughty, indifferent expression, gave what seemed like a half-smile that was not quite one, offered no reply, turned, and swept back out through the curtain.

Yuedeng — if not for the fact that it was an old woman — would have genuinely liked to roll up her sleeve and ask what she was so smug about.

Shen Weici rose and asked Yuedeng to bring the garments the seamstress had sent and help her change.

She knew that Lady Wen's gift of clothing was surface performance, but she also had to maintain the relationship from her end.

Yuedeng brought two sets over: "The colors are all peach-red and bright purple — these two are the quietest, one in rouge-pink and one in lotus-root green."

She muttered: "I did not notice Second Young Miss's clothes ever being this vivid — so why are Miss's clothes all so bright?"

When the seamstress had delivered the garments yesterday, Shen Weici had only glanced at them briefly. Looking again today at the colors and patterns, they were entirely different from the plain shades she ordinarily preferred.

In truth, Shen Weici could very easily guess: without a deliberate instruction from the Second Lady, the seamstress would never have made such vivid garments on her own.

She pointed to the rouge-pink — the color was somewhat vivid, but the pattern on it was plain, and it was not too conspicuous.

Yuedeng hurried to bring the garment with its fine qiong-branch border and helped Shen Weici dress it, asking as she worked: "Not a single visit from the Old Madam all these days — why the sudden summons today?"

Shen Weici shook her head: "Let us go and see."

Once fully dressed, both mistress and maid immediately sensed something was wrong. The garment was a touch too small — even without intent, the line of her figure was evident, and with the waist-sash drawn in, the effect was somewhat improper.

Shen Weici understood at once that the Second Lady had deliberately had this garment made this way.

But there was nothing she could do about it now — she only had Yuedeng tug and adjust the fabric, loosening the waist-sash somewhat, so the curves were slightly less pronounced.

She made no other changes, and without putting on any of the jewelry Shen Zhaozhao had sent, she remained quietly and simply dressed as she went with Yuedeng.

Before she even reached the veranda annex, she could already hear lively laughter and conversation. Shen Weici gathered her hands in her sleeves, paused outside the curtain and had a maid go in first to announce her arrival, then followed the maid inside.

The moment she entered, the chatter subsided, and all eyes turned toward Shen Weici.

This was Shen Weici's first time appearing before the full household, and everyone was naturally curious.

Dressed in rouge-pink with a pale yellow wide border, the sleeve and skirt hems embroidered with pale white butterfly patterns — her features were clean and gentle, blossoming like flowers. Though she wore not even earrings, the absence suited her perfectly. Like a radiant moon among flowers, she made it impossible to look away.

And those graceful, perfectly proportioned curves further dazzled the eye — yet she carried herself with propriety, her eyes refined and lovely, like a divine figure from a painted scroll. She truly drew attention, and the whispers began.

When it had first been said that the Second Branch had taken in a wild illegitimate daughter from the countryside, everyone had assumed she would be crude and common. No one had expected a beauty like this.

Song Zhang sat among the gathering in a deep crimson brocade robe, propped languidly with one foot resting on a low stool.

Behind him, two beautiful attendant-maids massaged his shoulders. Beside him, a half-kneeling maid held out a tray of fruit, and another beautiful maid peeled a sugar tangerine newly arrived from the south and placed it in his mouth, her delicate hand then reaching to catch the seed he spat out.

Song Zhang's gaze fell upon Shen Weici where she stood in the center of the room. His lazy eyes swept over her composed, slightly lifted gaze, then dropped to her slender waist.

The sash that hung along her waist outlined her elegant figure, and she had that tenderly charming appearance — Song Zhang's lips curved with a cold, mocking arch. Dressed this way, she was not without her scheming nature. He thought of the half-new, half-worn moon-white dress from before — pitifully touching, every inch — and now barely half a month later, she had revealed her true character, using this garment to draw attention.

The Third Branch's eldest son, Shen Siwen, standing beside Song Zhang, asked in a low voice: "You are not usually seen at these gatherings — what brings you here today?"

Song Zhang's eyes were faint: "Nothing in particular. Just came to watch a bit of liveliness."

Shen Siwen said nothing more.

On the other end of the room, Shen Weici bore those many stares and walked with her head slightly bowed to the center, first paying her respects to the Old Madam, then offering greetings one by one to each person in the veranda annex.

The Old Madam smiled warmly: "Good child — it has only been a few days, and you already look lovelier. Go sit beside your stepmother."

Shen Weici acknowledged the remark and went to sit quietly and carefully beside Lady Wen.

Then the Old Madam said to Shen Yanli: "This is your Third Sister's first proper time meeting the household, and there are many here she does not yet know. You may take her around and make the introductions."

Shen Yanli, unlike Shen Zhaozhao, felt no animosity toward this newly arrived Third Sister — in fact, he felt a certain fondness for the beautiful girl, and stood with a ready smile: "Gladly."

He walked to Shen Weici and said with a smile: "Third Sister, come along — let me introduce you around."

Shen Weici's face broke into a smile, and she stood and followed behind Shen Yanli.

Shen Yanli first brought Shen Weici to the First Branch for introductions. When they reached Song Zhang, Shen Yanli paused, considered a moment, and then said to Shen Weici: "Though Young Lord Song is of the Song Ducal Manor, he is also family here. By our order, he comes second. You may address him as Young Lord, or if you wish to seem closer, you may call him Second Elder Brother Song."

Shen Weici stood before Song Zhang, glanced at the maids surrounding him, and at a distance of three paces, her voice remained perfectly even as she said: "Young Lord Song."

A distance, deliberate and distant.

Song Zhang looked with a flat expression at the person standing before him. Shen Weici's face wore an estranged look, as if she did not recognize him at all. His expression turned cold and indifferent, as if she was beneath his notice — he could not even be bothered to respond.

chapters.title: A Game of Shuanglu
chapters.content:
Shen Yanli had long known Song Zhang's disposition. That he offered no response to Shen Weici was normal — he treated Shen Yanli the same way on ordinary days, giving him little acknowledgement.

He had not expected Song Zhang to show Shen Weici any warmth, and so he pulled her along to meet the Third Branch.

In truth, that Song Zhang paid her no mind was actually a relief to Shen Weici. She had feared he might suddenly bring up the jade pendant — and though she had no ulterior motive in what had happened, she had only just arrived at the Manor. Given that everyone seemed to suspect she was there to covet its wealth, if he were to speak of it now, it would only make her position more difficult.

The Third Branch was the largest: the Third Lord's health was poor and he had taken no official post, but he kept several concubines in his courtyard, and the concubine-born children were the most numerous. The eldest legitimate son had passed the hereditary examination and held a minor eighth-rank post in the capital; the second legitimate son was younger than Shen Yanli and still attending the clan school.

Then there were the two concubine-born daughters — Fourth Young Miss Shen Mingqiu and Fifth Young Miss Shen Yueqiu.

Shen Weici greeted them each in turn.

Her deportment was proper, her gaze composed, and her speech gentle enough to put people at ease. All except Song Zhang had smiling faces for her.

Moreover, everyone could see plainly that the Old Madam had asked Shen Weici to go around meeting people, which meant she had officially recognized Shen Weici's place in the household — putting her face before the whole family, meaning she was henceforth an acknowledged Third Young Miss of the Marquis Manor.

Whatever their private thoughts, they all had to put on a show of face before the Old Madam.

Shen Rongshen, watching Shen Weici move among the gathering without any small-minded awkwardness, felt gratified as well. As long as the Old Madam acknowledged Weici's standing, all would be well.

Once the round of introductions was complete and the younger generation had all been acquainted, the two concubine-born daughters of the Third Branch came over and pulled Shen Weici aside for a chat.

Having observed a full circle around the household, Shen Weici had now formed a rough understanding of everyone. In the First Branch, among people her own generation, there was only Song Zhang.

She had learned that Princess Consort Huimin had been previously married into the Song Ducal Manor. Her husband had been the Song Ducal Manor's heir and a newly minted number-one scholar — with a brilliant future. But fate cut his life short, and he died when Song Zhang was only three.

Afterward, Princess Consort Huimin had remarried into the Marquis Manor, and Song Zhang was taken to the Grand Princess — his grandmother — to be raised in the imperial palace for a few years before returning to live with his mother.

Song Zhang remained the heir of the Song Ducal Manor and merely resided in the Marquis Manor because of his mother.

Yet the First Lord and Princess Consort Huimin had produced no children afterward — something that was hard to understand.

Neither the First nor the Second Branches had any concubines — only the Third Lord had taken four or five, leaving the Third Branch with the most children of the next generation.

With the Second Branch suddenly producing an illegitimate daughter, the concubine-born daughters of the Third Branch came to draw her closer.

Shen Zhaozhao watched this from her place beside the Old Madam, her gaze cold and dismissive. She had always looked down on those of concubine birth — their mothers were of low status, some even former maids. When it came to marriage, the best of them would be sent into noble households as concubines; the rest would be married off to ordinary families. The difference from her own standing was like heaven and earth.

She was the Marquis Manor's legitimate daughter. Her parents were both of distinguished noble birth, and her future husband would be a peer of equal standing. To mix herself in with those concubine-born daughters would only lower her status.

She thought her mother was right: why should she spend any energy on Shen Weici? She would not be in the Manor for long. She herself was to be married into the Yong'an Marquis Manor in the coming year — and wasting time on Shen Weici was not worth it.

Still, seeing Shen Weici's hair without a single ornament, she ground her teeth with renewed resentment. She had sent her jewelry as a courtesy, and Shen Weici had the gall not to accept it.

And she had expected those gaudy colors to look terrible on Shen Weici — instead they had brought out her beauty even more vividly, which irritated her beyond measure.

She gave a cold laugh, walked over to where Shen Weici sat with the others, and said with a look of deliberate indifference: "Since we have nothing else to do, shall we play a game of Shuanglu?"

The two Third Branch girls glanced at Shen Zhaozhao. They did not often associate with her ordinarily, and Shen Zhaozhao had always carried a slight air of superiority around them. But since Shen Zhaozhao had taken the initiative to approach, and she was about to be married into the Yong'an Marquis Manor — not someone to offend — they responded agreeably: "If Second Sister has a mind to, we will keep you company."

Shen Zhaozhao gave a meaningful smile, then turned her eyes to Shen Weici's lowered gaze: "But just playing without stakes would be dull — the loser must accept a forfeit."

The Third Branch girls caught Shen Zhaozhao's intent, exchanged a glance, and understood. Since it was a matter entirely within the Second Branch, it was none of their concern. They smiled and agreed, even going so far as to pull Shen Weici into it.

Shen Weici naturally smiled and declined: "I will just watch while you all play."

Shen Zhaozhao folded her arms, making no effort to hide her distaste, and sneered: "I kindly invite Third Sister to join a game of Shuanglu — to foster some sisterly closeness — and this is how Third Sister repays my goodwill?"

In Shen Zhaozhao's mind, Shen Weici was surely unfamiliar with Shuanglu, having come from such a backwater county. Making her look foolish would be the easiest thing in the world.

Over in the men's area, Song Zhang was in the middle of a leisurely conversation with the Third Branch's eldest son Shen Siwen and Shen Rongshen, when he heard Shen Zhaozhao's sharp, pressing voice from the corner and glanced over.

He saw Shen Weici surrounded by several of the Manor's young women, her slight figure hemmed in by Shen Zhaozhao's imperious stance — rather like a situation with enemies on all sides.

Then he heard Shen Weici's gentle voice say: "Of course I would not dare refuse Sister's kindness. I am happy to play with Sister."

Song Zhang looked away expressionlessly.

At Shen Zhaozhao's agreement, Shen Weici accepted, so she immediately called for a maid to bring the game equipment.

Shuanglu was a common pastime among ladies of noble families. Shen Zhaozhao had played since childhood, and though the game depended partly on luck, the other half came from choosing the best move from the roll of the dice. She was most adept at Shuanglu and had almost never lost.

The board was set out. Shen Zhaozhao and Shen Weici sat facing each other, and the Third Branch girls stood on the side to watch.

On the other side, Shen Yanli noticed and went over with the Third Branch's second legitimate son to have a look.

Within the veranda annex, with all three branches present, along with the crowd of maids and servants, the atmosphere was lively and warm. The young women gathering to play board games was perfectly ordinary, and there were few people paying particularly close attention.

Shen Zhaozhao picked up a glass game piece and moved first. Shen Weici's eyes stayed fixed on the board throughout, her expression mild and warm, and she rolled the dice after Shen Zhaozhao.

Those watching were mildly surprised. They had expected Shen Weici to be unfamiliar with the game and stumbling over herself — yet her movements were perfectly composed.

The game went on for nearly a quarter of an hour without ending. By the time it was nearly over, the two players were each a single piece away from an impasse, and a winner could not be determined.

Shen Zhaozhao's expression darkened as she stared at the board, then looked at Shen Weici.

Shen Weici met Shen Zhaozhao's gaze, then lowered her eyes and asked gently: "Shall Second Sister continue?"

Shen Zhaozhao could barely contain the darkening of her expression. She had not expected Shen Weici to draw even with her. Draws were almost unheard of in Shuanglu, and she did not know whether it was Shen Weici's doing or just blind luck.

Shen Yanli looked at Shen Weici in amazement: "Third Sister is truly formidable — she managed to draw even with Zhaozhao."

Shen Weici heard this and gave Shen Yanli a smile: "Second Sister is still the more formidable one. I was only following Second Sister's lead, and my luck happened to hold."

Shen Zhaozhao, with a cold face, had the maid set up the pieces again and demanded another game.

Shen Weici was about to rise and let one of the Third Branch girls take her place, but Shen Zhaozhao grabbed her sleeve with a cold expression: "Where is Third Sister going? I expressly wanted to play against Third Sister — what would be the point if you leave?"

Shen Weici met Shen Zhaozhao's eyes. The hostility could not have been plainer — she was absolutely determined to make her lose and humiliate her.

She glanced around at those watching the game. Every face was calm, but they all wore something between a smile and not — as if waiting for the entertainment.

She lowered her lashes and pressed her lips briefly together.

She looked at Shen Zhaozhao and said quietly: "Since Second Sister is in the mood, I will keep you company."

chapters.title: A Slap
chapters.content:
In truth, Shen Weici was no stranger to Shuanglu. She had once watched a female teacher at her private school playing it and had grown fond of it. After classes ended, she would often stay behind to play with the teacher, sometimes staying so late that her mother had to come and fetch her.

The game was popular in Yuyang as well, though mostly among the wealthy — it was uncommon among ordinary people. Shen Zhaozhao had simply assumed that nowhere like Yuyang would have such things, and in her heart she looked down on Shen Weici entirely, naturally concluding she would not know how to play.

But Shen Weici did not intend to win against Shen Zhaozhao — nor would she allow herself to be beaten and humiliated. A draw was the best outcome.

Shen Weici studied the board. If she advanced her piece one step after the horse move, it would trap Shen Zhaozhao out of her home base — Shen Zhaozhao would then either block one of her pieces, or concede. If she blocked, it would be a draw again. Given Shen Zhaozhao's temperament, she would certainly choose a draw.

Song Zhang let his gaze drift over, and found Shen Weici's figure already blocked by those watching the game. He paid no further mind to the conversation Shen Siwen was still holding with him, rose from his seat, and walked over to watch the game.

Shen Siwen looked at Song Zhang's retreating figure, gave a surprised sound that went unanswered, and then followed along to have a look.

Song Zhang studied the layout of the board for a few moments, then turned his gaze to Shen Weici.

He watched her. She remained silent throughout, her moves steady and seasoned, clearly guiding the game toward a draw while never appearing to take the upper hand against Shen Zhaozhao. This made him raise an eyebrow.

At this point, just as Shen Weici was about to move to block one of Shen Zhaozhao's pieces, her wrist was seized by Shen Zhaozhao. Shen Zhaozhao's other hand casually toyed with the dice, narrowing her eyes at Shen Weici: "Third Sister, make sure you see clearly before you move."

Shen Zhaozhao changed the dice this brazen and openly, her lips curled in a cold smile — as if she knew with certainty that no one would speak up for Shen Weici.

Shen Weici's eyes flickered to the Third Branch girls and to Shen Yanli on either side. They had all seen what happened, yet none of them said a word. On the contrary, they all maintained a studied silence — waiting to watch the show.

Of course they would. Compared to her, a girl who had been in the Manor only days, Shen Zhaozhao was far more familiar to them.

There was nothing to be done about it. Not capping the piece was merely losing one move — Shen Weici lowered her eyes and changed her strategy.

Song Zhang watched as this unfolded, arms folded, his gaze settling on Shen Weici's face. He wanted to see what she would do.

With Shen Zhaozhao no longer playing by the rules — swapping the dice whenever she was unsatisfied, pressing hard at every step — Shen Weici had no way to win.

Shen Weici looked at the state of the board and paused. She placed the glass piece she was holding back in the side vessel, and looked at Shen Zhaozhao: "Second Sister's chess skill is superior. Weici is no match and cannot manage."

Shen Zhaozhao gave her a cool look: "Oh? Is Third Sister conceding?"

Shen Weici said quietly: "Though the game has not yet produced a winner, I know I am outmatched and do not dare continue against Sister. If Sister considers this a concession, then so it is."

Shen Zhaozhao tossed down her piece and looked at Shen Weici: "Since Third Sister concedes, she must take the forfeit, must she not?"

Shen Weici shook her head: "Earlier, Sister said the loser would take the forfeit. As of now, the game has not yet determined a winner."

Shen Zhaozhao had not expected Shen Weici to dare say this, and fury choked her; she reached out and grabbed the front of Shen Weici's collar and threatened her: "Do you dare play games with me? Try it and see — I can make you regret this day."

Shen Weici's collar was seized by Shen Zhaozhao; her body tilted across the board and game pieces scattered everywhere. She braced herself against a chair with one hand, and looked at Shen Zhaozhao with neither deference nor defiance: "Does Second Sister think I said something wrong?"

Shen Yanli, seeing how things were going, hurried to restrain Shen Zhaozhao and tried to pacify her in a low voice: "Zhaozhao, let it go. Third Sister already conceded — why hold on to this?"

The whole game had been transparent to everyone watching. It was clear why Shen Weici had conceded — she couldn't continue playing. By conceding on her own terms with a half-finished board, she was offering both sides a way to save face. The matter should end there; as her elder brother, he was finding it hard to watch.

Shen Zhaozhao had been deliberately trying to humiliate Shen Weici from the start. And now hearing her elder brother speak for Shen Weici on top of it, she was furious enough to gnash her teeth.

She shoved her elder brother's hand aside, raised her palm, and slapped Shen Weici across the cheek — gritting out the words: "A loss is a loss. I said from the beginning that the loser would take a forfeit. One slap is the price you pay for losing."

"I have wanted to slap you for a long time. Since you are greedy for the wealth of the Marquis Manor, you should know that the Manor is not a place you can enter as you wish."

"You deserve this slap. You have no cause for complaint."

Song Zhang stood with his arms folded, his gaze falling upon Shen Weici with a flat expression, yet his fingertips shifted.

Shen Weici, no matter what, had not expected Shen Zhaozhao would slap her in front of so many people. She pressed her hand slowly against her cheek, trembling slightly. Every person in the room — and there were many — not a single one had moved to stop it. They had all watched with amused interest.

Even Shen Yanli, who had only moments ago spoken up, said not a word now. On the contrary, he stepped to one side and positioned himself to block the view from where the Old Madam and the others sat, so they could not see this scene.

Her heart, in this moment, plunged into ice-cold water.

Her collar was still held in Shen Zhaozhao's grip, strands of hair falling loose. She did not look at the onlookers — only at Shen Zhaozhao — without a trace of cowering. Her voice was quiet and clear: "Does Second Sister not know why I lost?"

Shen Zhaozhao sneered and looked around: "Which of you can say — did I win or not?"

"Was she wronged or not?"

No one spoke. Everyone looked at each other.

Shen Zhaozhao pointed to the Third Branch's concubine-born daughter Shen Mingqiu: "Fourth Sister — tell me, how did I win?"

Shen Mingqiu hesitated. This was purely a Second Branch matter, and she had no wish to involve herself. But choosing between Shen Zhaozhao and Shen Weici was not a difficult choice. She smiled: "I only know that Second Sister's skill in Shuanglu is superb — I could never beat her."

The words were ambiguous, but their meaning was unmistakable.

Shen Weici's eyes blinked. She looked at Shen Zhaozhao: "Since Second Sister's skill is so superior, why not invite the Old Madam to bear witness, and let us play one more game? If I lose again, I will accept any punishment Second Sister sees fit to impose."

Shen Zhaozhao's face went cold: "You are not qualified to play another game against me."

Shen Weici smiled faintly: "Is it that Second Sister does not dare play against me? Or is Second Sister afraid of losing?"

Shen Zhaozhao's expression underwent a great change. She raised her hand high and brought it down across the other side of Shen Weici's face. Shen Weici had anticipated it and moved to block — but Shen Zhaozhao's force was too great, and the blow landed squarely regardless.

Yet this was precisely what Shen Weici had intended. She had already received one slap — if she was going to take it, she would make a scene that the Old Madam could see, let the ladies of each branch witness it; and most importantly, she wanted to push her father, to force him to see even one part of her predicament.

Shen Zhaozhao had been baited beyond reason. She called her maidservant to hold Shen Weici's arms and raised her hand to strike again: "You low country girl — how dare you say I cannot beat you at chess."

"Today I will show you what I am capable of, and teach you to keep your tail between your legs from now on."

The commotion Shen Zhaozhao caused was now large enough that the Third Branch lady-of-the-house nearby came over to see. She called out loudly: "What is the matter here? How did it come to a fight among the young ladies?"

Third Lady-in-law Wang's voice was not quiet, and others in the room came over as well — just in time to see a maid holding Shen Weici's arms while Shen Zhaozhao stood across from her, hand raised and swinging down.

Fortunately, Song Zhang beside them reached out and caught her wrist, and the blow did not land.

Looking at Shen Weici's flushed cheeks, it was clear enough what had happened.

The expressions of those from the First and Second Branches varied. Princess Consort Huimin looked at Lady Wen and gave a cold, amused sound: "Tsk, tsk. The daughters raised by the Second Branch truly open one's eyes."

"Bullying a younger concubine-born sister who has no mother — truly a sight to behold."

Lady Wen's expression changed, and she snapped at Shen Zhaozhao: "Zhaozhao, stop this at once!"

Shen Rongshen came forward and took in the scene — Shen Zhaozhao's ferocious expression, every trace of her usual sweet innocence gone, and Shen Weici silent, not making a sound. Though Shen Weici had not said a word, the fingermarks on her flushed cheeks, the plain look about her, and the slightly loosened pins in her hair all showed plainly what she had endured.

On top of that, Shen Zhaozhao had slapped a concubine-born younger sister in front of the whole household — a clear failure of upbringing. He felt his face flush with shame, and immediately spoke sharply: "Outrageous!"

"Release her at once."

chapters.title: Mockery
chapters.content:
At Shen Rongshen's sharp command, the maid who had been holding Shen Weici immediately let go and retreated to stand behind Shen Zhaozhao.

This whole drama had been witnessed by everyone in the veranda annex. Lady Wen's expression was stiff and grim. She told a matron to go and coax Shen Zhaozhao away.

Shen Zhaozhao was reluctant to leave. She shot Shen Weici a venomous glare, then rushed to throw herself into Lady Wen's arms, weeping: "Mother, she lost the game herself. What was wrong with me slapping her twice?"

Shen Zhaozhao was the only legitimate daughter of the Marquis Manor. In ordinary times she was sweet-tongued and in the Old Madam's favor, indulged by both father and mother, and had never been made to suffer in any matter. Even the other girls in the Manor treated her with some degree of flattery, and so in all things she thought only of herself.

Shen Weici was freed by the maid. She saw Shen Zhaozhao throw herself into Lady Wen's arms, bowed her head, and quietly withdrew into a corner.

Still and composed, as if the scene that had just played out had nothing to do with her.

Shen Rongshen looked at Shen Zhaozhao, then heard her words. His expression dark, he reprimanded: "You and Weici are sisters of the same branch. Even if she did lose, what justifies slapping someone? I have clearly been too indulgent of you. Go back to your room at once!"

At this point the Old Madam was helped forward by her matron. She frowned at Shen Yanli: "What exactly happened?"

Shen Yanli glanced subtly at Shen Weici, then turned to the Old Madam: "It was nothing of consequence, really. Third Sister lost at the game, and Zhaozhao thought it was fun and so patted Third Sister's face as a forfeit — she simply misjudged how much force to use."

Shen Weici listened quietly, her expression carrying the faintest trace of irony.

The Old Madam looked at Shen Weici's reddened cheeks — still faintly bearing fingermarks — which could not possibly have come from a single light touch.

Princess Consort Huimin, not waiting for the Old Madam to speak, said coolly: "Those marks are still showing. Who would have thought the Second Young Miss had such strength? A pat was all it took to leave those marks."

She then looked over at Song Zhang: "璋儿, I do not suppose even the feathered guards under your command have fighters this capable?"

Song Zhang's gaze lingered a moment on Shen Weici, his face cold: "There are some, but they are all brutes fit only for rough and dirty work. I simply do not know where Second Young Miss trained such consummate fighting skills."

He snorted: "Losing at a game and then striking someone — on a level with the common street shrews. Or perhaps surpassing them."

Song Zhang's words were cutting, sparing no dignity. Lady Wen's face went from green to pale, and she could not find anything to say in response.

The First Branch, though they seldom involved themselves in the Manor's affairs, had never been afraid of anyone. Even the Old Madam showed a degree of deference to Princess Consort Huimin, let alone that Song Zhang was a trusted intimate of the Emperor. As an Old Madam without any title, her only real authority was her seniority.

Those in the Third Branch hearing Song Zhang's words could not help but burst out suppressing a laugh, all of them smiling meaningfully — the situation was now perfectly clear.

Words from Song Zhang's mouth were invariably the truth.

Someone murmured low: "Nothing more than the Second Branch bullying someone — and she is their own blood. To be so intolerant of one's own kin...  tsk, tsk, tsk..."

One quiet whisper after another drifted through the room. Shen Zhaozhao's face went white, but she dared not confront Song Zhang and buried her head in her mother's arms.

Lady Wen's face was equally unpleasant. Those stares pressing in from all sides made it seem as though she had been privately mistreating Shen Weici all along.

The Old Madam's own expression showed that she found this ridiculous — but she also had no real intention of blaming Shen Zhaozhao, and so she said with a frown: "Let this matter go no further. The young ladies were just playing, a little too rough — nothing more."

She looked at Shen Weici: "Weici, have you anything to say?"

The favoritism in these words was unmistakable. Shen Weici also had no intention of letting this blow up further here. She understood the Old Madam's meaning: she did not want her to pursue it.

She stepped forward, pressed the corner of a cloth handkerchief to the corner of one eye, and said in a husky voice: "Today's matter was truly not Second Sister's fault. I have caused everyone to come over, and for that I owe the Old Madam and all the ladies an apology."

She then turned and curtseyed to Shen Rongshen: "Please do not blame Second Sister, Father. Weici provoked Second Sister's anger while playing chess — it is only right that I should be punished."

"Yet Weici's appearance is currently disheveled, and she has no wish to disturb everyone's enjoyment further. With Father's permission, she will take her leave."

These words, from beginning to end, were proper and gracious — not a single one assigned blame. She stood among them all, quiet and composed, her beauty undeniable — and despite the fingermarks still on her face, her peach-blossom complexion in spring bloom, her misty, smoky eyes — the contrast with Shen Zhaozhao, who had run sobbing to Lady Wen and still refused to accept what had happened, was apparent to everyone who had a scale to weigh it.

By submitting this way — not contending, not grasping — it showed only that the Second Branch had been too partial, that this newly arrived concubine-born daughter had been mistreated behind closed doors, and even dared to strike her in public. One could only imagine what she endured in private.

The First Lord frowned at Shen Rongshen: "Since you've brought her in, raise her properly. You are already being watched by the Censors — do not let them find grounds to censure you again for conduct unbecoming a gentleman."

In a lower voice he continued: "The household also needs managing. A man who lets himself be ruled by his wife will have a disordered household sooner or later."

Shen Rongshen looked at Shen Weici's downcast brow, at the faintly red corners of her eyes, and felt her silent grievance. A faint sense of guilt toward this daughter rose within him.

He replied quietly to his elder brother: "Elder Brother speaks rightly. I understand."

Then he walked to Shen Weici and sighed: "Go back for now. I will have medicine sent over shortly."

Shen Weici nodded, then raised her face to look at her father, blinking back tears: "Father should not trouble himself over this matter further. Weici is not aggrieved."

She lowered her eyes and, with the maids behind her, quietly withdrew from the veranda annex.

Shen Weici always had a way of gently saying a word or two of comfort to Shen Rongshen — as when she had said on her first day that she did not want to make things difficult for him.

Time and again she considered him, this father of hers, not wanting to cause him trouble. Gradually, his sense of debt had transformed into guilt.

If he were to be honest, he felt little genuine care for this daughter. Since her return, he had barely looked in on her — most of his time was still spent with Shen Zhaozhao.

The words "Weici is not aggrieved" still rang in his ears. He looked at Shen Weici's careful, quiet retreating figure and let out a long, heavy sigh.
