Song Qingxiu continued, "I hear the Emperor is thinking of giving the Fifth Princess to you—would that also mean he's signalling that he intends to name the Fourth Prince as Crown Prince?"

"The Duke of Song's Mansion commands military power. By giving you the Fifth Princess..."

Before Song Qingxiu could finish, Song Zhang cut him off. "I am not going to marry the Fifth Princess."

Song Qingxiu stared. "The Fourth Prince is extremely powerful right now. People at court have already begun choosing sides. If you marry the Fifth Princess, and the Fourth Prince becomes Crown Prince, the Duke of Song's Mansion will be the Emperor's closest confidants—why would you refuse?"

Song Zhang did not answer. He simply reached out and lifted the carriage curtain to glance outside, then looked back at Song Qingxiu across from him. "Third Uncle, don't be in a hurry to take sides. I am not going to marry the Fifth Princess. The Duke of Song's Mansion has always stayed out of factional struggles—wouldn't Third Uncle be better off watching from the shore?"

With that, Song Zhang called for the carriage to stop and stepped out.

chapters.title: Why Would Young Lord Song Help Me?
chapters.content:
By the time Yuedeng made it back to the Marquis Manor, the sky outside had gone completely dark.

She had held herself together the entire way. The moment she reached Linchun Courtyard and stepped through the door, she let go — rushing to the bedside and collapsing into tears: "Miss, that Zhang Yuanheng truly cannot be relied upon. He… he is now…"

The instant Shen Weici saw Yuedeng come running in with tears on her face, her heart went half cold.

She gently patted Yuedeng where she had fallen against her, rubbing her back, and said quietly: "Tell me plainly. That is all."

Only then did Yuedeng lift her face from Shen Weici's embrace. Her eyes were red as she choked out: "He has let Miss down. He is already making arrangements for another marriage."

"A faithless man like him will get his due sooner or later. And to think Miss has been making a pouch for him all these days — he was never worth Miss's heart."

Although the sight of Yuedeng just now had already told Shen Weici seven or eight parts of the story, hearing it said plainly from Yuedeng's lips still stung her heart like a needle.

She had believed she would not grieve. It turned out she grieved a little after all.

She closed her eyes, concealing the feeling that had risen in them, and held Yuedeng's hands tight while using her handkerchief to dab Yuedeng's tears: "In a way this is for the best. With a character like his, I am fortunate not to have married him — the life afterward would certainly not have been good."

"Besides, it is not I who was faithless. I have done nothing wrong by anyone."

Yuedeng heard this and wept all the harder, asking through her tears: "Then what will Miss do?"

"Now the Old Madam and the Second Branch all want Miss to marry Zhang Tingyi, and Young Master Zhang is no longer willing to marry Miss. Where is Miss's way out?"

Shen Weici's eyes fell, and she spoke quietly: "A way out…"

"There is always a way out. We have not yet reached the worst of it."

Yuedeng looked at Shen Weici through tearful eyes: "But this servant's heart is aching terribly right now. Isn't Miss's heart aching?"

Shen Weici lowered her brows: "Naturally it aches somewhat. I did, after all, give my genuine heart. But it is also fate."

As she spoke, Shen Weici's eyes did grow red at the rims. She sighed inwardly at herself for failing, once again, to see someone clearly.

Song Zhang stood outside the courtyard wall. His dark eyes rested on the silhouette cast against the window — that gentle, warm shadow that had a way of settling the restlessness in him whenever he looked at it. He pressed his lips together, and thought of what she had suffered these past days, and of the bloodstain still on her collar. His heart gave a small, sharp ache.

Yan'er, the maid keeping watch at the courtyard gate, saw Song Zhang standing there but not moving, and did not dare open her mouth. She glanced at the sword at his waist and felt a small thrill of fear.

Everyone in the Marquis Manor knew that the Second Young Master was the last person you wanted to cross — he spared no one's feelings, and offending him left you without any escape.

Song Zhang glanced at the maid at the gate, who was watching him with timid eyes, then walked into the courtyard without further ceremony, utterly unconcerned that no one had announced him, as naturally as though this were his own yard.

Hexia, who had been sitting at the main doorway tending to a boiling pot of medicine, saw Song Zhang come in and scrambled to her feet in fright, calling: "Second Young Master."

Song Zhang lowered his eyes to glance at the medicine brazier, where something burbled softly and sent out a bitter fragrance.

He said nothing. His expression remained cold. He stepped over the threshold.

Hexia, only after Song Zhang had gone inside, came to her senses and went to follow — but by then she could already see his back disappearing behind the curtain.

Inside the inner room, the air was thick with the smell of medicine, a white curl of incense from the high shelf unable to mask it. Threaded through the smell was a warm, gentle fragrance — Shen Weici's scent. Song Zhang found himself thinking, strangely, that even this air was something he did not mind.

He came in with the sweeping ease of a man accustomed to commanding rooms — expression cold, manner arrogant, his cinnamon-red round-collar house robe belted in black leather, black wrist guards on his forearms, a face like carved jade and eyes like a phoenix's — like a frost-dusted pine — and stood in the center of the room meeting Shen Weici's gaze.

Shen Weici had been sitting with a weight in her chest, and started slightly at Song Zhang's sudden entrance. Seeing him only look at her without speaking, she braced herself up a little and asked: "What brings Young Lord Song here at this hour?"

Song Zhang's gaze dropped to the front of Shen Weici's garment, where the bloodstain still showed. Her dark hair lay obediently against her shoulders, and the candlelight falling across her made her look softer still.

He looked at her face with a kind of quiet hunger — at her alluring red lips, at her eyes which still held the glimmer of unshed tears. He took another step closer.

Was she grieving because Zhang Yuanheng would not marry her?

Shen Weici watched Song Zhang continue to say nothing and continue to walk toward her bed. She was wearing only her inner robe; he was, after all, an outsider man — and even if by seniority he might be counted as a sort of cousin by marriage, the connection was remote, and he bore a different surname. It simply did not feel appropriate. She quietly drew the quilt up around herself and asked again: "What has Young Lord Song come for?"

Song Zhang looked at the wariness in Shen Weici's eyes and the motion of her drawing up the quilt. His phoenix eyes half-lidded. He finally spoke: "Have your maid step outside."

Shen Weici was already miserable, and had no heart for any of this. Hearing Song Zhang's words, she raised her reddened eyes to look at him: "Why does Young Lord Song want my maid outside again?"

Song Zhang met Shen Weici's gaze, raised an eyebrow — and then, in the next moment, to Shen Weici's astonishment, swept his robe aside and sat down on the edge of her bed.

"No particular reason. If you will not send her out, I shall simply sit here until she goes."

He looked at Shen Weici with perfect composure, not the slightest hint of jest: "Staying the night would also not be beyond the pale."

Shen Weici truly had not expected Song Zhang to be this shameless. She was startled for a moment, but in the end she had no desire for a prolonged standoff with him — at worst she would simply have to listen to a few more of his cutting remarks.

She told Yuedeng to wait just outside the curtain, and turned her face slightly to one side to conceal the glimmer in her eyes: "Can you speak now?"

Song Zhang breathed in the fragrance that was so close at hand, edged a little nearer to Shen Weici, and kept his expression entirely unmoved.

He asked her: "Are you feeling better?"

Shen Weici had never in her life expected Song Zhang to ask after her health. This man, who had never once regarded her as anyone worth caring about, was being strangely unlike himself tonight.

She could not read Song Zhang's intentions, but she had been performing serious illness for the household's benefit, and maintained the same careful caution before him — she coughed softly twice, as though the illness were still heavy upon her, but then shook her head and said slowly: "A little better."

Song Zhang heard Shen Weici's cough and frowned. He looked at her slightly pallid face, at the redness still at the rims of her eyes. His fingers closed and then loosened again.

From inside his robe he produced a small medicine bottle, palm-sized, and held it out toward her: "I will handle the matter of Zhang Tingyi. He will not dare come to the Marquis Manor to propose again. You need only rest and recover."

Shen Weici looked at the white jade bottle between Song Zhang's fingers, then lifted her gaze slowly to him, unable to understand why this person would suddenly have any intention of helping her.

Song Zhang waited as Shen Weici made no move to take the bottle and said nothing. His hand hovered in mid-air for a long moment. Then he simply reached over and took the hand she had resting on the quilt, and placed the medicine bottle in it.

Shen Weici's fingers were slightly cold. They closed around the bottle — soft and smooth against his palm. Song Zhang could not resist a moment of letting them rest in his hand before releasing her.

Shen Weici looked at the medicine bottle, still warm from his body, carrying something of his scent. She looked up at Song Zhang in bewilderment and asked: "Why would Young Lord Song help me?"

chapters.title: He Wanted to Taste
chapters.content:
The room had grown very quiet. Song Zhang's face, compared with its usual cold arrogance and casual mockery, seemed tonight to carry feelings Shen Weici had never seen on it before.

In truth, Shen Weici had never had a particularly good impression of Song Zhang, and had never thought of asking for his help. She still remembered every cutting word he had ever said to her.

She would not believe Song Zhang had suddenly developed this kind of goodwill, nor did she have any wish to lean on another person.

Song Zhang looked into Shen Weici's pale, steady eyes and said quietly: "I am helping you because that old reprobate Zhang Tingyi has no shame, and I am after all half a member of this household. Doing this for you is nothing out of my way."

"It is not any great difficulty."

As he spoke, Song Zhang's slightly lowered gaze drifted to the embroidery lying on the pillow beside her, then back to her: "Though I am not helping you for nothing. You ought to offer me something in return."

Shen Weici paused and looked at Song Zhang.

Everything in her room put together was likely not worth a single object in Song Zhang's. She remembered the last time she had been to his quarters — every item on the display shelf alone was probably of considerable value.

She kept her guard up and asked in a low voice: "What does Young Lord Song wish me to offer in return?"

Song Zhang's eyes rested on Shen Weici's face with unhurried ease — those eyes still faintly red at the rims, moisture flashing in them at intervals, arrestingly lovely: "I noticed a few days ago that my sister was embroidering a pouch. Why not embroider one for me as well?"

Shen Weici was taken aback. The gentleness beneath her brow gave way to a flicker of feeling: "What does Young Lord Song mean by this? Is it truly only a pouch you want?"

Song Zhang raised a cool eyebrow at the surprise in Shen Weici's eyes: "Is Third Young Miss Shen unwilling to give even a pouch?"

Shen Weici, having had that turned around on her so abruptly, found herself momentarily at a loss for words.

She was not unwilling — only astonished that Song Zhang's condition could be so simple.

She lowered her brow and considered for a moment, then raised her eyes to Song Zhang: "In a few days I will send the pouch to Young Lord Song."

Song Zhang looked at that one upward glance, at the rippling dark eyes, at the hair cascading down in black waves, at the white face with its trace of allure in the candlelight. What most beguiled him was her eyes — those flushed peach-blossom eyes, the outer corners slightly tilted, the irises bright with moisture, a shimmer of vivid color across them.

When those eyes fell, there was another kind of fragile beauty — the kind that made a man want to pull her close and hear what her voice might sound like with even more softness in it.

Song Zhang felt, without quite meaning to, a heat spreading through him.

He was at an age when the blood ran high, and his desires for a woman had been growing keener.

In his years at the frontier, beautiful women had been plentiful in their offerings — yet not one had moved him at all.

Looking at those lovely faces, their coquetry so deliberate as they pressed themselves against him, baring their chests in front of all and sundry — the interest vanished in him at once.

Song Zhang, though his manner was at times loose and free-ranging, having grown up without much of the capital's noble discipline, was deep down a traditional man. Where his own woman was concerned, he would never allow even half a measure of her to be exposed before another's eyes — and as for those women who posed and preened for every man in the room, he had only ever toyed with them at the table. He had not the slightest wish to take any of them away.

Song Zhang's breathing had gone a degree warmer, yet he kept his composure. He breathed in the warm fragrance at the tip of his nose, and despite himself his gaze fell once more on Shen Weici's lips.

Perhaps it was her illness, but her lips were less vividly red than they had been that other evening — and yet they still made Song Zhang's throat move.

He wanted to taste.

Not that Song Zhang was without experience of kissing a woman. At eighteen, he had led his army and subdued the Eastern Lin kingdom. The Eastern Lin had sent many beautiful women as tribute. He had been young and high-spirited, fresh from a victory, and had looked the offerings over with certain intentions.

He had gone around twice and chosen the most beautiful one, intending a night of pleasures.

The woman had considerable skill. Song Zhang had been inexperienced with women and had been drawn into a dizziness by her arts — he had been lured into letting her draw him close, his big hands kneading her body, falling back with her onto the bed, her boneless hands moving over him.

At that moment Song Zhang had felt all the blood in his body concentrated in one place. He had been on the verge of acting — and then, for reasons he could not explain, a chill suddenly ran through him. He turned his head and found a gleaming blade suspended at the back of his neck. Another breath's delay and it would have been buried there.

Song Zhang had barely dodged in time, scrambling up and kicking the woman until she spat blood.

Questioning his men afterward revealed that several had been similarly ensnared. He was furious. That same night he led his troops and killed more than a thousand members of the royal household, hung the Eastern Lin king's head on the city wall, set one of his own subordinates up as the new Eastern Lin king, and left the populace without a soul who dared defy him.

After that, Song Zhang had carried the shadow of it and never again touched a woman sent by a conquered nation.

In this way, it could be said that Song Zhang had still not truly been with a woman — and that woman deserved a generous share of the credit.

Now, looking at Shen Weici, Song Zhang's mind was full of those roving thoughts — he had already, in imagination, held her close and kissed her several times.

But Shen Weici had no idea what Song Zhang was thinking at that moment. She only saw his gaze fixed on her, deeply, the shadowed phoenix eyes sharp and unfathomable — and felt, looking into them, something like the cold intent of a man who had taken many lives.

Perhaps it was because Song Zhang was a military man, the blade at his waist having felled countless enemies. Shen Weici always felt there was something of a blood-edge about him. Sometimes she would glimpse a displeased look in his brows from a distance and feel as though he might draw his sword on someone at any moment.

She saw Song Zhang continuing to look at her without speaking, and felt she had no purchase on his intentions. She opened her mouth again, softly: "Young Lord Song?"

The voice — slightly bewildered, carrying a trace of soft hoarseness — made Song Zhang draw in a long breath and push hard against the rising impulse.

He looked into Shen Weici's eyes and suddenly asked: "I came in just now and your eyes were red. Have you been crying?"

Shen Weici looked at Song Zhang in astonishment, sensing something different about this visit. The man who had always been cold and cutting to her was asking why she had cried.

She paused, then said quietly: "It is nothing. The hot tea steamed my eyes. It will pass."

Song Zhang did not press further. He had already guessed the reason in his heart.

He rose from the edge of the bed and looked down at Shen Weici, who had been momentarily lost in thought and was now looking up at him. He pointed to the medicine bottle in her hand: "The imperial physician says two pills per day. When you have finished them, tell me and I will bring you more."

Shen Weici felt it wrong to accept things from him without cause. Suddenly the medicine bottle in her hand felt as though it were burning.

She held it back out toward Song Zhang and said, with gentle roundabout care: "Weici thanks Young Lord Song for his kindness, but my illness is not serious — I do not dare accept any more things from Young Lord Song."

Song Zhang pressed his lips tightly together, looked down at Shen Weici with a genuine frown of displeasure: "Vomiting blood is not serious?"

Then he gave a cold laugh: "If you don't want to accept what I give, just say so plainly. There is no need for these hollow courtesies. I will simply consider it a case of casting pearls before swine."

Shen Weici froze. Song Zhang's words put her in an impossible position.

Song Zhang had come to give her medicine and said he would handle Zhang Tingyi. He had said he would help her — she simply could not yet tell whether it was genuine goodwill. But looking at his darkening expression, she thought: if Song Zhang truly could resolve the matter of Zhang Tingyi, she could not fully trust him, but she could at least acknowledge his intention.

chapters.title: The Impulse He Felt Toward Her
chapters.content:
The candlelight swayed in the room, as though trembling with the unspoken stirring passing between the two of them.

Song Zhang's face, framed by the cinnamon-red robe, was as fine as carved jade — those expressive brows and bright eyes carrying the fierce edge of a young general. In the warm candlelight, even he seemed to hold, for just a moment, a sliver of tenderness.

Shen Weici turned the matter back and forth in her heart for a long while, and in the end drew her hand back.

She lowered her eyes, her gentle brow perfectly quiet, and said softly: "Thank you, Young Lord Song."

Something shifted in Song Zhang's expression. He looked down at Shen Weici's lowered brows and lashes — that tilted nose catching the warm light, that white robe also dusted in gold — already tender enough to seem as though one might wring water from her. Now she looked softer and more fragile still, and a single glance was enough to undo a person.

For the first time in his life, Song Zhang felt an impulse toward a woman that he could not suppress.

The only thing holding him back was the pride buried deep inside — the refusal to expose his every longing on his face the way Zhang Yuanheng had, like a besotted lapdog, letting the woman see that she could effortlessly captivate any man.

He would not let her think she could draw him in as easily as all the rest.

Song Zhang looked once more at the graceful white robe she wore, then at the strand of hair that had slipped from her shoulders and was slowly falling down her back. On an unguarded impulse he bent, reached out, and tucked that strand of hair behind her ear.

Shen Weici looked at Song Zhang in surprise; Song Zhang himself went still for a moment when he met her eyes.

He withdrew his fingers, annoyed at himself in a vague, minor way, and said abruptly: "It looked worse hanging loose."

And with that he turned and walked out.

Outside, Minhe immediately stepped to Song Zhang's side and murmured: "Just now, Zhang Yuanheng came to the front gate to ask to see the Second Lord. He was turned away. He must have come looking for Third Young Miss Shen."

Song Zhang's expression was cool. He glanced at Minhe: "If any one of his letters so much as reaches Linchun Courtyard, do not expect to escape military discipline."

"And anything sent out from Linchun Courtyard is to come to me first."

Minhe hurriedly said: "General, rest assured — there are four or five men watching. Not even a fly gets through."

He then leaned in and murmured: "Also, the message just arrived that Zhang Tingyi has been drawn away."

Song Zhang's face went cold. He glanced once more at the warm glow of the window within the courtyard, then clasped his hands behind him and walked away in long strides.

Shen Weici watched Song Zhang's retreating figure and did not quite follow what he had meant by 'it looks worse.'

Was he saying her hair looked worse when it fell down?

Yuedeng, seeing Song Zhang leave, quickly pushed the curtain aside and came in. The moment she entered she saw Shen Weici's gaze fixed on a distant point, and hurried over: "Miss?"

Shen Weici came back from her absence of mind and looked down at the medicine bottle in her palm.

She opened it. A medicinal scent drifted out.

Yuedeng asked curiously: "Miss, what is that?"

Shen Weici tipped one pill out into her hand — a dark brown pill with a slight sheen — looked at it, then tipped it back into the bottle without answering Yuedeng, and set it beside the pillow.

She had no actual illness and no real need for medicine.

She looked down at her own inner robe. She had been thinking about this for two days now — anyone who needed to see should have seen by now. She told Yuedeng to have water brought for a bath.

In the bath, Shen Weici leaned against the rim of the tub, and the matter of Zhang Yuanheng's broken promise came back to her.

The image she held of him — always gentle and courteous, almost bashful about looking at her for too long — and in the end she had still failed to see him clearly.

Behind her, Yuedeng was wiping down her back while murmuring: "The whole Manor is talking about Miss's situation now. It must have gotten out already. If the Second Lord and Second Lady hear it, what if they get even angrier and push even harder for Miss to marry Zhang Tingyi?"

Shen Weici gathered her thoughts and closed her eyes: "I can only see how severe the talk outside becomes. If it is only a minor ripple, it will not hurt the Second Lady much, and things will stay the same. But if it spreads widely, and Father and the Second Lady still insist on forcing me to marry Zhang Tingyi despite the public shame of it — then I will have to find another way."

As she spoke, Shen Weici also thought of Song Zhang's offer to help. She did not know whether what he said was true, and had no way to fully trust him.

In the warmth of the steam, Shen Weici let out another long, slow breath and looked toward some far point.

-----

The next day, as Shen Rongshen left the great hall after morning court and headed toward the Ministry of Revenue, his colleagues around him turned to point and murmur without the slightest restraint.

Those words were not intended to be kept from him — they all found their way into his ears.

They said: what a thing it was for the Jian'an Marquis Manor with its centuries of prestige to have sunk to this — a disgrace to the old families, an insult to the integrity of scholars, forcing a daughter into marriage with a man nearly forty years her senior, practically driving the girl to death.

Any noble family with any face in the capital, they said, would never push their daughter into a match like that. The Jian'an Marquis Manor's eagerness to curry favor was unsightly to behold — and now they had broken up a true match and nearly caused a fatality.

Others said he kept a tigress at home and could not manage his own household — that his daughter had been left to the cruelties of the mistress, robbed of charcoal in winter — and that even after coughing blood and fainting, they had not let up, coming to her bedside the very next day with the Old Madam to force the marriage. They were working toward killing someone outright.

More said the Old Madam of the Jian'an Manor was an old witch — not looking out for her own grandchildren but turning against an illegitimate daughter who had lost her mother.

He was walking with his face dark when someone else said nearby: "Heard from Imperial Physician Lin that the Third Young Miss of that household fell ill from accumulated grief. They say she had barely been back a month before she was driven to vomit blood. One can only imagine what she suffered in that Manor in that one month."

Shen Rongshen heard these words and immediately stepped forward to argue. But the men backed away a few steps, looking at him coldly: "Do not come and sully us with your presence. We are not the ones capable of such conduct."

Shen Rongshen's face had gone a terrible color. In the great hall that morning, memorial after memorial had been submitted censuring him for moral failings — a man ruled by his wife, his household in disorder, unworthy of his post. Now, seeing the others recoil from him as though he were a snake, he felt his dignity stripped from him entirely, and left with his face covered.

Ahead of him, Chen He blocked his path with a cold, mocking smile: "Not satisfied with skimming from the Ministry of Revenue's funds, and now going to flatter yourself into the Zhang family's favor too?"

"There are quite a few memorials censuring you now. Do not expect anyone to intercede for you this time."

Shen Rongshen's face went iron-gray. He had no wish to exchange words with Chen He and swept his sleeve and walked away.

Xu Zhian fared no better. Everyone knew he was connected by marriage to the Second Branch of the Jian'an Manor, and his friends were all laughing at him — saying he was about to bring home a little tigress too, to be managed and kept from taking so much as one concubine, and eventually forced to clear all the women from his household.

And they said his future father-in-law might not be able to hold onto his position — that the Jian'an Marquis Manor could only go further downhill.

Xu Zhian's face was drawn. For a brief moment he felt that having a marital connection to the Jian'an Marquis Manor was a humiliation.

A friend clapped him on the shoulder and joked: "Heard your mother-in-law-to-be is a fierce demon woman, and now you are bringing home a young tigress. Brother, I genuinely pity you."

"With this business spreading the way it has, which decent man among the upright will want to associate with the Jian'an Marquis Second Branch? They would be afraid of being tarred with the same brush — the name of selling a daughter for advancement, toadying to the powerful. Scholars from humble origins would think it beneath them to have any connection to the Second Branch. You marry that legitimate daughter of theirs, and people will start avoiding you too."

Xu Zhian heard this and flung off the man's hand and walked away.

Everywhere he went now he attracted pointing and staring, with people coming up to ask him about the Jian'an Manor. Xu Zhian had known nothing of any of this — Shen Zhaozhao had never mentioned it — and now that it had all blown up, he found it deeply embarrassing.

The ugliness was now known throughout the court. Zhang Tingyi, from what was heard, was not much better off — the Ministry of Punishments had sent men to the Zhang household last night. The matter had not erupted publicly, but those who knew of it were not few. Zhang Tingyi had not appeared at morning court today.

All that was known was that Zhang Tingyi had gone in the night to prostrate himself before the Emperor and beg forgiveness for his crimes. What exactly had happened was still unclear, but he was clearly in no position to attend to anyone else's matters.

No one knew when this ugly affair would finally draw to a close.

Zhang Yuanheng, learning of all this, stumbled on his feet and nearly lost his footing.

He suddenly thought back to the time Shen Weici had urged him to come and propose sooner. Had she known what was coming?

He had no thought for anything else now. He only wanted to see Shen Weici at once.

chapters.title: Making Trouble for Linchun Courtyard
chapters.content:
Inside the Marquis Manor, Lady Wang of the Third Branch was sitting before an upstairs pavilion admiring the plum blossoms when she spotted Lady Wen in the distance, hurrying in the direction of the Old Madam's quarters with a handful of matrons.

She smiled, called out to her, and came down with her maids to stand in Lady Wen's path: "Where is Second Sister-in-law off to?"

Lady Wen's expression was far from pleasant. Seeing Lady Wang approach, she had no heart for conversation and only said: "I am going to speak with the Old Madam."

Lady Wang covered a smile with her hand and looked at Lady Wen: "Is Second Sister-in-law going about the business of the Third Young Miss?"

Lady Wen's manner stiffened. She looked at Lady Wang with a face that had gone a shade darker.

Lady Wang looked at Lady Wen with a smile: "What is Second Sister-in-law looking at me like that for? The whole city is talking about it now. Who isn't?"

"Just yesterday when I went back to my family for my nephew's hundredth-day feast, my own relatives were asking me about it."

"They also said I have two concubine-born daughters in my household and reminded me a thousand times not to follow that example and do something so disgraceful."

"Though they were worried for nothing. I am not so cold-hearted as Second Sister-in-law. I could never do such a thing."

Lady Wang was finally able to hold her head high for once. The Third Branch had always been a step below the Second Branch, which came down ultimately to her husband being the lesser man — though at least her son showed some promise.

But Lady Wen, with her slightly superior family background, had always put on airs in front of her, and was forever rubbing in how clean and orderly her own inner quarters were. Well — however orderly, men would still stray. And had she not had a daughter brought home from outside? And then been unable to tolerate it and done this, and had it all come out? She deserved every bit of it.

Lady Wen's expression went thoroughly black. She understood perfectly well that Lady Wang was saying all of this to needle her.

She gave a cold laugh and looked at Lady Wang: "Fourth Young Miss should be of marriageable age next year, should she not? With Second Sister-in-law so principled as she is, I am quite looking forward to seeing what kind of household she finds for her, and how generous the dowry."

Lady Wang paused and then said with an acid smile: "That need not concern Second Sister-in-law. At least I will not be cruel enough to marry a good daughter off to an old man."

"Nor will I drive a perfectly good girl to her death."

Lady Wen's expression underwent a violent change. Even her mask of forced composure cracked — she pointed at Lady Wang, grinding her teeth: "Wanting Shen Weici to marry Zhang Tingyi was a matter of considering his household's standing, and she herself was willing to go. I did not force her."

Lady Wang found this so funny she actually laughed: "I must admit I have developed a new admiration for Second Sister-in-law. Saying something this false without so much as a blush or a flicker — I simply do not have Second Sister-in-law's ruthlessness."

"If Third Young Miss had been willing to marry that Zhang Tingyi on her own, why did she suddenly cough up blood last time?"

"Surely Second Sister-in-law is not going to say she was so happy she coughed blood."

Lady Wen's face went the color of iron. She said nothing more, swept her sleeve, and walked away.

Lady Wang watched Lady Wen's retreating figure with deep satisfaction. She had been about to bring up all the memorials censuring the Second Lord at court, but thought better of it — the Old Madam might think she was taking too much pleasure in others' misfortune and make trouble for her. So she let it go.

She watched Lady Wen go with a cold smile: "Give it a few more days, and she will not be holding that head so high."

With that, in rather good spirits, she went back with her maids to enjoy the plum blossoms.

Meanwhile Lady Wen went to the Old Madam's quarters with a face full of grievance, wanting to discuss what was to be done.

The Old Madam was chatting and laughing with her maids when Lady Wen came in looking crestfallen. She frowned with displeasure: "Why do you come in looking like that? Do you mean to show me on purpose?"

Lady Wen had not expected the Old Madam to read it that way. She hurried to sit down: "Old Madam is misjudging me. Have you heard the rumors that have been going around these past days?"

The Old Madam's heavy eyelids lifted toward Lady Wen: "What rumors?"

She frowned at her personal maid Yuehong: "What else are you lot hiding from me?"

Yuehong heard this and dropped immediately to her knees: "Those rumors are false, and we were afraid if Old Madam heard them your health would suffer, so we did not tell you."

The Old Madam had been confined to her warm room these past two days, drowsy and seldom going out. With her maids keeping things from her, of course she had not heard what was being said outside.

Hearing Yuehong's words, her expression darkened: "Tell me exactly what is being said outside."

Yuehong knelt on the floor and looked at the Old Madam, head bowed low, speaking in a halting whisper: "They are saying outside that Old Madam is cruel — that she is driving her own granddaughter to death…"

"And also…"

Yuehong did not dare continue. She trembled on the floor and kowtowed: "These are only wild talk from outside. Old Madam, please do not take them to heart."

The Old Madam almost fainted from fury at just this one line. She hurled the teacup in her hand to the floor and pointed at Yuehong with trembling fingers: "Continue…"

Yuehong looked at the shattered teacup that had landed beside her. Her voice shook even harder, but she had no choice — she raised her head and continued: "Outside they are also saying that it is because Old Madam indulges cruelty that the Second Lord was willing to do such a thing, selling his daughter for advancement…"

"And that the Jian'an Marquis Manor's growing decline is also because of Old Madam…"

When Yuehong finished the last sentence she was drenched in sweat, her forehead pressed to the floor, not daring to raise her eyes even a fraction.

The warm inner chamber fell so silent that the drop of a pin could have been heard. The maids standing nearby all went rigid with fear, not a sound among them.

Even Lady Wen did not dare open her mouth.

In truth, the words about the Old Madam were among the milder things being said. The accusations against Lady Wen herself — calling her a tigress, a she-demon — were far more numerous. The Manor was now using 'tigress' for her behind closed doors. Lady Wen had already punished several servants over it, but could not stop their mouths.

The Old Madam sat for a stunned moment, then came to herself, nearly unable to draw in a breath. She brought her hand down hard on the table: "Who on earth started spreading this talk?!"

Lady Wen looked at the Old Madam: "I also felt something was strange about how quickly this spread. I specifically sent maids outside to trace where it began — and what they found was that it started with several storytellers."

"Those storytellers are vicious. They have painted me as a demon mother who drove her stepdaughter to death, and said things equally awful about Old Madam. When my maids asked the storytellers who told them to say all this, they only said: if you don't want it known, don't do the deed — and no amount of questioning could get anything more out of them."

The Old Madam's expression went cold: "Who would spread these things without cause? It must be that courtyard — Linchun."

"And here I thought she had been so quiet. She has been working from behind the scenes."

She looked at Yuehong: "Go and bring all the gate boys from the main gate and every side gate. I want to ask which ones have gone in and out recently."

chapters.title: The Old Madam's Fury, and Zhang Yuanheng's Second Visit
chapters.content:
Within minutes, the warm inner chamber of the West Small Compound was crowded with servants kneeling in a solid mass across the floor.

The Old Madam's gaze pressed heavily down upon one of them: "You are saying that yesterday afternoon Linchun Courtyard's Yuedeng went out? How long before she came back?"

The gate boy immediately replied: "She went out in the afternoon, carrying the Second Lord's token. She was back within about an hour and a half."

The Old Madam looked at the coachman from that day: "Where did she go?"

The coachman knelt before the Old Madam and gave a truthful account: "Yuedeng went first to a pharmacy to collect medicine, then to the Yiyong Earl's Manor. Yuedeng said the Third Young Miss was no longer connected to the Earl's Manor and asked her to return the keepsake. This old servant did indeed see Yuedeng hand back the item she carried to the master of the Earl's Manor in person. Second Young Master Song happened to also be present at the time."

Lady Wen heard this and frowned, looking sternly at the coachman: "You are certain every word is true?"

The coachman kowtowed repeatedly: "Second Lady, Old Madam, every word is the truth. I have hidden nothing."

Lady Wen thought about it — the coachman had no reason to hide anything. And besides, she had heard the full story of Shen Weici and the Second Young Master of the Earl's Manor from her husband — she knew that Zhang Yuanheng had indeed been intending to come and propose, and that he had even given her a keepsake.

Now that Shen Weici had returned the keepsake, perhaps she had simply accepted her fate and was preparing to marry Zhang Tingyi.

There was not a single fault to find in any of it — on the contrary, the girl had been remarkably obedient.

She turned to the Old Madam with a darkened expression: "Could it be that the gossip was started by maids who went home to visit their families?"

The Old Madam's face was grim as she instructed the housekeeper standing nearby to bring every maid who had left the compound in the past few days.

The housekeeper complied, and quickly compiled a list of everyone who had gone out over the past three days for the Old Madam to review.

The maids on the list included rough-work girls, Third Branch maids, and First Branch maids — seven or eight in total.

The housekeeper said awkwardly: "The maid from the Second Young Master of the First Branch's rooms may be a little difficult to summon."

The Old Madam's brow furrowed. She looked at the names on the register in her hand, and with a sudden surge of fury threw it to the floor.

"Then bring the rest of the maids to the front courtyard and give each of them thirty strokes of the board. Have the other servants watch. Let that be a warning — if anyone dares gossip outside again, they will face the same."

The housekeeper hurried to carry this out, taking with him everyone kneeling in the room as he went.

Lady Wen looked at the Old Madam: "Even if we beat and kill a few servants now, the gossip outside has already spread."

"And I have been thinking — those storytellers gave such a vivid, detailed account. Maids simply whispering to each other would not produce that. A few servants gossiping at most would keep it to whispers. Would they dare take it out in public and broadcast it?"

"I keep feeling that with the way this has blown up, someone must be behind it, fanning the flames."

The Old Madam gave Lady Wen a cold look: "What use is there in saying all this now?"

"The story is already out. You cannot silence everyone outside. Now you should be thinking about how to stop the talking!"

Lady Wen, jolted by the Old Madam's shout, looked at her and said: "What if Zhang Tingyi steps in to help?"

The Old Madam's expression went colder still: "You fool. Do you think the situation needs to get any bigger?"

Lady Wen fell silent and then asked timidly: "Then what should we do now? We have already offended Zhang Tingyi — who else can we turn to for help?"

The wrinkled face of the Old Madam went dark and low as she said: "The only thing now is to get Shen Weici's illness to clear up as quickly as possible, get the marriage done, and have her stand up at the wedding banquet and say she married Zhang Tingyi of her own free will. That way we neither offend Zhang Tingyi nor have to confront this matter directly, and the whole thing blows over."

Lady Wen asked hesitantly: "But will Shen Weici be obedient enough to say at the wedding banquet that she married willingly?"

The Old Madam looked at Lady Wen mildly: "Did you not hear just now? She has already returned the Earl's Manor keepsake. That means she has accepted her fate and is willing to marry Zhang Tingyi."

"She herself has accepted it — what does it cost her to say one sentence at the banquet?"

"At most you can give her a little more in the way of wedding gifts."

Lady Wen heard the Old Madam's words and felt this was the only viable option left. She nodded: "I will go and check on her this afternoon and see how the illness is getting along."

The Old Madam looked at Lady Wen: "Go and settle her emotions carefully. Speak with more warmth. Tell her about all the advantages of marrying into the Zhang household."

"A girl from a small place like her — how much of fine living has she seen? Tell her all about the Zhang household's wealth. She may even end up grateful to you."

"But do not tell her about the rumors outside. She has not left her courtyard these days and should still not know what is being said. Remind the maids in her room as well not to breathe a word of it to me."

Lady Wen nodded: "Then we will follow the Old Madam's plan."

News of the flogging in the front courtyard spread through the entire Manor within moments, leaving everyone walking on eggshells. The whispered conversations dropped even lower — a few maids behind closed doors in the servants' room at most.

When Yuedeng went out to pick plum blossoms for tea, she heard the news and ran with Hexia to the front courtyard to have a look.

There were more servants gathered at the front courtyard than ever before. Yuedeng saw the person strapped to the bench being beaten half to death without being able to cry out, the cloth at their hips soaked red. She felt a chill run up her back.

Nearby someone murmured: "Old Madam really is cold — flogging people whether they were guilty or not. At that pace, the woman might not be able to have children after this. No wonder there are all those rumors outside…"

Before the words were out, someone beside her clapped a hand over her mouth: "Are you mad? Saying that at a time like this?"

The first woman hurriedly shut her mouth.

Yuedeng looked a moment longer, the scene all red in her eyes, and quickly pulled Hexia away.

Back in Linchun Courtyard, Yuedeng told Shen Weici about the front courtyard: "Old Madam really is vicious. Miss didn't see what that maid looked like — all blood. They say she will probably never carry a child after this. It must be because the rumors outside got pretty loud, and Old Madam heard and called in all the servants who had gone out in the past few days to take the beating."

Shen Weici was sitting at the window sewing her embroidery pouch. She heard Yuedeng's words and her needle paused. She looked out for a moment and sighed: "After all, others have been implicated because of me."

"But I had no choice…"

Yuedeng heard Shen Weici say this and hurried to say: "How can Miss be blamed for that?"

"This whole thing was wrong of them in the first place. Miss only told that small medicine boy — who would have thought he was such a talker? In just this short a time, and already this many people know?"

Shen Weici frowned: "I do not know exactly what is being said outside. I cannot go beyond Linchun Courtyard these days. The maids in here had best also stay put — otherwise it will arouse the Second Lady's suspicion."

"In ordinary circumstances it should not have traveled this fast."

Yuedeng, seeing Shen Weici frowning, said: "The faster it spreads outside, the better — it will show the Old Madam and the Second Lady whether they still have the face to force Miss into marrying Zhang Tingyi."

Then she asked: "I also went out yesterday — how come Old Madam didn't punish me?"

Shen Weici looked up at Yuedeng: "She didn't punish you for two reasons. First, you were only out a short while and went to the Earl's Manor to return the keepsake — which satisfies Old Madam that I am being obedient. Second, you are my closest maid. If Old Madam beat you, how would she get me to go along willingly with marrying Zhang Tingyi?"

"If you had gone somewhere else yesterday, or gone to the Earl's Manor without telling the coachman, you would probably be in that front courtyard right now."

Yuedeng nodded in understanding: "No wonder Miss specifically told me to tell the coachman truthfully what we were going to the Earl's Manor for. Otherwise, knowing Old Madam's tricks, she would have decided right away that I was the one who spread the gossip outside."

Shen Weici squeezed Yuedeng's hand and said quietly: "From now on, wherever you are, do not use words like 'old witch.' The people around us in this Manor are not necessarily trustworthy — we arrived here as strangers and don't know who might turn on us. You also have to be careful and not tell everyone everything."

Yuedeng bowed her head and said softly: "I just dislike Old Madam's way of looking so compassionate and yet showing not a shred of kindness to the servants."

Shen Weici lowered her head and embroidered one more stitch in the pattern on her work, then paused and put another embroidery hoop from the table into Yuedeng's hands: "That is not something for you to think about. Come and embroider with me."

Yuedeng took the hoop and had no choice but to sit obediently beside Shen Weici and keep her mouth shut.

Hexia came in carrying tea made with plum blossoms, and a faint fragrance drifted in with her. A sliver of winter sunlight through the window fell on Shen Weici. She looked down and took a sip of the warm tea, then narrowed her eyes and looked out the window.

---

That afternoon, Shen Rongshen arrived home to find Zhang Yuanheng waiting at the main gate — evidently there for him.

Shen Rongshen felt he had lost face before Zhang Yuanheng too, having been the one who orchestrated the match between them in the first place. Now for this to have happened was mortifying.

He did not dare meet Zhang Yuanheng's eyes. Averting his gaze as though he had not seen him, he tried to walk straight through the gate. But Zhang Yuanheng came after him calling: "Lord Shen."

He called twice. Pretending any longer would have been too obvious. Shen Rongshen had no choice but to turn around.

He was bracing himself for an awkward exchange when Zhang Yuanheng unexpectedly folded his hands and bowed deeply, then offered his apology: "I should have come to propose marriage earlier. But my household encountered some difficulties, and I was delayed. I come today specifically to offer my apologies."

Zhang Yuanheng looked at Shen Rongshen: "If my failure to come to propose is why Lord Shen has arranged for Third Young Miss Shen to marry Lord Zhang, I ask Lord Shen to give me one more chance. I will persuade my family, and will come to propose very shortly."

In truth Zhang Yuanheng had already come the previous day, only to be turned away by Shen Rongshen. Today he had come earlier and waited at the main gate.

When he had returned home that time, he had been planning to have his mother and a matchmaker come to propose the very next day — but to his complete surprise, that next day a representative of the third branch of the Song Ducal Manor arrived saying they were interested in joining the two families by marriage. His father and mother immediately changed their minds.

He had been in the palace at the time and knew nothing of it. He still thought his mother had already gone to propose. Only when he returned home did he learn she had done no such thing.

His father had urged him to reconsider. Zhang Yuanheng had said, firmly and without hesitation: he would marry no one but Shen Weici.

The third concubine-born daughter of the Song Ducal Manor's third branch — he had never met her. And even if the Song Ducal household was the most powerful and prestigious in the capital, with a pedigree of a hundred years of prominence, holders of military power, intimates of the Son of Heaven, and virtually the first among noble families — that was all quite beside the point. He had no interest whatsoever.

But his father had placed every hope for the Earl's Manor's rise on him, convinced that marrying a daughter of the Song Ducal household would instantly elevate him, and by extension restore the Earl's Manor's standing in the capital.

Zhang Yuanheng had never been the kind of man who needed to climb on another's power. He wanted to rise on his own ability.

Yet his father and mother held firm. He had missed his moment, was too ashamed to face Shen Weici directly, and had written a letter asking her to wait a little longer — he would definitely come to propose.

But then, within just a few days, came the news that she was to marry Zhang Tingyi.

And the day before, he had seen his father return the keepsake he had sent her. The pain that struck him was immediate. He knew Shen Weici had misunderstood him. He rushed over that very night to seek an audience, only to be turned away by Shen Rongshen. He had the letter passed to the gate servant, only to have the servant return it to him with the word that his letters could no longer be delivered.

Zhang Yuanheng's heart had gone completely cold in that instant. He walked home in a daze and did not sleep all night.

Thinking of Shen Weici being pushed to the point of coughing up blood, he hurried back today the moment he left his duties, wanting to see her just once.

Shen Rongshen stared at Zhang Yuanheng in confusion, bowing and apologizing like that — he had assumed he was coming to reproach him for breaking faith.

He suddenly recalled that Shen Weici had said the Earl's Manor intended to come and propose the day Zhang Tingyi came. How was it that now he was bowing and saying he had been delayed and could not come?

Was this a roundabout pleasantry?

But given the current situation, he could not agree to Zhang Yuanheng's request yet.

Zhang Tingyi had run into difficulties for now, but his younger sister Lady Zhang Consort had been in solid imperial favor for years. As long as Lady Zhang whispered in the Emperor's ear, Zhang Tingyi could weather any storm. And if he now reversed course and refused, would that not earn him the name of kicking a man when he was down? Zhang Tingyi would never forgive him.

Yet all that pointing and whispering had stripped him of his dignity, and he was filled with a deep, bitter regret.

Shen Rongshen was torn. He glanced at Zhang Yuanheng, who was still bowing, then quickly helped him straighten up and went along with his words: "At Lady Zhang's birthday banquet, Lord Zhang took a liking to Weici, and you still had not come to propose. So the Zhang household sent a matchmaker."

He sighed as though helpless: "You know that Zhang Tingyi commands his own power at court, and with the crown prince still unestablished, I could not afford to offend him. That is why I had no choice but to agree. But I also do not want Weici to marry him. Give me a little more time — let me see if there is still room to turn this around."

Shen Rongshen was already taking precautions on both fronts: stabilize Zhang Yuanheng for now, and redirect the blame onto Zhang Tingyi — leaving himself in the position of the helpless man caught in the middle.

Zhang Yuanheng heard Shen Rongshen's explanation and understood its meaning. Though pained, he raised his head and looked at Shen Rongshen: "I understand Lord Shen's difficulty. I will wait."

He added: "I heard Third Young Miss Shen has been seriously ill. Could I go in and see her?"

Shen Rongshen would certainly not let Zhang Yuanheng in to see Shen Weici at this point. He frowned and sighed: "Weici is seriously ill and cannot receive visitors just now. Please go home first. If the two of us can still find a way to make this match, nothing would be better."

Zhang Yuanheng heard Shen Rongshen's words and understood that much of what had been said was probably meant to put him off. Zhang Tingyi, however powerful, could never simply take a woman in broad daylight. The Yiyong Earl's Manor and the Jian'an Marquis Manor were both households of standing — Zhang Tingyi would have to show at least some restraint. He had not yet gone so completely lawless.

There was also the possibility that Shen Rongshen, seeing the Zhang household's greater prestige and the growing likelihood of the Fourth Prince becoming crown prince, had simply stopped considering him.

But today he absolutely had to see Shen Weici. No matter what, he had to make everything clear to her.

chapters.title: With Young Lord Song Here, Who Dares Make Trouble?
chapters.content:
Yet no matter how Zhang Yuanheng pleaded, Shen Rongshen would not let him through in the end.

He knew Zhang Yuanheng's genuine feeling for Shen Weici and humored him with assurances that she was perfectly well, before finally feigning a headache and dismissing him.

Shen Rongshen watched Zhang Yuanheng's retreating figure, saw him board his carriage — and let out a long, heavy sigh.

He went back to the Second Branch courtyard with worry written all over his face.

The moment he arrived, Lady Wen stepped forward to meet him: "My lord — have you been to see Lord Zhang yet?"

The sight of Lady Wen now filled Shen Rongshen with a dull irritation. He shook off her hand and went straight to the inner chamber to change out of his official robes.

Lady Wen, caught off guard by the shove, stumbled back several paces. It was only Shen Zhaozhao, standing behind her, who caught her before she could fall.

Shen Zhaozhao looked at her father's behavior in confusion: "What is wrong with Father today?"

Lady Wen stared blankly at the swaying curtain, then patted Shen Zhaozhao and pushed through after him.

Inside the inner chamber, one maid was helping Shen Rongshen out of his official robes while another brought his house clothes.

Lady Wen had just been shoved and still had not recovered from the shock. Since their marriage she had always been the one deferred to, every whim accommodated — to be treated this way, suddenly and without warning, was not something she could accept. Her temper came up at once and, with the maids still present, she pointed at Shen Rongshen: "If you have suffered outside, do not come home and take it out on me."

"Shen Rongshen. You owe me nothing."

Shen Rongshen heard these words and was furious in an instant. Heedless of the fact that he was only half into his new clothes, he kicked the maid aside, took two steps to Lady Wen, and brought his hand across her face with full force: "If not for your meddling and going behind my back to force Weici onto Zhang Tingyi, would any of this have happened?!"

"Now the whole court is talking about me, pointing at me, saying I have failed in my duty and sold my daughter for gain. One by one they avoid me as though I were a disease."

"Two days running with memorials censuring me reaching the Emperor, and now my post is about to be taken from me — are you satisfied?!"

Lady Wen was stunned by the sudden blow. She heard the words he roared and went dazed, covering her face and staring at him in disbelief: "How can it have gotten this serious? You only wanted Shen Weici to marry Zhang Tingyi. Say outside that she chose it herself — what selling daughter for gain?"

Shen Rongshen had been holding down a full day's worth of fury. Hearing Lady Wen's stupid words, he nearly choked with rage: "Do you know how it is being described outside right now?"

"They say Shen Rongshen is a spineless man, entirely ruled at home by a vicious wife, unable to manage even his own daughter's life affairs — standing by while the vicious wife wrecked the daughter's proper match and forced her onto an old man. Practically trying to push the girl to her death."

"They also say you abused her daily, and then, unmoved by her coughing blood, went straight to her bedside again to pressure her — only waiting to drive someone to an actual death."

"And they say the Jian'an Marquis Manor grows more decrepit by the day, reduced to relying on a concubine-born daughter to flatter the Zhang household. They say I have shamed the honor of scholars."

"Now if I say Weici went willingly, do you honestly think anyone will believe it?!"

Lady Wen backed away several paces, frightened by his voice growing louder with each sentence. Shen Zhaozhao, who had just come in behind her, froze at her father's shouting and went to hold her mother up: "My mother is Shen Weici's legal stepmother. Mother may marry her to whomever she wishes. What right do people outside have to say a word against Mother?"

"Even if Mother gave her to a beggar, she would not dare say no. How is it that now that she is being given to Zhang Tingyi, people are blaming Mother?"

"Even if the Earl's Manor intended to come and propose, they came too late — Mother did nothing wrong!"

Shen Rongshen pointed at Shen Zhaozhao with trembling fingers and turned to Lady Wen: "This is the daughter your upbringing has produced. With a character like this, if she does not change, she will come to grief."

Lady Wen, now at something of a loss, looked at Shen Rongshen: "What is the point of saying all this now? You are being censured — think about what to do."

"This all started because of Zhang Tingyi. Have you gone to speak with Zhang Tingyi about it?"

Shen Rongshen looked at Lady Wen coldly: "Do you think I have not been to see Zhang Tingyi?"

"When I went to look for him this afternoon, I was told Zhang Tingyi had been kept at the palace. Apparently there was some matter from last night. I tried to ask through the palace attendants when he would come out, but could not find out — I will have to wait until later and go to the Zhang household again."

Lady Wen hurried to say: "Then what about your brother? Let your brother help again."

Shen Rongshen gave a cold snort: "My brother has been dragged into this mess because of me too. Today in court when I was censured, not a single word did my brother say in my defense. Afterward I went to speak with him, and he swept his sleeve and walked away without a backward look. He wants no part of it."

Lady Wen's expression shifted: "How can your brother be like this? We are all one household — if one falls, all fall. Being demoted serves no one, including him."

Shen Rongshen slumped in the armchair, propping his forehead: "My brother has always cared most about his reputation. He is a man of upright character. When something like this comes out, he feels it has damaged the Manor's name and refuses to help at the cost of his own reputation."

Lady Wen, agitated, came to his side: "Should we not ask the Old Madam to persuade your brother? And also have Princess Consort Huimin put in a good word with the Emperor — that might still save your position."

Shen Rongshen paused, brow deeply furrowed: "I suppose it is the only way."

"Though right now Princess Consort Huimin is still at the temple in prayer. I cannot disturb her. The only other hope is to have Song Zhang say something favorable in front of the Emperor."

He told a maid to hurry up with his clothes, then went to find the Old Madam.

Shen Zhaozhao watched her father leave and said, dissatisfied: "What is the matter with Father today? I have never seen him this angry before."

"It is only a matter of marrying Shen Weici off to Zhang Tingyi. What is wrong with that, given her origins? If you ask me, she ought to be bowing down and thanking Mother for it."

Lady Wen cut Shen Zhaozhao off and frowned: "You are not to say those things anymore. Your father's heart is currently set on that wretched Shen Weici, and the rumors outside cannot be suppressed. Your father is already in a foul mood. If you say this in front of him again, he will only get angrier."

Shen Zhaozhao pursed her lips and looked at Lady Wen: "I truly cannot understand who started those rumors, or how they spread so badly. I dare not even go out now — the whole city is talking about our Manor. It has almost become common knowledge. They have painted Mother as utterly monstrous. It is truly infuriating!"

Lady Wen also sat down, mildly irritable: "I also never imagined it would spread this far. But those rumors themselves cannot actually harm me in any real way — it is only words from common people. What I never expected was for your father's position to come into danger as well. The most pressing thing now is truly to find a way to stop the spread."

Shen Zhaozhao suddenly had an idea: "Those rumors started with the storytellers, didn't they? Why not have Second Brother round up those storytellers and put a stop to it? Have them go back and say everything they said was false, that Shen Weici chose this willingly — wouldn't that fix it?"

"And then have Shen Weici stand alongside the storytellers and make the clarification — who could still doubt it?"

"And have Second Brother come along too — with him there, who would dare make any trouble?"

chapters.title: Which Matters More — Your Face or the Manor's Face?
chapters.content:
The moment Shen Zhaozhao's words landed, the tight frown on Lady Wen's face smoothed entirely. She looked at Shen Zhaozhao: "That is actually a real plan."

"Have Shen Weici stand alongside the storytellers and retract everything — the rumors will collapse on their own, and the Manor's reputation will be restored. Your father's name will be protected too."

"We will need Song Zhang's help for this. Have his men round up those storytellers and compel them to cooperate. They will fall into line quickly enough."

She instructed the matron at her side: "Go to the front gate and let me know the moment the Second Young Master returns."

The matron nodded and hurried off.

Lady Wen rose and, with a full retinue, headed for Linchun Courtyard.

Inside Linchun Courtyard, Hexia came rushing in to say the Second Lady and Second Young Miss had arrived. Shen Weici heard this without much surprise, gave a quiet acknowledgment, set down her embroidery hoop, and told Yuedeng to bring tea.

When Lady Wen came in, she found Shen Weici sitting before the charcoal fire, a thin blanket draped over her lap, a cup of warm tea in hand, leaning against the chair with a wan, sickly air.

Lady Wen was deeply displeased by Shen Weici's constitution — always catching colds, always coughing blood. People who didn't know better would think she had been pampered like a daughter of the highest household, more delicate even than a princess from the palace.

Shen Zhaozhao behind her looked at Shen Weici's pallid face with equal disdain. She could not fathom what Zhang Yuanheng had ever seen in her.

When Shen Weici saw Lady Wen come in, she moved to put down her tea and stand. Lady Wen glanced at her: "You are ill — stay seated. There is no need for formalities."

Lady Wen took the stool a maid brought, accepted her tea, and looked at Shen Weici with a manner of visible concern: "Are you feeling any better these past days?"

Shen Weici let a look of touched feeling cross her face: "I have caused Stepmother to worry. I have taken two doses of medicine and am feeling much improved."

Lady Wen gave a performed sigh of relief and nodded at Shen Weici: "I had not imagined your constitution was this fragile. It was probably a hard life in Yuyang that left your foundations weak. Stay here in the Manor and take good care of yourself — build up your health."

Yuedeng, standing behind Shen Weici, found every word of this transparently hollow. She did not believe for an instant that Lady Wen had suddenly grown any goodwill.

Shen Weici heard Lady Wen's words and looked up softly: "I know Stepmother cares for me. Only — the weather has been getting colder, and Stepmother should also dress more warmly."

Lady Wen blinked, then smiled: "You are even more considerate than Zhaozhao. No wonder your father always says how sensible you are."

Shen Weici lowered her eyes and coughed once, then said quietly: "Father taught me to be respectful and attentive to my stepmother. I have always remembered that."

Lady Wen thought to herself that this Shen Weici was one she had been underestimating. The girl spoke with not a drop out of place. Even Lady Wen herself could not read whether it was genuine or not.

She looked at that fragile face and could not find a single crack of falseness. This whole mess had started entirely because of her, and yet here she sat, as though the whole thing had nothing to do with her.

Lady Wen smiled faintly, leaned back against the chair, drank her tea at leisure, but kept her eyes fixed sharply on Shen Weici's: "Have you heard the talk that has been going around outside?"

Shen Weici looked up in apparent surprise: "What talk? I have not left the courtyard these past days and truly do not know."

Lady Wen smiled mildly and looked into Shen Weici's eyes: "Outside they are saying I am a cruel woman who abuses her stepdaughter. That your father nearly drove you to your death in his eagerness to sell his daughter for advancement."

"Even the Old Madam has been denounced. Everyone in the Manor is troubled by it."

She smiled again: "You are the one who knows nothing here. I suppose that does spare you a good deal of worry."

Shen Weici looked at Lady Wen with a slightly pale face: "How did it come to be said like that outside?"

Lady Wen replied: "Some storytellers in the capital — no one knows where they got their information — have been holding forth in teahouses. The whole capital knows about it now. Your father's reputation has been destroyed by those storytellers."

"And there are those who are censuring your father over it. If your father loses his post because of this, your life will not be easier for it either."

"Furthermore, all of this may have given offense to Zhang Tingyi. When you are married into his household, he might well take it out on you."

Shen Weici listened to Lady Wen and, seeing her come here now, felt something jump in her chest.

She had not understood how it had reached the storytellers. Though the effect she had wanted had been achieved, the outcome had not quite gone as she intended — Lady Wen still had not given up the idea of marrying her to Zhang Tingyi.

In her original plan, Lady Wen and her father, under the pressure of public opinion, might have abandoned this marriage. She had not anticipated that their fear of offending Zhang Tingyi would prevent them from letting go.

She understood: as long as Zhang Tingyi remained in imperial favor, this matter would not be resolved so easily.

Shen Weici looked down slightly and sipped her tea: "That it has spread like this is something I truly did not foresee. But these are only rumors — the Emperor is perceptive enough to distinguish what is true. He would surely not punish Father on the basis of unfounded hearsay."

Lady Wen's expression stiffened slightly. She had not expected Shen Weici to fail to follow her lead.

The response should have been panic and a plea for what to do — to which Lady Wen would say: go out and make a public retraction. Instead this oblique little thrust at her had arrived.

Everyone in the Manor knew whether the matter was true or false, and the rumors differed little from reality. If it were genuinely false, Lady Wen would not be this helpless. But because it was true, there was no rebuttal to be made.

Lady Wen's face flickered. She was about to speak when Shen Zhaozhao stepped forward, impatient: "What use is any of that? What is urgent now is to go out and make a clarification."

She glared at Shen Weici: "I want you to go out tomorrow and make a clarification alongside the storytellers. Once you have cleared it up publicly at the teahouse, people will stop spreading it."

Shen Weici now fully understood why they had come.

She said with apparent alarm: "But as a woman who has not yet married, to go and show my face in a teahouse like that — what will people think of me afterward?"

Shen Zhaozhao gave a cold snort, her eyes arctic: "What matters more — your face or the Manor's face?"

"You are going to marry Zhang Tingyi regardless — why worry about what people think?"

"This situation arose because of you — of course you should be the one to explain it. Or would you prefer everyone in this Manor to be denounced by people outside on your behalf?"

"Even Grandmother has been slandered. Can you truly feel at ease staying in Linchun Courtyard, without even a shred of filial feeling?"

"Besides, Young Lord Song will go with you. What are you afraid of?"

The room fell silent in the wake of Shen Zhaozhao's words.

Lady Wen sipped her tea calmly, but her eyes were sharp and fixed on Shen Weici's face. She wanted to see how she would refuse.

chapters.title: Adding More Fuel to the Fire
chapters.content:
The room was silent. The maids all looked at Shen Weici where she sat with her eyes quietly downcast.

Yuedeng was almost trembling with the urge to leap to her feet. They had done this unreasonable thing and now had the audacity to accuse the young mistress of having no conscience.

Yuedeng looked down in worried agitation at Shen Weici, fingers clenched tight.

After Shen Zhaozhao finished her volley of pressing words, Shen Weici let out a quiet breath, passed the teacup to Yuedeng beside her, then pressed her handkerchief to her lips and coughed a few times.

Her voice was very soft. She spoke: "Second Sister need not put it that way. My face is of course less important than the Manor's."

"Only — going out in public looking this ill would only confirm that I am gravely sick."

"And as for the storytellers — words once spoken are difficult to take back. If I go to the teahouse and say I am marrying Zhang Tingyi of my own free will, Second Sister — how many people do you think will believe it?"

Shen Zhaozhao gave a cold snort and stepped forward: "Whether they believe it or not is beside the point. You yourself have gone to say it. Even if they don't believe it, they will stop spreading it."

"And anyone who still dares say otherwise, Second Brother will have them hauled off to prison."

Shen Weici looked at Lady Wen: "Is Stepmother of the same mind?"

Lady Wen looked at Shen Weici and sighed: "Right now this is the only approach. I am afraid we must trouble you somewhat."

Shen Weici nodded: "Since Stepmother is asking me to go, I naturally would not dare refuse. I will do as Stepmother says."

Lady Wen saw how obedient Shen Weici was and smiled, looking at her: "We have no choice in this. You are also now a daughter of the Marquis Manor — its reputation is part yours too. If you go out and give an explanation, when you come back I will not treat you badly."

"The Old Madam will not treat you badly either."

Shen Weici smiled back: "I know all that."

She then coughed more severely — a long spell of it — and the pallor of her face flushed with a brief pink. Her jade skin beneath the rose glow of that color was startling enough to make even Lady Wen, watching, feel a small shock.

Shen Zhaozhao looked at Shen Weici being this beautiful even while this ill, and clenched her hand inwardly with dark envy. If Zhang Tingyi had not set his sights on her, she would have loved to ruin that face.

Lady Wen frowned at Shen Weici: "Why are you coughing so severely?"

Shen Weici smiled faintly: "It is nothing serious — only the cough is a little worse at times."

Lady Wen gave an uncertain nod and said a few more words of comfort before concluding: "Rest well today. Tomorrow I will have someone bring you out. Get yourself ready in the morning."

The moment Lady Wen and Shen Zhaozhao were gone, Yuedeng came at once to Shen Weici: "Miss, are you really going?"

Shen Weici's face at this moment had none of the wan discomfort it had worn before. She leaned back in her chair and looked at Yuedeng: "The Second Lady has still not given up on forcing me to marry Zhang Tingyi. Going out tomorrow might be another opportunity for me."

"The talk outside has spread this far, which means the method was right. So we just add more fuel to the fire."

Yuedeng started at this, then asked urgently: "How do we add fuel?"

Shen Weici gave a quiet sigh and said in a low voice: "I will tell you tonight. Right now — go to Father's study and see if he is there. If he is, come back and tell me. I will go find him."

Yuedeng went and was back quickly, reporting that Father had gone to the Old Madam's and she had come away empty-handed.

Shen Weici heard that her father had gone to the Old Madam, and the last small hope inside her dimmed.

She had meant to go to her father and gently suggest he give up the marriage to Zhang Tingyi — to take the wind out of the rumors. But from the look of things, he had not once thought of giving up.

She frowned slightly and looked down at the needlework in her hands.

She truly did not want to make things this difficult for everyone.

---

In the imperial palace, Song Zhang sat across from the Emperor over a meal. The table was laid with a dozen dishes, almost all of them things Song Zhang had liked when he lived at the palace.

The Emperor looked at Song Zhang: "You have not stayed to eat with me in quite some time. Sit with me today and have a few more cups."

Song Zhang smiled and raised the gilded cup before him, draining it in one: "Then this subject first drinks to Your Majesty."

The Emperor laughed: "You are still as forthright as ever."

He looked at Song Zhang: "Among the memorials presented to me lately, a good number have been censuring your Second Uncle of the Jian'an household. I have been sitting on the matter. It is not, in itself, a significant affair — only a matter of marrying a daughter off to Zhang Tingyi."

"This subject does not find it particularly troubling. What is your view?"

Song Zhang looked at the Emperor: "Does Your Majesty wish to know my opinion?"

The Emperor arched an eyebrow: "Why else would I keep you? After all, your mother is in the Jian'an household. I thought I ought to look after them somewhat, on account of that connection."

Song Zhang rose and bowed: "In truth, if Your Majesty asks this subject, he also thinks the censures have a point."

The Emperor looked at Song Zhang in surprise: "How so?"

Song Zhang said: "The matter of the Jian'an Manor is now known throughout the court. The Censorate has submitted memorials, and the remonstrating officials raised it in the great hall. If Your Majesty takes no action, the favoritism becomes too obvious and difficult to justify. How then would Your Majesty command the confidence of your officials? If the fashion for flattery and self-advancement grows unchecked, the court will rot from the inside out."

The Emperor paused, then smiled ruefully at Song Zhang: "Only talking to you do I feel at ease. Only you will speak the truth to me."

Song Zhang sat back across from the Emperor: "This subject is only thinking of Your Majesty. Giving Second Uncle a measured lesson this time will make the officials feel Your Majesty is even-handed."

The Emperor nodded: "Since you say so yourself, you cannot later come to me and intercede for your Second Uncle."

Song Zhang smiled: "I certainly will not."

The Emperor looked at him once more, set down his chopsticks, and dismissed the attendants, then said to Song Zhang: "As for the business with Zhang Tingyi — turn a blind eye for now. Aside from his excessive appetites, I am otherwise satisfied with him."

"And he did have one eye put out and an arm broken over this matter by your people, and is still recovering — that is punishment enough."

Zhang Tingyi's talent for flattering the Emperor was without equal. He could always leave the Emperor flushed and pleased. He also supplied the Emperor with alchemical tonics, and everyone in the palace knew the Emperor's trust in Zhang Tingyi knew no bounds.

The Emperor had grown noticeably more muddled these past two years. He went straight to Lady Zhang's quarters after court, and some memorials were even processed by palace eunuchs on his behalf. The Second Prince had made a suggestion before the throne recently, only to be scolded for it, while the Fourth Prince — born of Lady Zhang — was frequently summoned to keep the Emperor company.

It was no wonder that people at court were gravitating toward the Fourth Prince. Anyone watching could see that the Emperor seemed inclined to establish the Fourth Prince as crown prince.

Song Zhang observed all of this. He had been at the Emperor's side for many years and understood the imperial mind — the Emperor indulged those he was fond of, and was especially generous with those close to him. While still not quite a foolish ruler, he had grown noticeably more muddle-headed over these past two years.

Song Zhang had long anticipated that Lady Zhang would beg the Emperor for mercy and the matter would be papered over.

He had never expected a single affair to bring Zhang Tingyi down entirely.

chapters.title: Has He Offended You, or Someone You Care About?
chapters.content:
The great hall was very quiet. Sovereign and subject spoke of affairs of state.

Song Zhang looked at the Emperor: "If the woman who died had been a slave or a person of degraded status, a rush mat to wrap her in would be nothing of note. But the woman Zhang Zhengqing tormented to death this time was a freeborn commoner who performed at an entertainment house without having signed any contract of indenture."

"When the body was carried out, many people witnessed it. My men suppressed the matter, but not before quite a number had already seen. According to the law, Zhang Zhengqing should be stripped of his office and imprisoned, or exiled for three years."

"Zhang Zhengqing already holds a position in the Court of Judicial Review. That a man who takes human life so lightly would command such a court — who among the people would dare trust in it again?"
