"Moreover, he attempted to flee afterward through a back gate, changed his clothes, and had an underling take his place. Had he not changed clothes and run, my men would not have mistakenly injured him — which he deserved."

"The Censorate is already aware of this. A memorial was submitted today. If Your Majesty is reluctant to punish him, you will chill the hearts of the people and the officials. Would that not do more harm than good?"

Then Song Zhang watched the Emperor's expression carefully: "Now that the talk throughout the court concerns Your Majesty's intention to establish the Fourth Prince as crown prince — if Your Majesty also pardons Zhang Tingyi, would that not signal to the court that whatever crime Zhang Tingyi commits, Your Majesty will never fault him? From that point on, only more people will seek to attach themselves to him, and faction-building will grow."

The words 'faction-building' struck the Emperor in the very place that mattered most. As a ruler, nothing was more to be feared than ministers forming factions.

His fingers tapped the table, his brow knitting deep: "That aspect of it I had not considered."

Song Zhang smiled: "This subject is a military man and does not associate much with the civil officials. His only duty is to stand close by Your Majesty and manage the palace garrison, keeping Your Majesty safe."

"These words are said entirely with Your Majesty's interests in mind. As for the schemes of the civil officials at court, this subject has no desire to pry into them — only to analyze what is at stake."

"The remarks just now were also prompted by the rumors now circulating outside that Your Majesty intends to establish the Fourth Prince as crown prince. If Your Majesty now pardons Zhang Tingyi as well, those rumors will only seem more confirmed."

The Emperor sighed. In his heart he did want to establish the Fourth Prince as crown prince — the Fourth Prince was his favorite, and though he could not match the Third Prince in battle or the Second Prince in depth of thought, he was the one who brought the Emperor the most peace of mind.

That was why he had been so indulgent toward the Zhang family.

But he did not want factions to form at court, and allowing the Fourth Prince's power base to grow too large was genuinely not in the court's interest.

The Emperor considered for a moment, then looked at Song Zhang: "Then how do you think I ought to punish him?"

Song Zhang bent slightly and filled the Emperor's cup: "How to punish is still Your Majesty's decision. This subject would not dare offer a conclusion."

The Emperor looked at his now-filled cup and then at Song Zhang: "Just now you said so much, and now at the critical moment you are deflecting again."

Song Zhang looked at the Emperor seriously: "This subject believes that having Zhang Tingyi imprisoned for three months, then demoted two grades in rank — would that not serve to balance things? The civil officials will keep guessing at Your Majesty's intentions and will not be too quick to form parties around him."

The Emperor frowned: "But Consort Zhang will be displeased…"

Song Zhang looked at the Emperor's knitted brow and said nothing more, staying silently at the Emperor's side.

When Song Zhang came out of the great hall, Lady Zhang Consort was waiting anxiously outside. Seeing Song Zhang emerge, she called to him: "Is His Majesty still inside?"

Song Zhang bowed: "His Majesty has had a little too much to drink and is being helped to rest by the attendants."

Lady Zhang's expression was uncertain. Her bewitching eyes fell on Song Zhang: "I know it was General Song's people who dealt with my brother's matter. Would the General have a moment? I would like to speak with you privately."

Song Zhang bowed: "This subject still has matters to handle at the Left Palace Guard, and subordinates waiting to make their reports. I am afraid I have no time."

Lady Zhang had not expected Song Zhang to dare refuse her. Her expression clouded.

But she also understood that the Emperor trusted Song Zhang more than he trusted her own brother. Song Zhang had, after all, grown up under the Emperor's eye — the Song Ducal household had been at the Emperor's side when he was crown prince — and besides, Song Zhang's grandmother on his mother's side was the Grand Princess. He was closer to the Emperor in every way than her brother ever could be.

Her eyes shifted through several calculations, and then she smiled: "Then go slowly, General."

Song Zhang bowed respectfully and walked into the night.

Lady Zhang watched Song Zhang's retreating figure — like jade-stacked stone, a lone pine standing apart, upright as a crane against the wind. If her daughter could marry Song Zhang, then the Emperor establishing the Fourth Prince as crown prince would become a certainty.

She withdrew her gaze beneath the palace lanterns and glided back into the inner chambers.

After leaving, Song Zhang went to the Palace Guard headquarters, where he found the Second Prince, Prince Ming, already waiting for him.

Song Zhang raised an eyebrow as he entered the main hall and looked at Li Rongshan, offering a proper bow: "Your Second Highness."

Li Rongshan smiled and raised Song Zhang from his bow: "Seeing you has become something of an undertaking these days."

Song Zhang's relationship with Li Rongshan at the palace had been the closest of any of the princes — not for any particular calculated reason, only because Li Rongshan's mother had been a mere palace maid, leaving him constantly bullied within the inner palace. Song Zhang had not been able to stand by and watch, and had helped him several times. One thing led to another and the two became close friends.

During the years Song Zhang had been posted to the frontier, whenever he returned to the capital to report, Li Rongshan was always the first to come and greet him. The bond between them was naturally unlike any other.

Song Zhang, hearing Li Rongshan's words, smiled and went with him into the inner hall, asking: "What does Your Highness want of me?"

Li Rongshan was direct: "Was the business with Zhang Tingyi your doing?"

Song Zhang looked at Li Rongshan and raised an eyebrow: "I have no such leisure."

Li Rongshan smiled: "No need to confirm it. I will add fuel from behind — I will make it so Zhang Tingyi cannot recover."

Then he smiled: "But I did not expect this from you. You have always kept out of court affairs. What made you move against Zhang Tingyi this time?"

"Did he offend you? Or did he offend someone you care about?"

Song Zhang heard this and looked at Li Rongshan: "And you — you are willing to act now? Are you not afraid the Emperor will suspect your people are in the Censorate?"

Li Rongshan sat across from Song Zhang: "As long as Lady Zhang is there, even with your persuasion, Father may not be able to bring himself to make a decision. But if the entire court memorializes together, that is different."

Song Zhang's fingers paused on his teacup. He looked up at Li Rongshan: "There are not a few of Zhang Tingyi's men in the court. There will naturally be those who defend him."

Li Rongshan smiled: "But there is still you. You push from behind — let the woman whose daughter died make more noise, and getting Zhang Tingyi dismissed is not impossible."

He looked at Song Zhang: "That ought to be nothing too difficult for you."

Song Zhang smiled: "I only wanted Zhang Tingyi behind bars for a few months and put through some suffering there — Your Highness wants him stripped of his office entirely."

Li Rongshan sighed: "As long as Zhang Tingyi remains at court, he will only draw more people toward the Fourth Prince. How can I be at peace?"

Song Zhang heard this and only said to Li Rongshan: "Your Highness need not be anxious. The Third Prince will be returning soon."

Li Rongshan looked at Song Zhang. Seeing the trace of seriousness behind those easy eyes, he rose and came to stand before Song Zhang, reaching out to rest a hand on Song Zhang's shoulder, and said in a low voice: "Song Zhang, you know that I have always been the loneliest of men. In all these years only you have understood me."

"Whatever the outcome — I will make sure you walk away from it whole."

chapters.title: Going to Ask Song Zhang
chapters.content:
When Song Zhang returned to the Manor that night, the steward at the gate came to meet him: "Second Young Master, the First Lord asks that you stop by the Old Madam's quarters when you return."

"The First Lord is also there."

Song Zhang raised an eyebrow. He rarely made any show of filial duty at the Old Madam's — he had visited just a handful of times since returning to the capital, and even those had amounted to little more than a few words of greeting. Being summoned there now almost certainly meant someone wanted something done.

Song Zhang felt a mild irritation at the prospect of going, and was on the point of ignoring it — then paused, changed his mind, and headed toward the Old Madam's quarters.

What could they want at this hour? It had to be something to do with the Second Branch. He was moderately curious to hear what it was.

Two junior servants walked ahead carrying lanterns to light the way. The hour was already late, the path dark and empty. Song Zhang's steps were unhurried, and he became aware of the wine making itself felt. He breathed out slowly.

The matrons at the courtyard gate saw Song Zhang coming from a distance and went to announce him. By the time he entered the main hall, he looked around — his father and the Second Branch people were all there. He offered an only barely respectable bow of greeting, then took the seat nearest to him with total self-possession.

Shen Shen, catching the smell of wine on Song Zhang, asked: "You have been drinking again?"

Song Zhang smiled: "A few cups with the Emperor."

Those words made Shen Rongshen's expression shift. He looked up at Song Zhang: "Did the Emperor say anything about this business of censuring me?"

Song Zhang lounged back in his chair, accepted the tea a maid brought, and drank a calm sip: "He did not bring it up."

Shen Rongshen looked at his brother in a panic: "Brother, what do I do?"

Shen Shen frowned and shot Shen Rongshen a look: "This is entirely because you failed to manage your own household and let the matter leak out. Now you have dragged the Manor's reputation through the mud. Chen He has been censuring you for three days straight. Save yourself if you can."

Shen Rongshen, having been spoken to sharply by his brother, looked ashamed. Then he turned to Song Zhang: "Song Zhang, all those rumors started with those storytellers. Can you have your Feathered Guard men round them up? The Feathered Guard patrols the streets — you can arrest them on some charge and they will stop their talking."

Song Zhang crossed his legs and looked at Shen Rongshen: "If I have people arrested, will that stop the rumor? When it is then said that the Manor is abusing its power to silence people, the rumors will only grow worse. Has Second Uncle not thought of that?"

Shen Rongshen heard this and hesitated, looking first at the Old Madam and then at his own elder brother.

Shen Shen sighed and spoke to Song Zhang: "Tomorrow your Second Uncle intends to have Weici go to Sanrun Residence — the largest teahouse in the capital — to make a public clarification. Yanli will go along as well. Send some of your men too, to maintain order if things get out of hand."

"And have those storytellers gathered together in one place to hear what they should be saying going forward. After this, they will not dare open their mouths again."

Song Zhang heard this and raised an eyebrow. He frowned at Shen Rongshen: "Would Third Young Miss Shen be willing?"

He gave a cold, unapologetic snort: "From what I hear, those rumors outside do not sound like mere wild talk. If they are not wild talk, what exactly is she going out there to clarify?"

What everyone knew to be true, said outright by Song Zhang — the faces of the Second Branch and the Old Madam all went uncomfortable.

Lady Wen's expression stiffened and flickered several times. She forced a smile and looked at Song Zhang: "This does concern the Manor's reputation. The way your Second Uncle and the Old Madam have been described outside is genuinely excessive. Your Second Uncle's post is at risk as well. Quieting those rumors is the only way to turn things around."

"We are also doing this for the Manor's sake."

Before Lady Wen's words had finished landing, Song Zhang's cold gaze swept across. That gaze carried, unmistakably, a trace of disdain and disgust: "If Third Young Miss Shen goes to make a clarification — does that make her responsible for damaging the Manor's reputation?"

"The woman has been coughing blood and is still in her sickbed. And your plan is to drag her out and put her through all this?"

Shen Shen heard Song Zhang say all of this and was surprised. This kind of small favor was the sort of thing Song Zhang, in any other circumstance, would have sorted out with a few men and not thought twice about. That he was now saying all of this was something else entirely.

In truth, Song Zhang had still shown some degree of respect to Shen Rongshen and Lady Wen as elders. The words he might otherwise have said would have been considerably harsher.

After speaking, he had no patience to remain. He stood directly: "I have no interest in getting involved in these matters."

Song Zhang said his piece, and without caring how the hall of people reacted, turned and walked out. Even when the Old Madam called after him, he had not the patience to look back.

He had come tonight only to accompany the Emperor, and had drunk a few more cups than intended to please him. Now to come here and be made to listen to plans for how to bully a young woman — forcing her to go out and show her face in public, to say she had not been wronged when she had — it was something he genuinely could not watch.

With Song Zhang's departure, everyone exchanged glances. The expressions were all unpleasant.

Lady Wen looked to the Old Madam for help: "Now that Song Zhang will not help either — what do we do?"

The Old Madam's expression went dark and tight. She murmured: "Then send Weici to Song Zhang's quarters first and tell him what tomorrow is about. From what I just observed, Song Zhang seemed to be shielding her. Let her go and ask Song Zhang herself — see if there is any room to work with."

Lady Wen heard this and knew it was the only remaining option. She rose, took her leave of the Old Madam, and hurried with her maids toward Shen Weici's courtyard.

——-

Shen Weici had only just come out of her bath. She was sitting in a chair, leaning back while Yuedeng dried her hair, working on her embroidery pouch.

Lady Wen came in and stood over her with an air of authority, launching into a long explanation.

Shen Weici listened with her head slightly bowed, the candlelight falling on her eyes and casting the shifting of her feelings there into shadow.

When Lady Wen finished, she asked softly: "If I go to Young Lord Song — and he does not agree?"

Lady Wen looked at Shen Weici: "If you go and he still refuses, that is that. The Manor will send some guards to go with you. Tomorrow Yanli will also be there. You must remember to speak carefully and not cause any further trouble."

Shen Weici paused, then only nodded.

Lady Wen saw how compliant she was being and was already somewhat satisfied.

She stood and looked at Shen Weici: "In a moment, the matron from my quarters will accompany you. Tidy yourself a little and go now. Early is better. Do you understand?"

Shen Weici did not lift her head to look at Lady Wen's face, only gave a docile sound of assent.

Lady Wen narrowed her eyes at Shen Weici — always that same soft and gentle manner, always obedient and compliant in front of others, almost never openly defiant. There was truly no way of knowing what was going through her heart.

Compared to Zhang Yuanheng's open devotion, was she genuinely willing to marry Zhang Tingyi?

The thought came and went in a flash. Lady Wen glanced at Matron Chang at her side: "You go along with Third Young Miss when she visits Song Zhang. Come back and tell me whether he agreed or not."

Matron Chang quickly nodded: "Madam, rest assured. I will remember."

Lady Wen had no desire to stay any longer, and gathered her sleeves and left.

The moment Lady Wen was gone, Matron Chang looked at Shen Weici: "Third Young Miss, shall we tidy up and go?"

Yuedeng frowned: "Miss's hair is not fully dry yet."

Matron Chang raised an eyebrow at Yuedeng, a trace of displeasure crossing her face. She was not accustomed to having a junior maid push back at her.

Her expression cooled. She looked at Shen Weici and said respectfully but with an underlying condescension: "Third Young Miss, the Second Lady is waiting."

Shen Weici looked at Yuedeng: "Since Matron Chang is in a hurry, let us go now. No more argument."

Yuedeng started: "But it is cold outside and very windy. Miss's hair — "

Before she could finish, Shen Weici had already risen. She turned and placed her hand gently over Yuedeng's and looked at her with calm eyes: "It is fine. Stepmother is waiting for Matron Chang to bring word back, and I would not want her to feel I was being slow about it. Bring my cloak — better to go sooner and be done with it."

Shen Weici's quiet gaze silenced Yuedeng, who turned and went to fetch the cloak.

Matron Chang stood to one side, watching Shen Weici's silhouette where she stood against the light — slender and graceful, the cascade of dark hair to her waist, her curves perfectly formed. Skin like snow, glowing faintly under the light sage-green of her robes — no wonder Lord Zhang was insisting on having her.

Yuedeng stood behind Shen Weici and gathered her hair, helped her put up the cloak's hood, then told Hexia to hurry and light a lantern.

Out in the corridor, a slant of moonlight lay across the steps. Shen Weici's embroidered shoes touched it, and in the soft blur of it her skirt hem caught the light like rippling water.

Matron Chang walked ahead to lead the way. Yuedeng walked at Shen Weici's side and murmured: "Miss's constitution is not strong, and there is always that cold ailment. If your head starts to ache later, what then?"

Shen Weici said only quietly: "It will be fine."

When they reached Guansong Residence, the guards at the door were still blocking the way. Matron Chang smiled and spoke with the guard, who went to have the matter announced. The message came back: "The Second Young Master says only Third Young Miss may come in."

Matron Chang was taken aback, then pulled Shen Weici aside and whispered: "The fact that the Second Young Master is willing to see you is a good sign. Go in and speak well. Do not let the Second Lady down."

Shen Weici looked at Matron Chang for a moment. That kind of expectation was rather amusing.

She gave a lowered-eyes, docile nod.

The guards stood aside. Shen Weici followed the maid who had come to guide her inside. The maid led her to an inner chamber and said softly: "The Second Young Master is still bathing. Third Young Miss, please wait a moment."

Shen Weici knelt on the cushion and glanced around the room. This was not the study where she had come before — it felt more like a private sitting room.

The space was generous, all the hanging blinds let down, the gauze moving faintly in the air. The charcoal fire was generous and warm. The room held low tables and a daybed. By the window there was also a wide wooden lounging bed, with a game of chess in the center — black and white pieces occupying much of the board, a game left unfinished.

Shen Weici glanced at this once and looked away. She knelt on the cushion at the low table. A maid knelt nearby and filled her cup, then quickly withdrew.

Shen Weici drank. The tea was more bitter than usual.

chapters.title: Is This How You Ask a Favor?
chapters.content:
When Song Zhang came in, the first thing he saw was Shen Weici waiting there in perfect silence.

The layered fabric of her robes pooled on the floor. Both hands rested properly on her knees. Her back was straight. The silver pin in her dark hair was especially striking — the loosely wound hair with a few strands already fallen, soft and hanging against her graceful shoulders, swaying into gentle curves as his entrance stirred the air.

Song Zhang walked into the room, his gaze drifting downward and remaining fixed on Shen Weici. He walked past her back, glancing over the nape of her neck. He watched her long lashes give a faint tremble, her skin like white jade with a cast of gold.

As he came around to her side, his gaze fell to the collar of her robe, where a clean white inner collar neatly enclosed every inch of skin. Only the sharp point of her chin revealed a hint of alluring charm.

Above that, half-veiled by her hair, her white earlobe — unadorned, appearing and disappearing.

Though she was covered from head to toe without a sliver of skin exposed, Song Zhang felt she could draw more impure thoughts from him than any other woman.

In the few steps it took to cross the room, Song Zhang had already looked Shen Weici up and down several times.

"Third Young Miss Shen — what brings you to find me?"

Shen Weici knew Song Zhang had come in. Only when he had stopped in front of her did she look up at him.

But that single glance gave Shen Weici a start — she quickly averted her eyes: "Would Young Lord Song please make himself presentable?"

Song Zhang wore only white trousers below, and above, only a black crane-patterned robe draped loose over his shoulders. She had caught a glimpse of water still dripping down his chest as he stood before her, entirely unconcerned.

She had never seen a man's body before and naturally looked away, while keeping her composure on the surface.

Song Zhang saw Shen Weici turn her face aside, those lovely eyes blinking rapidly as though somewhat flustered.

He raised an eyebrow slightly, looked down at his exposed chest, gave a low, quiet laugh, and drew the robe together as he sat down across from her.

He had not meant any impropriety — he had always been casual in this way. In his quarters, surrounded by men, wearing nothing on top was unremarkable. He had simply forgotten that Shen Weici would not have seen such things.

He sat across from her with relaxed ease and looked at her composed face: "Can you speak now?"

Shen Weici brought her gaze back. She had now noticed that his robe, though gathered, was only casually so — the collarbone still very much visible, right in front of her.

But this time looking over, Shen Weici noticed that a strikingly beautiful woman was kneeling beside Song Zhang, quietly pouring his tea, then kneeling and using a handkerchief to carefully dab the water still on his neck.

Her voice, soft as a warbler's, murmured: "Why did you come out so quickly, sir? In this cold weather, you really should take care of yourself."

Shen Weici looked at the woman without meaning to. Her skin like congealed fat, gleaming white, her slender fingers clearly not those of a maidservant.

Song Zhang seemed slightly annoyed by the woman's attentions: "Go out."

The woman looked at him as though hurt, then quietly, silently withdrew.

Song Zhang noticed Shen Weici's gaze follow the woman. He felt a brief impulse to explain, then caught himself with a private laugh. Whether he had ten or twenty women, no one could say a word. Why on earth should he explain himself to Shen Weici?

After the woman had gone, Shen Weici looked back at Song Zhang and lowered her eyes: "Tomorrow I am to go to the teahouse to make a clarification about the rumors outside. Father and Stepmother are asking me to request that Young Lord Song send some men to come along."

Song Zhang frowned, looking at Shen Weici: "I said I would handle the business with Zhang Tingyi. Why do you still need to go out?"

Shen Weici lowered her eyes: "If I do not go, they will find other ways to make things difficult for me."

Song Zhang gave a cold laugh: "Spineless."

Shen Weici pressed her lips together and was quiet a moment before: "If Young Lord Song is unwilling to send men, then I will take my leave."

Song Zhang heard this and raised an eyebrow. He looked at her with narrowed eyes: "Is this how you ask a favor?"

Shen Weici looked up. Her gaze met Song Zhang's — those keen, invasive eyes — and she looked aside again.

She had not actually held out much hope that Song Zhang would agree.

On the way here she had already thought it through: how could Lady Wen possibly be the one to send her? It must be that her father had already failed to persuade Song Zhang, and so she had been sent instead.

She also understood her own position: this visit was a performance for Lady Wen. Whether Song Zhang's men came or not had no real bearing on Shen Weici's plans.

On the contrary, she had not wanted Song Zhang to help her father.

She said quietly: "It is for Young Lord Song to decide as he sees fit. I will take my leave."

She braced her hand on the table and began to stand.

A warm, large hand closed around her wrist. Then Song Zhang's mildly scattered voice came: "Third Young Miss Shen — what is the rush? Have I said I refuse?"

Shen Weici froze and looked up at Song Zhang. His dark eyes were rolling with some unusual feeling she could not make out.

She was about to speak — and then Song Zhang stood abruptly. His hand still held her wrist, and in the moment of her startled uncertainty, he came and sat beside her.

The loosely held robe shifted with his movement and fell fully open, now spread wide right in front of her.

She blinked, unable to understand what Song Zhang intended. She moved her wrist, trying to signal him to let go — but his grip tightened and pulled her forward, and she had to throw out her other hand to catch herself, otherwise she would have fallen into his arms.

By the time she recovered, she was glaring at Song Zhang with genuine irritation: "What does Young Lord Song think he is doing?"

Song Zhang had it in mind to say: I have always only known how to bully people, and I only want to bully you.

But looking at Shen Weici's eyes lit with that rare flash of indignation — bright and pretty — he released her wrist, and the corner of his lip curved: "Has the pouch been finished?"

Shen Weici blinked: "Not yet."

Song Zhang's gaze settled on the faint residual pink still on her cheek. His voice dropped to a low rasp: "Third Young Miss has come all this way. Of course I will agree. Tomorrow I will personally escort Third Young Miss — how would that suit?"

From Shen Weici's perspective, Song Zhang's men not coming was already the best outcome. Him coming personally was even more undesirable.

She had no wish to debate this further: "I would not dare impose on Young Lord Song."

She rose to leave.

Song Zhang felt the unruly thoughts she stirred in him ignite — a prairie fire in a young man's blood-hot years, the desire for a woman growing only keener.

The shadow from his youth had suppressed it for a time, and returning to the capital had gradually let it come loose again.

Yet Song Zhang felt he had been cursed. The concubines and beautiful women the Emperor sent him stirred nothing in him whatsoever.

chapters.title: In What Way Is He Less Than Zhang Yuanheng?
chapters.content:
Only the two of them were in the room. The swaying candlelight was like the restless stirring rising in his chest.

He watched the jade-green skirt hem sway, the wide sleeve brush across his fingers, trailing a soft, intoxicating scent. His gaze fell on Shen Weici's slender waist.

The blush-white sash hanging down drew him before he knew it. He reached out and caught Shen Weici's wrist.

He held it — still slender — and for a moment Song Zhang thought that with a little more pressure he could snap it in his hand.

He squeezed gently. But it was soft, with a slight yielding give. It only looked fragile.

He looked up at Shen Weici's startled eyes, and said with affected ease: "Third Young Miss Shen — if you do not wish to go tomorrow, you do not have to go. If they make trouble for you afterward, come and find me."

Shen Weici heard Song Zhang's words and nearly thought she had misheard.

The expression on Song Zhang's face now was nothing like his usual cold aloofness, nor his occasional careless irreverence. There was a note of genuine sincerity in it.

This was the first time Shen Weici had ever seen that expression on Song Zhang's face. She was momentarily still, and then gave a quiet shake of her head: "Young Lord Song's kindness is appreciated. But I have nothing with which to repay Young Lord Song, and can only disappoint his goodwill."

She drew her hand from Song Zhang's, lowered her eyes, and gave a half-bow: "If Young Lord Song is unwilling to send men tomorrow, then I will take my leave now and go back to give my stepmother an answer."

It was not that Shen Weici was opposed to accepting Song Zhang's goodwill. First, she simply did not yet dare trust that Song Zhang would so suddenly be this kind to her. Second, even if Song Zhang were willing to help, she was still a member of the Second Branch — Lady Wen would always have ways to get at her afterward. Song Zhang certainly could not be in the Manor at all times. She could not afford to brazenly offend Lady Wen in the open.

Besides, she had always understood that no one is ever genuinely kind to another person without cause — even the nearest relatives harbor private motives. She would not trust anyone.

The warmth on Song Zhang's face gradually cooled. That briefly heated heart, beneath Shen Weici's composed and quiet manner, began to die down.

She could accept Zhang Yuanheng's goodwill, could be bashfully charming in front of Zhang Yuanheng. In front of him, it had never happened.

Even when he reached out to her, she still would not respond.

Song Zhang truly did not know how to read Shen Weici. If she wanted to climb higher, to marry into the Earl's Manor — he was incomparably better than Zhang Yuanheng in family background, position, official rank. In what way was he less than Zhang Yuanheng?

Or was it that she had genuinely fallen for Zhang Yuanheng?

Song Zhang's eyes gradually, dangerously narrowed. He gave a cold laugh. He had with some difficulty set aside his pride and taken the first step — and she had trampled it underfoot. He had never in his life thought about trying to please a woman, and now he felt rather ridiculous before Shen Weici.

Song Zhang stood with a darkening face. His tall shadow fell across Shen Weici entirely. He looked down at those eyes of hers, still perfectly calm. The faint flush of pink from just moments ago was gone — like that faintly beating, warming heart of his.

He restored his arrogance to his face, pressed his lips into a cold hard line: "At least you know your place. You are not worth my goodwill."

His sleeve swept past her shoulder as he walked away in long strides.

Shen Weici heard Song Zhang's words and paused. She did not feel she had said anything wrong. Song Zhang had always been cold and cutting toward her — she did not trust him.

The faint cold fragrance he had left behind still lingered at the tip of her nose. She calmly gathered her sleeves, took the cloak hanging on the stand nearby, and turned and walked out.

She stood in the corridor, pulled on the cloak, and was crossing the courtyard when she felt a gaze fall on her from behind. She turned to look — and saw Song Zhang standing at the window.

Behind him was a broad band of bright light. His face was in the alternating dark and shadow.

She could not read his expression from here, but she could feel the vast weight of feeling in his gaze, and it gave her a small, quiet jolt.

Shen Weici looked away and pulled the cloak's hood up over her head.

Matron Chang, waiting at the courtyard gate, came hurrying forward the moment she saw Shen Weici: "What did the Second Young Master say?"

Shen Weici considered for a moment, then opened her mouth: "Just now when I spoke with Young Lord Song, he did not say yes and did not say no. He only told me to go back first."

Matron Chang's face creased with difficulty. One could not press Song Zhang for more — she had no choice but to nod: "Then let us go back."

Back in Linchun Courtyard, Yuedeng took the cloak from Shen Weici's shoulders and immediately asked: "Is Miss's head aching?"

Shen Weici shook her head. She sat sideways in the chair, her pale slender fingers held near the fire basin, warmth spreading from her fingertips. The pallor of her face began to take on a little color again. She stared at a point on the floor, lost in thought.

---

Very early the next morning, Matron Chang from Lady Wen's quarters came to remind Shen Weici to dress herself promptly.

Matron Chang had also brought face powder, lip rouge, and blush — she set them on the table and smiled at Shen Weici: "The Second Lady says Third Young Miss has natural beauty. Even without making up your face you are lovely, but a little color would improve your complexion."

Shen Weici put out a hand and stopped the matron's fingers mid-reach toward her face: "Matron need not bother with that. Let us go now."

Matron Chang's hand froze in mid-air. She had not expected Shen Weici to stop her so directly.

She saw Shen Weici already standing and asking Yuedeng to fetch the cloak. She could only pick up the lip rouge: "At least let Third Young Miss put on this, then — it will give you more color."

Shen Weici glanced at what Matron Chang was holding, and concealed the contempt that rose in her eyes. She said nothing more.

Matron Chang quickly applied the lip colour to Shen Weici's lips. The previously bare, natural lips took on a deep crimson, and the already alluring face became suddenly more vivid.

Matron Chang stared for a moment. Truly a beauty to unsettle the heart.

Shen Weici did not speak more. She looked at Matron Chang and asked: "Are we leaving now?"

Matron Chang came to herself and went ahead to lead the way.

When they reached the front gate, Shen Rongshen was unexpectedly waiting there.

Shen Weici went over to greet him with the same quiet obedience and asked: "Why is Father here at this hour?"

Shen Rongshen looked at Shen Weici's plainly dressed figure — though now there was no longer just that silver pin in her hair. A kingfisher-blue hairpin had replaced it, lending a touch of refinement.

He stood with his hands clasped behind him, the guilt in his heart spilling out of his eyes: "I came home from court early because I was uneasy. I wanted to see you."

These words sounded as though they came from a caring and protective father.

Shen Weici's eyes did not so much as flicker. She replied as she always did, gently and without any edge: "Daughter thanks Father for his concern."

Shen Rongshen sighed: "I know you are sensible. Having you go out to give this clarification is something we had no choice about. Do not blame your father."

Shen Weici raised her face and shook her head: "Daughter understands Father also has his difficulties. She will not blame Father."

Hearing Shen Weici's words, the guilt inside Shen Rongshen eased slightly. He called Shen Yanli over: "Accompany your Third Sister. Make sure she is looked after. No mistakes."

Shen Yanli said: "Father, don't worry. I go to that teahouse often. Nothing will go wrong."

Only then did Shen Rongshen nod with a small measure of relief.

chapters.title: He Came After All
chapters.content:
Standing at the front gate, Shen Rongshen gave a few more instructions. Beside him, Lady Wen said: "The hour is about right, my lord. Let them go."

Shen Zhaozhao, standing to one side, gave Shen Weici a cold look: "Remember clearly what you are supposed to say. If you say the wrong thing, do not expect me to let it pass when you return."

Shen Rongshen heard Shen Zhaozhao's words and frowned, speaking low: "Zhaozhao, no more of that."

Lady Wen caught the displeasure on Shen Rongshen's face and looked at Shen Weici: "All right, off you go."

Shen Weici's steps paused for a moment. Just before leaving, her previously downcast eyes lifted slightly toward her father: "Father — I am going."

A strange sensation moved through Shen Rongshen — as though calling up the memory of that old departure, when he had told that woman he would be back soon and she had sent him off with such gentle compliance, helping him dress and adjust his clothes.

Shen Rongshen closed his eyes and sighed: "Go."

Shen Weici lowered her eyes again and went toward the carriage.

Shen Zhaozhao watched Shen Weici's figure disappear into the carriage curtain, and could not help whispering to her mother: "Can I go along and watch?"

Lady Wen patted Shen Zhaozhao's hand: "That place is a mixed crowd of all kinds. What business does an unmarried girl have there? What if someone recognizes you?"

"Those people are not worthy of seeing you."

Shen Zhaozhao nestled against her mother's shoulder: "I just want to see how Shen Weici says it, in case she makes a mess of it."

Lady Wen smiled: "Your elder brother is going along, and there are guards. She will not dare say the wrong thing."

"And besides, Song Zhang's men are not going — things might get unruly. If you were there and something happened to you, what then?"

Shen Rongshen stood nearby, listening to the mother and daughter exchange these words. He watched the carriage gradually move away, and gave Lady Wen a cold, silent stare. He felt only a deepening revulsion for the woman beside him.

He told his attendant to prepare his own carriage, and made ready to go to the palace.

Lady Wen, struck by that look, stood watching his carriage recede down the alley without a word being spoken to her, and she felt, clearly, that Shen Rongshen had grown colder and more distant these past days — nothing like the devoted, accommodating man who had always deferred to her in everything.

The handkerchief in her fingers was twisted tighter and tighter. All of this had changed the moment Shen Weici arrived.

Her eyes gradually went cold. Only when Shen Zhaozhao came to her side did she warm her expression again, and she took Shen Zhaozhao with her back inside.

Over at the teahouse, Shen Weici's carriage drew up in front. Shen Yanli came down from the carriage behind and walked to Shen Weici's curtain: "Third Sister, wait a moment. I will go up first and speak with the proprietor, and then speak with the storytellers."

There was only a quiet "mm" from within before he took a few guards inside.

The moment he entered, he found the teahouse — usually bustling and noisy — completely silent. Every patron sat properly at their table, heads bowed over their tea, not daring to breathe too loudly.

He looked around. The entire three floors of the teahouse were lined with guards, whose sheer presence had silenced the room.

Looking toward the storytelling platform on the second floor, a dozen or so storytellers stood to one side, as though waiting for something.

Shen Yanli was delighted. He thought: Song Zhang must certainly be here. He went upstairs quickly, grabbed a tea server and asked: "Where is General Song?"

The server pointed in a direction. Shen Yanli looked — and there in a private booth across the floor, Song Zhang was seated in his usual grand and languid sprawl, with the teahouse proprietor attending nervously at his side.

Those indifferent eyes turned at that moment and landed on Shen Yanli.

Shen Yanli blinked, then went over quickly, and called a servant down to go and fetch Shen Weici.

Truly, getting Song Zhang to handle something was something else. Everything had been arranged perfectly.

The servant rushed down and delivered the message at the carriage curtain. Shen Weici heard and asked Matron Chang, in a mild tone: "Is there a gauze hat with a veil?"

Matron Chang was startled and replied before thinking: "Third Young Miss is meant to be seen by the people in the teahouse. If your face is covered, how can they believe you?"

Yuedeng could hold back no longer and stepped forward: "My young mistress has not yet married. If all those people in the teahouse see her face, what family of good standing would accept her afterward? This is a mixed crowd with all manner of people."

"She is not refusing to go and clarify the matter. She can simply unveil at the end when she speaks. What is the harm in that?"

Matron Chang heard these words and could find no rebuttal. Every word was reasonable, and she had simply not thought of it when setting out.

She did not particularly care whether Shen Weici's reputation was preserved — only that she achieve what her mistress needed. But now that the point had been raised, she could hardly tell her to just endure having everyone stare.

And yet — where was she to find a gauze veil hat right now?

She looked at Shen Weici with a manufactured expression of difficulty: "Third Young Miss's concern is reasonable, but there is no veil hat now. Third Young Miss will simply have to bear with it."

This was something that could be borne. Yuedeng was nearly boiling with anger, but Shen Weici's soft fingers gripped hers.

She saw Shen Weici's lovely eyes turn and fall on Matron Chang with a quiet, composed gaze. Her voice carried a trace of grievance: "Matron need not put herself to trouble. If the Manor's face is more important than my own — then let it be more important. I will simply endure."

And she lifted the carriage curtain and stepped out first.

Matron Chang watched Shen Weici's retreating figure and felt a small jolt of wrongness. That tone had sounded quite genuinely aggrieved. She felt something was off and hurried to follow.

She went forward and asked: "Third Young Miss, what is the matter?"

Shen Weici looked up at her, pale: "Only that I have never been looked at by this many people."

The fear in her looked unfeigned. Matron Chang was beginning to offer some comforting words when she realized Shen Weici had already bowed her head and was walking into the teahouse, and quickly hurried to stay close behind.

The moment they went in, they felt something was wrong. Why was it so quiet? Every patron sat with bowed head, as though afraid to look at the people coming in.

Shen Yanli was waiting by the door at this point. He saw Shen Weici enter and smiled: "Do not be afraid. Second Brother is here, and he has arranged everything well."

Hearing that Song Zhang was also inside, Shen Weici gave a faint start, then lowered her brow and bit her lip, and nodded, following Shen Yanli toward the second-floor storytelling area.

chapters.title: Carried Away by Song Zhang
chapters.content:
The second floor was packed — yet every person there sat with their head down, silent as stone. Not even a breath was audible, for when that dark mass of Feathered Guard soldiers had entered earlier, they had said: listen only — do not look at the person. With the fearsome Cold Judge of the Feathered Guard seated above and watching, no one dared make a noise.

Shen Yanli felt an inexplicable gratification, though he puzzled at why no one was lifting their head. But he had no time to worry about it.

He walked beside Shen Weici as he guided her upstairs, bending toward her and saying: "Say what you need to say the same way Mother taught you this morning. Try to make it sound heartfelt, so people believe you. Once you have said it, I will take you home."

He seemed to notice that Shen Weici's color was poor — a faint dampness on her forehead as though she had broken into a light sweat. He bent to look at her more carefully: "Third Sister, are you all right?"

Yuedeng stepped forward and said quietly: "My young mistress is frightened. And this teahouse is full of men. Miss has not yet married — having this many people see her face is not right, and goes against propriety."

"Just now I asked Matron Chang to find a veil hat for Miss, but she said there wasn't one. So Miss had no choice but to come with her face uncovered. She must have been frightened by it."

Shen Yanli heard this and saw the sense in it immediately. He had not considered Shen Weici's reputation at all, only thought to have her come and clear the matter up.

But it was too late now to find a veil hat. He quickly reassured her: "It is all right. Say your piece and I will step in front of you when you are done, so as few people as possible see your face."

Shen Weici then gave a pale nod.

Up in his booth, Song Zhang watched Shen Weici come upstairs. Shen Yanli bent close beside her, his tall frame almost entirely blocking her small figure from view — only the occasional glimpse of a pink skirt hem visible. Even that was enough to make his gaze linger.

His expression was cold, his sharp eyes never leaving Shen Weici for a moment. He seemed to be searching her quiet, fragile face for some trace of regret.

Regret for not having asked him for help.

But Song Zhang saw nothing. That gentle face was always composed.

Only when he was cruel to her did vulnerability show on it, and tears would tremble on the brink. Only then would she fix him with those indignant eyes.

And in front of Zhang Yuanheng she would wear a faintly shy smile, a becoming charm warming her cheeks.

The cup in his hand was gripped tighter and tighter. The darkness in his expression deepened, frightening the proprietor hovering nearby, who could not imagine what he himself had done wrong.

Until Shen Weici stood before the storyteller's table — and the grip finally broke. Shards of porcelain fell one by one to the floor.

Shen Weici stood at the table with her head down, looking at the teacup Yuedeng placed before her. She raised it with delicate fingers and drank a light sip.

Shen Yanli smiled beside her: "Third Sister should wet her throat first."

Shen Weici's eyes moved, glancing at Shen Yanli, then back. She coughed twice.

Not loud, not soft — but in the hush of the teahouse the sound carried clearly.

Then Shen Weici began to speak. She said everything Lady Wen had instructed her to say that morning.

Her voice was pleasant — soft and clear, tinged with a faint coolness, her tone as gentle as river water, flowing steadily.

The listeners found themselves imagining, at the sound of that voice, a woman who must be cultured and gracious, good-tempered and beautiful — a proper lady of breeding.

But curious as they were, not one dared look up. They whispered furtively among themselves, feeling something suspicious about this whole arrangement.

What family would send their unmarried daughter out to show herself in a public place like this? From this one fact alone, the story of the Jian'an Marquis Manor mistreating its concubine-born daughter was probably not far from the truth. They had almost certainly forced the girl here.

Shen Yanli watched the reactions of those below with a vague satisfaction, thinking they would hold their tongues from now on.

He was thinking this when Yuedeng let out a piercing cry: "Miss — you are coughing blood again!"

The sound of it made Shen Yanli's heart seize. He spun to look — and saw Shen Weici with one hand pressed on the table, the other gripping a handkerchief tightly to her mouth. The handkerchief was soaked red, and two drops of blood dripped from it — a sight to stop the heart.

Hearing Yuedeng's shout, several people in the audience instinctively raised their heads. They did not see the face clearly, but they saw two hands stained with blood clutching a handkerchief to the lips, the cloth drenched red, bloodstains along the cuff of her sleeve.

What the audience saw was enough to make them reel. Someone cried out: "For the Jian'an Marquis Manor to treat an uncherished daughter like this — have they no conscience?!"

"They forced her here to make a public statement, and now she is coughing blood again — they are not human beings!"

"The Jian'an Marquis Manor is going to have a death on their hands! They are going to drive someone to her grave!"

Uproar broke out.

The Feathered Guard soldiers started forward to intervene — but Minhe waved them off. They halted at once and let the scene unfold.

And Song Zhang was no longer in his seat. He was already crossing the room toward Shen Weici — and seeing her fingers clenching into the edge of the table, the bloodstains at her fingers and collar, pain closed around his heart as though he could not breathe.

That copper-salt smell spreading outward — it made Song Zhang's eyes go red.

He swept her up into his arms, kicked aside Shen Yanli who had gotten in the way, and with her held sideways against his chest he went striding rapidly down the stairs.

Yuedeng stood frozen for a moment, then came to her senses — Song Zhang was already downstairs with her young mistress.

Heart jumping, she rushed down the stairs after them.

Shen Yanli had never imagined things would turn out this way. He wanted to shout an explanation, but the people around him were already pressing toward him, furious, rolling up their sleeves.

Shen Yanli covered his head and ran — seeing the Feathered Guard also leaving with Song Zhang, he bellowed for his guards to form a line, then bolted through the back door in a panic.

Matron Chang was also caught in the surge and could not escape. She was seized by the agitated crowd and slapped twice before finally squeezing out — looking more or less like a battered pig's head.

Yuedeng rushed out to find no trace of Song Zhang or her young mistress. She spotted Minhe coming out behind her and went straight to him: "Where is my mistress?"

Minhe looked at Yuedeng: "Your mistress coughed up that much blood — the General brought her away for her own good. Stop asking so many questions. Go home and wait for the General to send your mistress back."

Yuedeng's heart gave several rapid thumps. Her young mistress had only pretended to cough blood — if Song Zhang found out, it would be over.

She grabbed Minhe's robe in desperate urgency: "I cannot manage without my young mistress. Could you take me to her?"

Minhe thought: I certainly cannot make that decision, and besides, a small maid like her could not hold him. He shook his sleeve free.

Mounted on his horse, he looked down at Yuedeng, on the verge of tears: "Do not be afraid. My General will not harm your young mistress."

"In fact, by now the General has probably already called for a physician to see her."

He rode off, leaving Yuedeng standing there even more terrified. She could only pray that Song Zhang would not figure it out.

She dared not even think what would happen if he did — her lord and his wife would know then that the previous time had also been a pretense, and the consequences would be beyond anything she could imagine.

chapters.title: I Will Not Let Anything Happen to You
chapters.content:
The carriage wheels outside turned at a rapid, urgent pace. Shen Weici, held tight in Song Zhang's arms, came back to herself — and could barely catch her breath.

In her heart she had simply never expected Song Zhang to throw caution to the wind and carry her away. The situation now was more complicated than she had imagined.

She had the sense that Song Zhang was not easily fooled.

She had bitten through her tongue — there was real blood mixed in — but if the blood were examined closely, the color would not be quite deep enough. Without thinking, she tucked the handkerchief soaked with vermillion paint into her sleeve.

The light inside the carriage was dim. Song Zhang held Shen Weici pressed against his chest with his palm, and used his fingers to touch near her eyes.

Feeling the faint trembling of those lashes, Song Zhang's grip tightened slightly. He said in a low voice: "Do not be afraid. I will have a physician come."

"Nothing will happen to you."

His words had barely fallen when he felt a soft hand catch his fingers. Then a quiet, slightly hoarse voice came: "Young Lord Song, taking me away like this — the Manor will be in an uproar…"

That voice was faint and thin — like a feather brushing across the heart. She always spoke in this careful, measured way, so pleasant to the ear.

And still worrying about whether the Manor was in an uproar.

Song Zhang took her hand in return. It was so small that he could close his entirely around it. He looked down at her face, half-lit and half-shadowed in the dim space of the carriage — at the faint trace of blood at the corner of her lip — and his voice, without his noticing, carried a certain gentleness: "Let it be in an uproar. I was the one who brought you away. Do you think such a small thing is beyond me to sort out?"

Shen Weici was startled. Her hand was held in Song Zhang's and she could not pull free with force. She performed weakness: "I know Young Lord Song means well, but I cannot stay away — Father and Stepmother will worry."

Song Zhang heard Shen Weici mention those cold-hearted parents and frowned, looking down at her: "Do you truly think they will worry? If they truly worried, let them worry. I will send you home when you are better, and no one will dare say a word."

His fingertip brushed the corner of her lips, wiping away the trace of blood there, then cupped her lips with his palm. He said with some irritation: "You coughed up so much blood and you still have so much to say. Do you have any regard for your own health at all?"

A man's large hand — broad and burning — its scorching warmth sent a flutter through Shen Weici's heart.

She could not speak. Song Zhang's other arm held tight around her shoulder. Her cheek was pressed against his chest, and the strong, steady heartbeat entered her ear one beat at a time — matching the unease she felt now.

This level of closeness should never have existed between them. But Song Zhang had done it to save her, and Shen Weici could not say anything against it. She only feared that so many people had seen — that it might give rise to gossip, and make finding a marriage even harder.

At this moment Song Zhang's mind could only be described as wholly distracted. He knew well that Shen Weici had been ill and was not well, and yet he could not stop himself from thinking about how soft this body was, and even wanting to press it further.

Song Zhang was reckless by nature — he acted on his wishes. Only with Shen Weici did he feel himself constrained.

He thought her too tender and gentle — he was actually afraid of startling her.

He breathed in the faint blood-scent mixed with warmth that clung to her, and his heart quickened. Almost against his will, he bent just slightly, and held Shen Weici closer against him.

The carriage soon arrived at his private residence. Song Zhang carried her inside and went straight to his usual quarters. Minhe walked at his side and murmured: "Someone has been sent to the palace to fetch Imperial Physician Lin. He should arrive very soon."

Song Zhang did not reply. His broad back blocked Minhe's view as he carried Shen Weici inside.

Shen Weici did not know where Song Zhang had carried her to. Her mouth was full of blood — just now when Song Zhang had covered her lips she had been forced to swallow a mouthful of it, and her tongue ached terribly. She tugged at Song Zhang's sleeve: "Let me go back to the Marquis Manor first."

Song Zhang was not going to listen to a word of that. He carried her to the bed and set her down, drew the covers up around her, then sat at the bedside and looked at her pale face, at the blood-spatter on the pink collar of her robe, at those fine white fingers stained almost completely red.

The sight of it shook him every time.

He called for the maids to quickly bring warm water, and looked at the fingers still gripping tight to his sleeve, unable to understand why Shen Weici was so insistent on returning.

Her father and stepmother did not treat her very well.

His face was dark but his hands were gentle. He tucked aside the strands of hair that had fallen across her face, leaving that small, pale face completely unobstructed.

She was barely of age — and yet she carried at times a stillness that seemed beyond her years.

Song Zhang looked down and said, threatening her: "If you say the words 'Marquis Manor' one more time, I will throw you out into the street to fend for yourself."

"Do not blame me then for having no pity."

Shen Weici froze. She truly could not fathom Song Zhang's intentions.

She knew that speaking further would only expose more. Her tongue was numb with pain, and without anything pressed against the wound, the blood kept coming. She glanced at Song Zhang, and thought: letting Song Zhang see more blood might make the pretense more convincing.

The blood in her mouth could not be held anymore. Shen Weici let herself pretend to bring up another small amount, tilted her head, and braced a hand on the edge of the bed, letting a small mouthful fall to the floor.

Her fingers trembled slightly as they pressed on the bed. Song Zhang's eyes went red seeing it. He swept forward and pulled Shen Weici tight against him, then called toward the outside in a low, furious voice: "Get Imperial Physician Lin here now. Fast horses."

Minhe, not knowing what had just happened inside, heard this and immediately went.

Song Zhang held Shen Weici in his arms, took the warm cloth a maid held out and used it to wipe the blood from the corner of her mouth. His large hand moved gently up and down her back: "I will make sure nothing happens to you."

Shen Weici tried to push Song Zhang away, knowing she should not be capable of that kind of strength. She rested her cheek against his shoulder and said in a weak voice: "Young Lord Song, please let go of me first. This is not proper."

Song Zhang was so frustrated he nearly felt his own blood rising — he said through clenched teeth: "You are in this state, and you are still talking about what is proper? I am, by blood relations, close enough to count as your cousin. A man cannot hold a little sister?"

"If anyone in this room dares say a word about it, I will cut out their tongue and gouge out their eyes."

At these words, the maids standing in attendance dared not so much as glance sideways, and hurriedly lowered their eyes in unison.

The warm fragrance he had been dreaming of was right beside him now, soft breathing falling at his neck. Song Zhang felt a sweet, languid ache in his heart — and then he looked down and saw the blood Shen Weici had coughed up, and the tenderness wrung at him just as sharply.

He held her greedily, his fingers resting on her slender waist, holding her close and protected.

Whether it was private longing or that thread of genuine tenderness, Song Zhang would not release her — not a single fingertip.

Imperial Physician Lin arrived to find Song Zhang holding Shen Weici tightly in his arms. He immediately lowered his eyes and did not dare look further, bowing respectfully toward Song Zhang: "General Song."

Song Zhang's expression went cold the moment he saw Imperial Physician Lin. He had been the one who came last time as well, and the prescription he wrote had been completely useless — the girl had coughed blood again.

If it were not for the immediate need to save someone, Song Zhang could have kicked Imperial Physician Lin half to death on the spot.

books.title: We Agreed to divorce, Yet You Hold Me Every Night
books.author: Happy Pearl
books.synopsis:
Lu Huaixi had been slipped onto the list of girls entering the imperial palace. Left with no good options, she got engaged to Xie Yuanjing — a man she had absolutely nothing to do with. A one-year agreement. Each getting what they need. After the separation, their marriages would be none of each other's business. Lu Huaixi was perfectly satisfied with this.

But Xie Yuanjing seemed a little *too* good to her — and she found herself sinking in, just a tiny bit.

Xie Yuanjing brought home a young girl and treated her like a child to look after — proper and upright, letting her do as she pleased. But the girl was too good. He sank in. He couldn't stand to see her grow close to others, couldn't stand to see her smile at someone else, couldn't stand to see her distance herself from him. He wanted to trade everything good he had just to make her stay.

Later, when the Lu family patriarch was wondering where his daughter could go after the separation, Young Master Xie pulled her back behind him.

"Separation? There's no such thing."

chapters.title: Not Wanting to Become a Nun
chapters.content:
"Shu Mama has brought new portraits of eligible young men. If you still can't choose one, you might as well shave your head and become a nun."

In the front hall, a young man frowned as he flipped through a stack of portraits, his voice laced with impatience—yet he was scrutinizing each one more carefully than the person they were meant for, finding every candidate more unsatisfactory than the last.

Across from him, a girl who had just come of age leaned her cheek against her hand, her hair pinned up in a lively and playful style, though her eyes were heavy with drowsiness.

"I don't want to become a nun. The mountains are too cold, and you can't eat whatever you like."

"Still thinking about eating? If your marriage isn't settled this month, your only choices are the mountains or the palace. Given your 'brilliance,' the first might let you scrape by—the second would be a slow death sentence."

Having been scolded by her own brother, the girl finally sat up straight.

She lowered her head reluctantly and reached over to pull out one of the scrolls, unrolling it.

"This one won't do—his household has too many concubines."

She set it aside and picked up the next.

The young man glanced over and declined on her behalf without even looking up.

"This one is a decent scholar. His family background is modest, but with some support his future would be secure. The only question is whether he'd want to marry someone like you who despises reading."

"This one—forget it. There were rumors recently that he's been keeping a mistress. Even if you became his primary wife, you'd never hold sway over him."

"This one..."

One by one, the portraits were set aside. In the end, only four thin scrolls remained.

The man depicted in the topmost portrait had a thick, blade-like beard and a powerfully built frame. He looked nothing like a young man who had barely come of age—he appeared as someone who had endured years of rigorous training, fierce and imposing.

The siblings' eyes landed on the portrait simultaneously, and both fell silent for a moment.

"Brother, honestly—even if I were sent to the palace, I might not necessarily be selected, right?"

Silence fell over the front hall. No one answered.

The girl slumped her head in dismay.

In the Great Yu dynasty, participation in the imperial selection was not compulsory. But recently, a piece of news had surfaced—someone had placed her name, Lu Huaixi, on the Flower and Bird Envoy's list.

And along with the listing, her habits, mannerisms, and even her portrait had been submitted.

Such swiftness could only mean someone had been pulling strings behind the scenes.

But her elder brother, Lu Yuanzhao, would not say any of this to her.

He couldn't bring himself to tell her the truth: that just by virtue of being from the Lu family, the one in the palace could never afford to let her go.

Let alone the fact that Lu Huaixi was beautiful—her looks were like flowers in bloom, and with her lazy, sun-warmed charm and endearing sweetness, she was the kind of face that made hearts stir.

"Stop brooding. Look through the rest. As for this... this robust warrior—what do you think?"

Lu Huaixi looked up at her brother in surprise, her lips parting slightly. In the end, she swallowed whatever fear she'd been about to voice.

Smoothly, the portrait was turned to the next one.

But a moment later, Lu Yuanzhao glanced sideways at his sister and frowned.

"He Jian Hang—no. The He family has too much ambition, and this youngest son of theirs has eyes bigger than his stomach. Don't let him fool you."

As he finished speaking, Lu Yuanzhao's expression darkened of its own accord.

He had suddenly realized that the high-born young lords and scions of noble houses all harbored their share of shameful secrets.

Hearing about their dalliances in passing was one thing, but the moment any of it touched his sister, it was the kind of thing that could come to blows at any moment.

And that was to say nothing of the fact that the He family and the Lu family were now political rivals.

From neighbors and close friends to bitter enemies—that transformation had taken no more than a year.

Lu Huaixi blinked and said nothing.

In the quiet, the final two portraits were laid flat on the table together.

Lu Huaixi's gaze dropped to them, and for a moment, it stilled.

One was Zhao Luo—she vaguely recognized him, though they had never had much dealings.

And the other—

Lu Huaixi's gaze settled on the man's cool and naturally handsome face. Though it was only an inked rendering, the likeness still made her pause for a heartbeat when she first saw it.

"He—how did he end up in here?"

The young lord of the Chengen Marquis' household—Xie Yuanjing, the late empress' own nephew.

This man's looks were extraordinary. Both his features and his bearing were of the rarest beauty, yet his temperament was difficult to read.

Occasionally he smiled at people, but always with an undercurrent of cool detachment that never quite disappeared.

Lu Huaixi's words came out a little stuttery, as if she could see through the portrait to that moment when he had laid hands on someone.

"Isn't he that terrifying Xie Yuanjing?"

"I don't know either."

Lu Yuanzhao spoke, then hesitated for a moment.

"If nothing had gone wrong for the Chengen Marquis' household, Father would never have dared consider him. Actually, even with what happened, Father probably wouldn't want to get entangled with him either. The portrait must have been included by mistake."

Xie Yuanjing was ruthless and yet oddly principled, possessing the calculating approach of the old guard while striking with the speed and precision of the young.

Though Lu Yuanzhao had always believed the Chengen Marquis' household would regain its power under Xie Yuanjing's hand, he had absolutely no desire to get on his good side.

This man's mind ran too deep—he couldn't fathom it.

But one thing he was certain of: Xie Yuanjing would never allow himself to be distracted by marriage matters at a time when the marquis' household needed to make its comeback.

"He's out of the question—you don't even need to think about it, he's clearly not suitable—"

"Young Master, Second Young Miss."

Before he could finish, Shu Mama entered from outside, her expression carrying a trace of displeasure, her sharp eyes pressing down some concealed indignation.

"What is it, Shu Mama?"

Both siblings looked over.

Shu Mama met Lu Huaixi's lovely gaze, startled for a moment, then pressed her emotions back down and smiled at her.

"Nothing, nothing. It's just this old servant's poor memory—I forgot to remove a few portraits of young men who are already engaged. I only just remembered."

The explanation came smoothly. Lu Huaixi's lips parted in surprise, but she obediently closed them again.

Lu Yuanzhao's expression shifted.

An obvious excuse, easy enough to see through—someone must have let slip some news from the palace. Several families who had initially shown interest, upon hearing something, no longer dared to get involved, and turned their consideration elsewhere.

Quickly, Shu Mama took away several portraits.

Most of those that remained carried an air of frivolity.

The ones of high status were unwilling to marry into it; the ones of low status didn't dare. The matter ground to a halt somewhere in the middle.

In the whole front hall, only Lu Huaixi showed no sign of distress.

She had returned to her original languorous drowsiness, her fair and delicate hand propped lightly against one cheek, her long curled lashes drooping downward, her fingertips idly toying with the portraits on the table.

It seemed she was resigned to becoming a nun—but she really didn't want that.

The girl sighed, her unfocused gaze drifting at last to Xie Yuanjing's portrait, her wandering fingertip coming to rest on his flat, straight lips.

Thin lips. That must mean he's heartless.

Lost in thought, a small stir arose from outside the courtyard, followed by someone hurrying by, lowering their voice to instruct another.

"An honored guest has arrived at the mansion—hurry and go brew tea."

Lu Yuanzhao rose to his feet, his handsome brow faintly creased. He was about to ask what was happening when he looked up and saw his father returning home, engaged in conversation with someone across the courtyard.

And beside him—a flash of black.

A man of clean, upright bearing stood out unmistakably.

The surprise lasted only a moment before the visitors stepped into the front hall.

Lu's father noticed that both of his children were present—one standing there in a daze, the other impossible to read, whether lazy or drowsy, blinking with a vague, unfocused air. His brow twitched.

"Why aren't you back in your own courtyard? What are you two doing here?"

Lu's father naturally noticed the things laid out on the table.

He hadn't expected that his two children would be sitting there without a care in the world, boldly looking through marriage portraits right under everyone's noses. His head was starting to ache.

"Please don't laugh at us, Lord Xie."

"I arrived without notice."

The man's voice was somewhat low. He ignored Lu's father's hand gesturing behind his back for everyone to leave, and with an easygoing smile, he nodded amiably at the motionless Lu Yuanzhao.

But the smile was faint, a fleeting thing, like a perfunctory courtesy—languid and offhand.

Then his gaze swept past Lu Yuanzhao to what lay behind him.

After one glance at Lu Huaixi, the man's eyes dropped slightly at their outer corners, his gaze coming to rest on her fingertip—on his own portrait.

chapters.title: Xie Yuanjing Is Not Suitable
chapters.content:
Lu Huaixi didn't register it at first. She stared at the flesh-and-blood person before her, momentarily dumbstruck.

The ink had captured Xie Yuanjing's likeness with perhaps seventy percent accuracy. The brushstrokes at the outer corners of his eyes had left a faint touch of red, the subtle upward tilt lending a warmth to what was otherwise an inky, cold, and sharp gaze.

But even with such a beautiful portrait, it still fell short of the man himself by half.

Lu Yuanzhao was the first to come to his senses. He gave a light cough, then turned to give Lu Huaixi a look over his shoulder, wordlessly signaling her to clear the table.

Only then did Lu Huaixi remember—before this man had walked in, she had been studying him with the express purpose of sizing him up as a potential husband.

And it hadn't only been him. She'd looked at many others.

A sudden flush of heat crept up her face. Realizing how mortifying this was, Lu Huaixi shot to her feet, leaned forward to cover the table, and—in a completely futile attempt at concealment—shoved the portraits to the side.

She had just barely managed to block the face on Xie Yuanjing's portrait when the man smiled again.

"Second Young Miss Lu."

He had called to her, yet said nothing more—as if simply offering a greeting.

But he had just seen his own portrait laid out on the table. So when that address fell on Lu Huaixi's ears, it carried an inexplicable weight of deeper meaning.

On the small path leading toward the inner gate, Lu Huaixi still hadn't fully recovered from the earlier awkwardness.

She generally wasn't prone to temper, and her manner of speaking was soft and unhurried. Even now, if she tried to put on a fierce front, the fierceness in it wouldn't hold a candle to the new puppy someone had just brought into the courtyard.

Beside a resting pavilion stood a sweet osmanthus tree, and the two siblings stopped beneath it.

Lu Huaixi, ears still red, shoved the hastily gathered portraits into her maid's arms all at once, then glared at her brother.

"I told you I wanted to look at these in my own courtyard, but you insisted it was too hot to move!"

Lu Yuanzhao touched his nose.

For once, the usually sharp-tongued young man could find no words to argue back. He could only sort through what he wanted to say and pick a few lines.

"Don't worry. Xie Yuanjing would never bring this up on his own. He's a crafty old fox in disguise—even if a portrait of himself ends up in someone else's hands for inspection, he'd only ever act as though nothing happened. He wouldn't embarrass either family."

Lu Huaixi's indignation, which had been simmering a moment ago, deflated all at once along with her brow.

"Why was his portrait in there anyway?"

"No idea. Either way, it certainly wasn't his own idea."

With that confirmed and out of the question, Lu Huaixi relaxed somewhat—though she still let out a dejected sigh.

"But then what am I supposed to do? Out of all those portraits, his was the only good-looking one."

"...What do you mean? Did you take a liking to—no, don't even think about it."

Lu Yuanzhao mercilessly pierced through her little daydream. "Xie Yuanjing could never give his heart to marriage matters. Even back when he was riding high, he never showed any intention of settling down. Now—even less so."

"Oh."

Lu Huaixi pursed her lips.

This was really so annoying.

She didn't want to become a nun, and she didn't want to wait for death. Why did her brother have to say it with such finality?

"Actually, my luck is usually pretty decent. Even the abbot at Wénan Temple once said my fate has an unusual quality—I always end up with a little more good fortune than ordinary people. So what if—"

"What if you catch the eye of a young, talented gentleman of good character and passable looks? That's quite possible. But if that person is Xie Yuanjing, then it's absolutely out of the question."

Lu Yuanzhao cut her off.

"Give it up. Your fate and Xie Yuanjing's have no business crossing. And do you really think there's no one in the Chengen Marquis' household already pining for him? If even the moon right next to his window is out of reach, what makes you think someone on the outside has a shot?"

Lu Huaixi's curiosity had been piqued and she was about to ask who in the marquis' household had her eye on him, when the branches overhead suddenly rustled.

Birds chirped—several at once, gathering together.

The two siblings had just started to look up when several white specks came dropping from between the leaves.

They were aimed right at the gap between the siblings' overlapping sleeves, yet in the end, they landed with perfect precision on the cuff of Lu Yuanzhao's sleeve.

Missing Lu Huaixi by just an inch.

Watching her brother's expression crumple, Lu Huaixi's earlier unhappiness vanished in an instant.

"Quite the 'extra little good fortune' you've got there."

Lu Yuanzhao gritted his teeth, forcing himself to swallow his revulsion. "I'm going to change. You—get back to your own courtyard and stay there!"

Lu Huaixi couldn't hold back her laughter. She waved him off with eyes curved into crescent moons, watching her brother storm away.

In the front hall, a cup of hot tea was carefully set down before Xie Yuanjing.

Spring was drawing to a close. The days still carried some cool freshness after rain, but most of the time they came with heat.

Xie Yuanjing glanced down at the steam curling above the tea surface without reaching for it.

Lu Yandao had spent twenty-seven years in officialdom and had sharp eyes. Even so, he still found the young lord of the marquis' household somewhat difficult to read.

But he understood clearly that no matter how fallen the Chengen Marquis' household had become, the young man before him was not someone to be trifled with carelessly.

"Today's incident may be a misunderstanding. I hope Lord Xie will not take it to heart."

Lu Yandao's words were deliberately vague, but both men understood: he was referring to the matter of the portrait.

Xie Yuanjing's expression was blank, his demeanor unhurried.

Just as Lu Yandao began to think the man had no intention of discussing such things, Xie Yuanjing suddenly smiled.

"The grand selection is in the eighth month."

His tone was calm and offhand, as if commenting on the weather. "If a marriage engagement is settled too late, it may appear as deliberate evasion—a slight against His Majesty's wishes."

At that, even Lu Yandao—practiced as he was at keeping his emotions in check—couldn't help a trace of worry from surfacing.

But in order to avoid the palace by marrying off his daughter, a matter that could at any moment be seized upon as a handle against him, he absolutely could not let anything slip to another person.

"Lord Xie misunderstands. Our dynasty has never compelled the daughters of officials into the selection. My daughter's portrait viewing is simply a matter of a father wishing to plan ahead for her future. You must be laughing at me."

"Is that so."

Xie Yuanjing nodded, unhurried. "Then it seems I was misinformed."

Every shift in Lu Yandao's expression had fallen under Xie Yuanjing's gaze. His own face remained unreadable, yet inwardly he added a few more strokes to his impression of Lu Huaixi.

Deeply valued. Acceptable.

"Since it is a misunderstanding, let us not speak of it further."

Xie Yuanjing said no more on the matter, but Lu Yandao steered the conversation back.

"Even so—Lord Xie mentioned being misinformed. What did you mean by that?"

"Nothing of great consequence. Only that I had heard someone placed Second Young Miss Lu on the Flower and Bird Envoy's list, and I assumed Lord Lu was troubled by the matter."

"That piece of news—"

Lu Yandao was indeed troubled. But what truly alarmed him was that the information had somehow reached the ears of the man before him.

He pressed down his thoughts, not wishing to reveal too much.

"What a preposterous thing."

Lu Yandao frowned. "Then Lord Xie came today to offer a word of caution?"

"No. I came to put myself forward."

"What?"

"To speak of a marriage arrangement. I am, I believe, a suitable match."

When there was no conflict between them, Xie Yuanjing's manner toward others was naturally languid and indifferent.

Even when speaking of something as weighty as a marriage proposal, the words came from his mouth as casually as a passing remark about the day's weather.

"Of course—on the condition that Second Young Miss Lu is willing."

chapters.title: Never Mind if She Has Someone She Likes
chapters.content:
"Is that so."

Xie Yuanjing smiled slightly, the outer corners of his eyes lifting just a fraction. The cold air that usually surrounded him softened, replaced by something more measured and calm.

"But I appear to be the only one who can help Second Young Miss."

He said it unhurriedly. "I have my own aims in this. If Lord Lu agrees, I can prevent the Second Young Miss from entering the palace—and I can guarantee that after the wedding, while I attend to her needs, I will not harbor any romantic intentions toward her."

"One year after the wedding, I will sign the dissolution of marriage and give her her freedom. After that, should she wish to remarry, I will always be her support—without exception."

"I have no wish to speak in circles with Lord Lu. To put it plainly: I just saw Second Young Miss holding my portrait, and I believe this match is, in fact, quite suitable."

Lu Yandao was so infuriated his expression crumpled.

His gaze sharpened in an instant, carrying the weight and displeasure of a man accustomed to authority.
